items.title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
paragraphs: European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.
Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.

In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.
Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."

But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".
Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".

Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.

Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.

Zelensky and the three European leaders - Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron - were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."

The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".
"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.

He also said any attempts to divide Europe into sphere of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.
"A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.
Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.
The French leader also called urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.

There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.

But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.

It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials haven't budged from Russia's demands for Ukraine sovereign territory.

As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.
And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.
He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.
Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready for making compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.

"I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said, despite the fact that Russia has in recent months intensified its attacks Ukraine's critical infrastructure as cold winter approaches.

Kyiv and its European allies say that - in the absence of any major success on the vast front line - the Kremlin leader is seeking to break Ukrainian resistance by leaving millions of civilians without electricity and water supply.

items.title: Meta now sells 3D movies on Quest VR headsets
paragraphs: Use your Quest 3 to catch films like Avatar and Jurassic World Rebirth in 3D.
Use your Quest 3 to catch films like Avatar and Jurassic World Rebirth in 3D.
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Meta now offers more than 150 3D movies that you can buy or rent to watch in VR on its Quest 3 and 3S headsets, the company announced today. The movies are available in Meta’s TV app and include titles like Avatar, Spider-Man: Far From Home, Jurassic World Rebirth, Wicked: For Good, and a Billie Eilish concert film co-directed by Eilish and James Cameron.

The company suggests watching movies in a Theater view that’s rolling out with a new Meta Quest update. Theater view “provides a big screen and dims your surroundings to create a cozy, personal cinema experience,” Meta says.

Meta promises that the library will “keep growing, with thousands of titles and international availability coming” when it launches its VR Glasses next spring. If you’re a Disney Plus subscriber, you can also watch 3D movies on Meta Quest hardware in the Disney Plus app thanks to an update rolled out earlier this month.

items.title: UK-EU reset talks will go ‘down to the wire’ as crunch summit approaches
paragraphs: British and European negotiators were striving to put the finishing touches to a deal on Thursday night as they provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme.
The EU-UK reset talks were going “down to the wire”, sources said, as both sides battled over the nature of the UK’s role in shaping future European food and farming rules.

On the eve of a summit in Brussels, the EU was “going into a landing zone” on the question of a British voice in shaping the rules under a food and drink agreement the government hopes to unveil on Friday, an EU source said. The EU compromise emerged in late-night talks on Thursday, after a dispute among member states over how far Britain could be involved in shaping policies related to the food and drink deal.

Earlier on Thursday the UK made concessions to increase the quota of EU citizens who could take part in a new youth mobility scheme, agreeing a cap of 100,000, instead of 50,000-80,0000 as previously sought.
It was also agreed to raise the age cap from 30 to 31.

The number of young British people allowed to go to the EU under the scheme will be matched but could be higher, with some countries, including Germany, being prepared to take unlimited numbers each year.

With less than 24 hours to go before Andy Burnham was due in Brussels for the summit with EU leaders, the two sides still needed to resolve some central sticking points, including how much of a say Britain will have in new EU food rules.

Speaking in general terms about the disagreements, also including tuition fees for EU students in the UK, another EU diplomat said: “It will go down to the wire. Our feeling is that the Brits have to move if they want a deal.”

A spokesperson for the British prime minister also described the talks as close, saying if an agreement was reached, the government would bring forward legislation, the cutting costs bill, to parliament next week.
Another EU diplomat said ambassadors representing the EU member states would meet at 5pm and “will go until agreement is reached tonight”.
Sources said the UK was still resisting pressure from the EU on tuition fees for EU students coming to Britain under the youth mobility scheme.
“We are fighting hard on this and think we will get there,” said an EU insider. “But for us, one of the hardest discussions centres on this question of the UK being a rule taker or rule maker.”

At the long-awaited summit, the EU and UK hope to sign three agreements, including a highly prized food and drink deal that was a Labour manifesto commitment and is expected to add 0.4% to British GDP.
The deal, expected to come into force on 1 March 2028, requires the UK to align with EU rules on sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) standards, making Britain a rule taker.

Asked about Britain’s status as a rule taker, No 10 said the Labour manifesto had aimed to build closer ties with the EU, adding: “We were obviously elected on a manifesto that promised to reset the relationship and seek to deepen ties with our European friends.”
According to EU sources, the UK has been pushing to have a formal role in EU committees involved in implementing existing and setting new SPS rules.
An EU diplomat said: “They want to be able to shape decisions, not only implementation, but future decisions. That has always been a red line.”
Under the SPS proposal, the UK will agree to dynamically align with EU laws and will have a “voice” but “not be in the room” when laws are drafted.
A second diplomat from a country sympathetic to the British position said the European Commission had proposed an “extremely restrictive consultation mechanism” for the UK.
In contrast, the EU diplomat thought it was reasonable for a British representative to take part in the implementation of SPS legislation affecting the UK.
“Of course the UK cannot vote in the council as a non-member state, but we feel that we need to be pragmatic about coordination and implementation,” they said.

The issue proved difficult to resolve because it divided member states. France was perceived by other member states to be the main barrier to greater UK involvement in EU working groups on food and drink laws. “They are super principled on that point,” said a second EU diplomat.
The French government does not agree that it has been the main block, arguing that only a few member states wanted to accommodate the UK.
The issue raises the tensions at the heart of the UK’s status as a rule taker, and would be many times magnified were Britain to choose to enter the single market as a non-EU member state.
The precise details of how the UK would be consulted on future food and farming rules remain unclear.
Separately, the EU and UK remain deadlocked over whether EU students in Britain should pay the British or international tuition fee rate.
The draft proposal gives the UK two options: to agree to significantly reduced undergraduate fees or equal treatment with nationals.

Burnham’s spokesperson suggested there was an UK-EU consensus that there would be no further incremental reset summits beyond the one on Friday until a full negotiation commenced on a longer-term, more stable relationship, such as rejoining the single market.
“After the summit, we will begin those discussions with our European partners about the realistic options for our longer-term relationship,” he said.

The UK has prioritised seeking commitments on Britain’s position relating to the EU’s Made in Europe legislation. The trade defence policy will include tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles but will also affect British manufacturing. The sides are believed to be close to an agreement to language at the summit that would point towards UK inclusion, but nothing can be formalised until the EU passes its own legislation.

Burnham’s spokesperson said: “[The UK is] engaging constructively with the EU on that, and we’ve been clear about the challenges it could represent for British industries. We have deeply integrated supply chains with Europe, and we want to keep working together to boost growth and open up trade.
“The UK and Europe have shared economic challenges, and we believe shared challenges are best met with a collective approach that is in Britain’s best interests, and in Europe’s too.”

items.title: Meta’s Muse Charm might cost $300
paragraphs: is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Meta is planning to price the Muse Charm, a little gadget with a screen that lets you chat with your Muse AI agent, at $300, according to The Information. CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed the gadget earlier this year and said the company expected to ship the Charm “in time for the holidays in December,” but he didn’t provide a price at the time.

When he announced the Muse Charm, Zuckerberg said that the company had “packed the whole Muse experience,” including real-time voice and avatar technology, into the gadget. It has a fingerprint sensor, and you can tap it to be able to talk to a Muse AI agent without unlocking a phone or opening an app. The Information reports that the Muse Charm will come with a free 12-month 5G data plan from Verizon.

Spokesperson Tyler Yee wrote to The Information that “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” When reached for comment by The Verge, Yee provided the same statement.
The company is also working on a smartwatch, The Information says, but a launch for that has been pushed to 2027 as Meta tries to get Muse Charm out the door.
Meta also open sourced code to let users make their own Muse gadgets, which my colleague Sean Hollister used to make his own DIY Muse Charm.
Update, November 19th: Noted statement given by Meta spokesperson Tyler Yee.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto fans skip work and pull all-nighters to play new instalment
paragraphs: Grand Theft Auto fans around the world pulled all-nighters, skipped work and school, and attended overnight launch parties to vicariously embark on police chases and coordinate robberies as the latest instalment of the eagerly anticipated series arrived.
GTA VI, a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired crime adventure game set in the fictional US state of Leonida, was launched at midnight on Wednesday after a 13-year wait.

The hype around the release led to schools encouraging pupils not to miss lessons in anticipation of “GTA flu”, a term coined for the swathe of absences when GTA V was released in 2013, which is expected to recur over the coming weeks. The human resources platform Remote said there had been a 32% increase in leave requests worldwide on Thursday.
Birchgrove comprehensive school in Swansea, south Wales, had warned parents and carers that despite the “considerable excitement”, studies should remain a priority.

The Sandon secondary school in Essex entered students into a raffle for £10 Amazon vouchers, a lunchtime queue-jump pass and free Christmas dinners as incentives to stop them bunking off to play as the game’s dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia.

Narendra Modi, India’s prime minister, took a different approach in a country with an estimated 550 million gamers. Modi posted 10 images on X modelled ‌on the game’s artwork that compared India today with the time of GTA V’s release.
The Indian politician, who has stepped up efforts to appeal to younger voters since youth-led protests over jobs and education, wrote: “India is playing a whole new game!”

Downing Street said Andy Burnham would not be playing the new instalment. Asked whether the UK prime minister would be exploring Vice City, the Grand Theft Auto maker Rockstar’s fictional take on Miami, a spokesperson said: “His diary is very full.”
The launch of GTA VI generated more than 2.6m posts on social media in 24 hours, according to social media monitor Visibrain.
Approximately 1,850 messages about the game were published per minute – 7% more than the number of posts at the start of the 2026 men’s Fifa World Cup.

Among the game’s fans is Sean Little, a self-employed painter and decorator. He persuaded his wife and daughter to sign a “non-interference contract”, giving him a week off dad duties to play in peace in Dumfries and Galloway, Scotland.
Myles_Away, a UK-based streamer on the Twitch platform, told the BBC he planned to play for “13 or 14 hours” on Thursday.

He said: “I played all last night, and then I slept, woke up, and [came] right into this interview,” adding: “Obviously not everybody is able to drop the money required. [Consoles] are very expensive at the moment, so they are able to experience the story through streamers.”

Jacob Joel, a 30-year-old IT professional in Bengaluru, southern India, took the day off to play in a gaming cafe. “We waited around 13 long years to get into GTA VI,” he said. “That is a nostalgic feeling.”
In Bangkok, British tourists Kyle McKee and Emily Todd reserved a PS5 console, TV and a sofa at a gaming centre. McKee, 27, told the AFP news agency: “It’s the fear of missing out, honestly.”

The launch also surpassed broadband records in the UK. Virgin Media O2 said its evening traffic between 8pm and 10pm on Wednesday was 9.4% higher than the previous record, set last week by “pre-loading” for GTA VI.
BT and EE networks also recorded their highest-ever home broadband traffic peak in the lead-up to the release.

Data from the two brands found that Fort Augustus, in Loch Ness, Scotland, recorded the biggest percentage uplift in gaming download traffic anywhere in the UK since the start of the pre-downloads last week.
Sony’s shares were up 2.92% on the Tokyo stock exchange after the global launch, with the analytics firm Omdia estimating that GTA VI could generate $3.2bn (£2.4bn) in sales by the end of the year.

items.title: Google is putting AI chats right on the homepage
paragraphs: is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Google is updating its homepage to include AI searches. In a post on X, Google’s vice president of product, Robby Stein, shows how you can now open a collapsible sidebar to view and continue your AI chats.

Based on the GIF shared by Stein, it looks like you can open the sidebar by clicking the gray bar that appears on the left side of your screen. From there, Google will show a list of the searches you’ve made using AI Mode, along with the ability to start a new thread, search your threads, or connect a Gemini Notebook.

It’s yet another big change for Google’s homepage, which has long presented you with a single bar to kick off your web search. The company brought its AI Mode button to its search bar last year, which opens up a chatbot-like search experience within Google. In May, Google updated its search box to accommodate longer queries and added AI-powered autocomplete.

Stein says Google is rolling out the option because “people are coming to Search with more questions that aren’t just one and done,” adding that “in testing, this sidebar made a big difference for making progress & continuing to explore the web.” The new homepage is rolling out globally on desktop.

items.title: Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
paragraphs: The people who framed the Convention in the years after World War Two, led by Raphael Lemkin, a Jewish survivor of the Holocaust, deliberately set a high bar of proof.
That is why it has taken so long for the ICJ to deliver a ruling that genocide has been committed.
In an ideal world for lawyers and investigators, they would assemble evidence from government documents and military orders. In practice, that is hard if not impossible to get.

Governments harbouring genocidal intent do not publicise their objectives. Instead, the Court has inferred evidence of genocidal intent from the actions taken by Myanmar's security forces and local militias against the Rohingya people.

According to Janina Dill, Chair in Global Security at the Blavatnik School of Government of the University of Oxford, "Genocidal intent can be inferred from a pattern of conduct… It does not mean the commission of atrocities had to follow only one goal, genocide. If that were the case, demonstrating that atrocities also followed other goals (like counterinsurgency, punishment or displacement) would negate genocidal intent.
"The court was incredibly clear that these are plausible goals, but it ruled that the totality of the evidence cannot be explained without genocide being one objective."
In other words, even if a state has been attacked, and if it orders its forces on to the offensive claiming self-defence, the sum of its actions could add up to genocide.

The justices made clear that each case needed to be treated on its merits. But because the court's decisions affect the way the law is interpreted, the Myanmar case does have an impact on the other genocide cases that are being heard by the ICJ. The most prominent is the one brought by South Africa against Israel over the killing and destruction it has inflicted on Palestinians in Gaza.

The British barrister, Philippe Sands KC, part of the Gambia's legal team, was in the chamber of the ICJ in The Hague to hear the verdict. Sands told the BBC's World at One programme that when they were arguing the case against Myanmar at the ICJ in January this year, Gaza was "the elephant in the room. Everybody knew that the court's approach in this case would have implications in the next one".
The approach taken by the ICJ justices in the judgement on Myanmar, he told the BBC, clarifies the standard of evidence they require to prove genocide.
"If the Gambia had lost, South Africa's case would, in effect, be over.

"But the Gambia now having succeeded, the door remains open for South Africa. That doesn't mean that South Africa will win. It doesn't mean that the International Court of Justice will find there was a genocide in Gaza. It means that the evidentiary standard has been defined very clearly, and it will be now for the parties in that next case and in other cases to meet those standards."

The undoubted joy and relief felt by Rohingyas in the camps in Bangladesh will not deliver them an immediate improvement in the miserable and dangerous living conditions they have been forced to endure for almost a decade.
The court has no mechanism to enforce its rulings, but it has told Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingyas.
That will not be easy. Hundreds of villages have been razed to the ground, and the Myanmar government is unlikely quietly to accept the verdict of the court.

The UK, as the so-called "pen holder" on the UN Security Council with responsibility for diplomacy around the Myanmar issue, put out a statement saying it was "determined to act and ensure accountability for these appalling crimes… we must ensure the Court's ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity".
It has called for an urgent session of the Security Council, is expelling Myanmar's defence attaché in London and has promised other measures in the coming days.
Not much might be possible at the UN. A tough resolution against Myanmar could be vetoed by either China or Russia, or both.

Other rumblings have come from the Trump Administration about the case. Without waiting for the ICJ's verdict, former US President Joe Biden's administration declared in 2022 that the Myanmar military committed genocide against the Rohingya people.
But Mike Waltz, the current US ambassador to the UN, warned the court last month not to "lower the legal threshold for proving genocide".
Waltz said he was speaking out to protect "American and allied soldiers" but his post has been widely interpreted as support for Israel's defence at the ICJ.

He condemned what he called the "leftist, global, antisemitic agenda" of the international community, singling out Navi Pillay, this year's recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize, who was one of the judges in the Myanmar case.
She led a UN independent international commission that reported a year ago that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.

items.title: Oil firm fined for breaking environmental rules hundreds of times
paragraphs: In February 2019, between 15 and 20 tonnes of a chemical leaked into the ship canal after a vent was left open and a written procedure was not followed.
A month later, a contractor's vehicle ruptured an effluent pipe. During repairs, about 15 tonnes of partially treated sewage entered Thornton Brook, which leads to the protected Mersey Estuary.
Environment Agency officers reported a sheen of oil on local waterways, while vegetation downstream of the refinery's discharge point was blackened by oil in January 2020.

The company was fined £80,000 for each of the 10 offences, with no additional penalty for the two 2019 incidents. Three breaches from 2022 and 2023 were taken into consideration without further punishment.
Nigel Glasgow, the Environment Agency's area environment manager, said the case showed "a repeated failure to comply" with permit conditions.
An EET Fuels spokesperson said: "We take our environmental responsibilities extremely seriously and regret these historic incidents."

The company said its investment included rerouting wastewater to United Utilities' Ellesmere Port treatment works, resulting in "a significant improvement in environmental performance", including fewer discharges and reduced freshwater use.

items.title: Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days
paragraphs: Federal judges have issued temporary restraining orders to block construction of Trump's arch and keep East Potomac Park open. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP hide caption
A federal judge has extended her block on construction of President Trump's D.C. arch for two weeks, another short-term victory for those who don't want to see the 250-foot structure break ground.

D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended her temporary restraining order on Wednesday, the day before it was set to expire. She originally stepped in to block construction on the night of Nov. 5, after the National Capital Planning Commission and National Park Service gave the arch final approval and the Trump administration said construction could begin imminently.

Chutkan's new five-page order prevents the administration from "initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility-installation, or roadway-closure activity, or any other construction-related activity" at Memorial Circle through Dec. 3.

"The judge's order recognizes that the conditions that called for emergency relief two weeks ago remain unchanged," Nick Sansone, the Public Citizen attorney representing the original plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said in a statement.
The extension gives Chutkan more time to consider plaintiffs' request for a longer-term preliminary injunction, which would prohibit construction as the lawsuit against the arch plays out.
That lawsuit started earlier this year with a challenge from a group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian, but has expanded in recent weeks.

In late October, the governments of D.C. and Virginia filed another lawsuit, which was combined with the original. And nine members of the Kennedy family joined the fight last week, saying the arch will block historic sightlines and cast shadows over the graves of John F. Kennedy and others at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.

"This is one man who wants to build this arch. He's violated every rule. If this is a great idea, then bring it before Congress, follow the rules and get it approved," Max Kennedy, a son of Robert F. Kennedy, told NPR's All Things Considered.
Opposition to the arch — from area residents, veterans, local officials, Democratic lawmakers and more — has grown in recent months as the structure hurtled through the federal approval process.

Critics take issue with the arch's scale and location, saying it would interrupt the solemn and historic vista between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. Plaintiffs argue the structure violates several laws — including the Commemorative Works Act and D.C.'s Height of Buildings Act — and is fundamentally illegal without approval from Congress.
A jogger passes a mobile security camera truck at Memorial Circle, where Trump wants to build his arch. Tom Brenner/AP hide caption
The Trump administration has not sought that approval, arguing the arch is covered by Congress' authorization in 1925 of a pair of 166-foot columns at the same location, which were never built.

In court filings and a recently unveiled website, the administration characterizes building the arch as a matter of urgency — both to complete that century-old vision and to facilitate national security. Trump said in September that the arch would double as a military complex, but the plans that got final approval this month don't include any details to that effect.

In a declaration this week, Ricky Buria, chief of staff to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, told the court that the agency is "currently in the planning process to determine how to integrate national defense uses … into the Arch without changing the existing plans for the Arch."

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR on Thursday that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."

The arch is one of several construction projects that Trump has pursued with vigor in his second term. Some of them, like the White House ballroom and Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, are well underway. Others, like the Kennedy Center closure and East Potomac golf course redevelopment, are held up by various legal challenges.

Democrats have said they will use their forthcoming majority in Congress to push back on Trump's construction agenda, including by blocking federal funding. But experts say the fate of many of these projects will ultimately be up to the court.

Trump's dream of redeveloping a municipal D.C. golf course into a championship-level venue is also temporarily on hold, despite his repeated social media pronouncements that the park would close and work would begin on Nov. 15.
Another D.C. district judge, Ana Reyes, intervened Saturday to order the administration to keep East Potomac Park open for two weeks, on the eve of its indefinite closure.

But the golf course itself is currently unstaffed, since its operator lease expired on Sunday. That hasn't stopped locals from showing up and teeing off, finding creative ways to mark the holes after the flagsticks were removed from the course.
Reyes has ordered both parties to weigh in on whether she has the authority to order the government to keep the golf course open.
On Wednesday, the Trump administration officially appealed Reyes' restraining order as it had promised. That order is currently set to expire on Nov. 28, the Saturday after Thanksgiving.

Noting that timing, the plaintiffs in the case — local golfers and historic preservationists — have asked Reyes to extend her order by another two weeks, until Dec. 12, while she considers the underlying legal issues and decides whether to issue a longer preliminary injunction.

The government, on the other hand, said "the court already has everything it needs to promptly consider a motion for preliminary injunction" and has proposed a schedule that would enable her to issue a final ruling by Nov. 28.
National Park Service employees walk past a golfer at East Potomac Park on Monday, after a judge ordered the administration to keep the park open. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP hide caption

In the meantime, the administration took another step forward in the federal review process on Thursday. The Interior Department presented its plan for the golf course to the Commission of Fine Arts, one of two federal agencies which would need to approve the project.
Commission Secretary Thomas Luebke said some 700 members of the public submitted comments ahead of the meeting, all but three in opposition to the golf course proposal.

The biggest concerns had to do with making the park less accessible to golfers of all levels, as well as cyclists, runners and picnickers who use the park's perimeter loop, which would be eliminated. There were other concerns about the impact of major road races — like the Marine Corps Marathon — that use that road, the loss of historic cherry trees and the cost of the project (the Interior Department said deferred maintenance alone would cost $43 million but did not specify how much the renovations would cost).

Over a dozen other people spoke out in the room, sharing their personal experiences with the park, raising questions about gaps in the presentation and urging the commission to defer or outright reject any plan that does not leave the perimeter loop intact.

Commissioners — all of whom were appointed by Trump — did not have the quorum needed to vote on preliminary approval. Several offered praise for the idea of beautifying the space and overhauling the golf course, but questioned whether this plan is the best way to do it.

Vice Chair Rodney Mims Cook, Jr., a Trump ally, said there seems to be enough space in the park to accommodate the aspects that people care about, like preserving the historic mini-golf course. His comments prompted applause from many of the people who had crowded into the meeting room.

Cook asked the Interior Department to bring alternative designs to its next meeting, in late January. The administration has said it plans to present the same proposal to the National Capital Planning Commission at its meeting in early December.

Administration officials said in Thursday's meeting, as they have in previous court hearings, that their plan is not yet finalized. Judge Reyes, however, is not convinced and accused the administration of already taking steps to carry it out, like cutting down hundreds of trees.

Plaintiffs in the case argue the administration has violated federal environmental law by splitting the project into smaller parts, like the tree removal, to bypass necessary reviews. And they say the administration skipped required legal steps in its rush to close off most of the park, which Reyes seemed to agree with in her order.
"In its haste to meet an arbitrary deadline, the Government has likely violated at least the National Environmental Policy Act and the Administrative Procedure Act," she wrote.

Trump has repeatedly described the East Potomac golf course as decrepit and dangerous, and challenged Reyes' authority over the project. Over the weekend, he reiterated that Reyes was appointed by President Biden and slammed her decision as "highly destructive and political."

"Why would a judge want to delay taking a terrible and very unsafe golf course, one that is mocked all over D.C.(and far beyond!), instead of quickly turning it into a great and admired one?" Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Time is of the essence, or golf seasons, jobs, prestige, and much money, will be lost!"

Government lawyers asked Reyes to recuse herself from the case in mid-October, accusing her of bias and hostility. She denied that request on legal grounds. Tensions between Reyes and the administration have dominated this case so far, with the judge ordering a misconduct inquiry into whether government officials and lawyers misled the court about its plans for the park.
Government lawyers have pushed back, telling the court Thursday that such an inquiry is "not necessary."

items.title: Howard-era minister Sharman Stone dies via voluntary assisted dying, aged 75
paragraphs: Former Liberal MP Sharman Stone has died via voluntary assisted dying after spending much of her political career advocating that people should have autonomy over their bodies.
Stone died aged 75 on Wednesday surrounded by family after a long fight against glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer. She was minister for workforce participation from 2006-07.
During her political career, Stone championed contentious medical research and supported access to abortion, and readily – and publicly – disagreed with former leader Tony Abbott on both topics.
Stone was one of the first female superintendents in the Victorian Office of Corrections, the first female director of the Victorian Farmers Federation, and the recipient of an economics PhD.
She was elected to federal parliament in 1996, serving through the Howard years in what was then the seat of Murray in northern Victoria.
Stone was remembered as a strong voice for her local community, right up to her late days.
“She was born and bred in the heart of the electorate she served – a sixth-generation northern Victorian from a farming family,” the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said after her death.
“She understood the rugged and regenerative nature of the land and what makes regional Australia tick.”
Stone spent two decades in parliament and was characterised by her independence.
She held several roles during the Howard government, including as parliamentary secretary to the environment and finance ministers.
She also held the shadow environment portfolio after the Liberals’ defeat to Kevin Rudd.
Stone retired from politics in 2016, and served as the Australian ambassador for women and girls until 2020.
Her celebration of life is expected to be held after the 28 November Victorian election.

items.title: FCC greenlights rule allowing prisons to jam cellphone signals
paragraphs: is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

The Federal Communications Commission voted unanimously to allow state and local prisons to jam cellphones. In an announcement on Thursday, the FCC argues the rule will help combat an “influx of contraband cellphones” used to carry out crimes from prison.

Jammers are generally banned under Section 333 of the Communications Act of 1934, though they’re used at some federal facilities. FCC Chair Brendan Carr claims that giving correctional facilities access to this technology will help prevent prisoners from using phones for illegal activity. “These devices [phones] are being used by inmates to order hits, run drug operations, traffic women and children, and unleash mayhem on our communities from behind bars,” Carr says.

In the months leading up to the vote, trade groups and human rights advocates have raised concerns about the risks of blocking cellphone signals in prisons. The US Chamber of Commerce and the CTIA, a wireless association representing the nation’s biggest carriers, have both warned in letters to the FCC that jamming technology could disrupt lawful communications outside prisons, including 911 calls. Meanwhile, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) has long argued that cellphones can keep prisoners safe by allowing them to document safety and human rights issues that the outside world may not see.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, the sole Democrat on the Commission, voted for the measure despite the risk of “potential unintended consequences,” according to the Associated Press. “I want to make sure that we don’t harm public safety in the name of helping public safety,” Gomez added.

The FCC says prisons that choose to jam cellphone signals will need to obtain a license, adhere to “technical standards and testing requirements,” and ensure that the jamming technology doesn’t interfere with communications outside the facility. Prisons must also notify nearby communities of testing and when the technology is being deployed.

items.title: Sony’s WH-1000XM5 are cheaper than ever for Black Friday
paragraphs: is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Back in my day, the only “Doorbuster” sales were at physical retail stores. But now, you can get ultra-low prices before Black Friday whether you want to shop in-store or online. One that stands out is the previous-generation Sony WH-1000XM5 noise-canceling headphones, which are marked down to their lowest price ever, just $169.99 at Best Buy. While their MSRP is $399.99, they’ve been spotted as low as $198 in the last few months.

The WH-1000XM5 launched in 2022, and despite having been succeeded by the WH-1000XM6, they’re still an excellent set of headphones. Their active noise cancellation effect is one of the best out there — competitive with the latest models from Bose and Apple — and the sound profile is tighter and more balanced than the older Sony headphones. There are some minor downsides, like a bulky case and all-plastic design, but those seem easier to overlook at this lower price point.

The newer Sony WH-1000XM6 improve the sound and noise cancellation, with quality of life upgrades not present in the XM5, like a folding design and more comfortable headband. However, they’re significantly more expensive, currently discounted to $348 during Black Friday (Amazon, Best Buy), down from their MSRP of $450.

To make shopping a little more confusing, the newer WH-1000XM4C sit between the XM5 and XM6 in terms of price, and are a slightly updated version of the older XM4 model with its foldable design. Our reviewer John Higgins thinks the XM4C’s noise cancellation lags behind, so I’d opt for the XM5 over them, especially at the sale price.

items.title: You can now buy a Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist
paragraphs: is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.
Valve announced some updates about Steam Machine availability today, including good news if you want to buy one right now and potential bad news about future supply due to RAMaggedon.

The good news: You can now purchase a 512GB Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist. Initially, interested buyers had to get on Valve’s waitlist if they wanted to purchase one, but the console-like PC is now available in an “add-to-cart” status, according to the company. As I write this, the 512GB versions with and without a bundled controller are showing estimated delivery dates of three to five business days on Valve’s website. If Valve sells through its current inventory, the company says it will indicate that the product is out of stock instead of making another waitlist.

The bad news: If you’re on the waitlist for a 2TB model, you might not get a chance to buy one at all, as Valve says there are more people on the waitlist than there are units available. The company is closing the waitlists for its 2TB models.

Valve says that while it’s still building more Steam machines, “memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels” and that it doesn’t know the number it can make or “at what price we’ll be able to offer them.” The 2TB Steam Machine is “especially constrained.” The company anticipates “having more information” to share about additional supply in January.

After delaying the Steam Machine’s expected early 2026 launch due to the memory and storage crisis, Valve launched the product in June with a price starting at $1,049 for the 512GB model without a bundled controller. A 2TB model without a controller costs $1,349.

items.title: Some creators are skeptical of Instagram’s new affiliate program
paragraphs: For years, influencers have come up with workarounds on social media to figure out how to share affiliate links with followers. A new integration between Instagram and Amazon was announced earlier this month as a way to make it easier for influencers to make money from affiliate links — but some content creators are suspicious about who really benefits.

The new integration allows creators to connect their Instagram and Amazon accounts and automatically tag products with their affiliate links, from which they earn a commission when followers make purchases. Influencers will be able to embed up to 30 product links in a Reel or 20 in a feed post, but a permissions setting has led to concerns about what creators are actually agreeing to.

In connecting an Amazon account, creators must agree to allow the retailer and its brand sellers to create ads from “any public content” that includes a related affiliate link. Influencers must also agree to acknowledge that brands can edit their content and use their “testimonial, caption or media” for ads.

The wide-ranging permissions are giving creators pause. Some have urged peers not to connect their accounts without reviewing the permissions and understanding how the feature would affect earnings. People making money on social media spend years tweaking their content and strategy to maximize reach, engagement, and, by extension, their bottom line. For some, it appeared that they would be giving Amazon and its sellers the ability to use their content under unclear terms. On Instagram head Adam Mosseri’s post announcing the feature, influencers complained about the lack of clarity, questioned whether using the feature would decrease their reach (which some creators say happens when they link to outside products), and demanded answers to whether their commission rate would stay the same when Amazon or brands use their content for ads.

Linking products through the new integration won’t reduce reach, Jimmy O’Keefe, Instagram’s director of product marketing, said in an email to The Verge. O’Keefe also noted that creators will continue to earn commission through affiliate links when Amazon boosts their posts, and that they can stop the boosting in settings or disconnect the integration entirely. There’s also a separate, manual way to add products without linking accounts, if a creator wants to opt out of having their content made into ads.

Amazon has an enormous influencer program that reaches across social media platforms. It is so lucrative that some content creators are able to make a living almost exclusively by hawking products for sale on Amazon, building empires on the shopping habits of their followers. When it comes to putting those links in front of followers, though, social platforms have historically been a roadblock, hence the cottage industry of link-in-bio tools meant to circumvent limits. Slowly but surely, though, platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and YouTube — perhaps chasing the success of TikTok Shop — have added more and more shopping features. The result is that shopping and social media begin to feel more and more like the same thing.

items.title: England fined for fans' anti-Catholic chants in Spain
paragraphs: England have been punished by Uefa following anti-Catholic chanting from the away fans during their Nations League victory in Spain.
European football's governing body have fined the Football Association £12,572 (15,000 euros) and imposed a suspended one-match ban for England away supporters.
BBC Sport understands the charge of 'racist and/or discriminatory behaviour' relates to chants that were deemed anti-Catholic and anti-Irish.
A further offence within the next two years would mean a ban on away fans is enforced.

There had been concerns of the prospect of racist chanting from Spain fans before the game in Madrid with England boss Thomas Tuchel stating he would remind his players of Uefa's anti-racism protocol before the fixture.

Tuchel stressed he didn't expect any incidents, but the visit was England's first to the Spanish capital since a notorious 2004 encounter at the Bernabeu was overshadowed by racist chanting directed at their players.
That led to a firm response from Spain head coach Luis de la Fuente, who said: "What I'd tell you, and you can tell Thomas, is that in Spain, there's no racism.
"Just like that, crystal clear. Just like in England, there's no racism in Spain. We aren't racist, any of us."
England won the match 3-2 to end Spain's 43-match unbeaten run and top League A Group 3.

items.title: Star Wars actor 'thrilled' to voice the Welsh Luke Skywalker
paragraphs: Mark Lewis Jones, who voices the dark lord Darth Vader, said on the red carpet it was "nice to record the voice but not have the make-up" and joked that "the Rhosllanerchrugog accent lends itself to the dark side".
Llyr Ifans, who plays C-3PO, said he hoped the film was successful and that more Welsh-language versions would follow.
"C-3PO seems to be in all of them," he said.
"I'm quite confident it will go down well and there will be a lot of happy Welsh-speaking parents on Christmas Day."
Ifans said he been a fan of the Star Wars films since childhood, and getting invited to play the character was "surreal".
"When I first got the email through I thought 'wow, this is a bit weird doing Star Wars in Welsh' but playing C-3PO, one of the iconic parts, you can't say no, can you really?"
C-3PO is said to be fluent in six million forms of communication and Ifans said it was now one more.

items.title: UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries
paragraphs: The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document.

A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”.
Until now, the Home Office has been seeking bilateral agreements with third countries allowing the removal of migrants, but with no obvious success.
Last week, five EU countries – Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands – announced an agreement in principle with Rwanda to establish a migrant “return hub” there in 2027.

Burnham hinted at possible cooperation with EU countries last week when he told reporters that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that [the five-country deal] with interest, learning from what went on in the past”. He said: “The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
The UK has been fighting for deeper cooperation with the EU on migration, with the new deal on a “strategic dialogue” secured in the last two weeks by negotiators in Brussels.

It is a key part of the UK-EU reset pact, which also covers a youth mobility scheme, tariffs on Chinese imports, food and drink exports to the EU and a wider restatement of commitment on defence and security.
Informed sources confirmed this was the first time the UK and the EU had agreed to “open a dialogue on returns” after the launch of the bloc’s Channel action plan in June this year.
Whitehall sources said the UK was now open to the possibility of sending rejected claimants to Rwanda – a recent pivot from the position under Keir Starmer’s government, which rejected the move.
According to a draft of the joint agreement, negotiations over third-country hubs will be part of increased cooperation to tackle irregular migration.

The document states: “The EU and UK … will establish a structured dialogue on migration covering in particular the joint activities under the Channel action plan, action against irregular migration and migrant smuggling networks, strategic communication and border management, upstream cooperation and engagement with third countries, returns to third countries, pull factors for irregular migrants and legal pathway.”
In May, the UK and 45 other European countries signed an agreement that explicitly endorsed plans to send unwanted asylum seekers to third-country hubs.

A political declaration from the 46 members of the Council of Europe, the body that oversees the European convention on human rights (ECHR), said states had an “undeniable sovereign right” to control their borders.

It is understood that the UK has been seeking a deal with an unnamed third country, similar to the Italy-Albania agreement that allowed Rome to place detention centres in Albania. Albania has ruled out a bilateral agreement on a return hub with the UK.

Previous discussions have reportedly centred on 11 countries: Armenia, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, Libya, Mauritania, Rwanda, Senegal, Tunisia, Uganda and Uzbekistan. Montenegro has denied reports that it is considering housing refused asylum seekers.
Starmer scrapped a Tory plan to forcibly send small-boat arrivals to Rwanda where their asylum claims would have been processed.

Before the election, the Conservative government had spent £700m on its Rwanda returns policy, which was meant to deter Channel crossings. The scheme hit legal and political obstacles from the start, with the UK supreme court eventually ruling it illegal.

Under Burnham, the Home Office has refused to close down the possibility of sending asylum seekers to Rwanda. This week, when asked if the UK might ever send asylum seekers to Rwanda, a Home Office spokesperson said: “The UK, like other European countries, is exploring innovative approaches including returns hubs to tackle illegal migration.”
The UK has been looking for years to strengthen cooperation with France and other EU member states to tackle small boats carrying asylum seekers across the Channel.

But sources say it is only in recent months that there has been a change of mood in the EU, with member states realising that the intensity of criminal trafficking across the Channel is “proving [to be] a pull factor” to enter the EU. Those that fail to make it to British shores remain in the EU’s migrant support system.

Responding to the planned cooperation on migrant hubs, Madeleine Sumption, the head of the Migration Observatory at Oxford University, said: “Its inclusion in the statement would confirm the now relatively widespread interest in ‘third country’ options.”
In response, Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, said return hubs were likely to be difficult and costly to run.
“Removing people to places they have never stepped foot will be difficult and distressing,” he said.
“The last decade has shown that working with people to support their return to their countries is far more successful.”

A Home Office spokesperson said: “While we are not part of this EU member state initiative, there is widespread international agreement on the need to have practical and workable solutions to deal with the global challenge of illegal migration.

“We continue to explore innovative approaches, including returns hubs, to build on the 80,000 people with no right to be in the UK returned or deported since July 2024. We have consistently made clear that we support the principle of returns hubs.”

items.title: EU-UK talks going down to the wire, says No 10
paragraphs: Negotiations between the EU and UK are "going down to the wire" ahead of Friday's summit in Brussels, Downing Street has said.
The summit is aimed at reaching new agreements between the two sides on food trade rules, visas for young people and carbon emissions pricing.
The prime minister's spokesman said that if a deal is secured, the government will introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions and debates" of the Brexit referendum.
Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, she said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but added "not trade at any cost".
She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc.
Burnham's spokesman said Brexit had done "more harm than good".

"The choice over the coming days is clear: stand with Boris Johnson and Kemi Badenoch defending a broken status quo, or with Andy Burnham delivering change, cutting costs for business, helping with the costs of the weekly shop and creating opportunities for young people," he added.
One of the deals expected to be reached on Friday includes a new youth mobility scheme, which would make it easier for young people to work and travel in the EU and UK.
The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.
In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.
Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.

Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.

The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in the talks, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.
An agreement on trade could also remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.
The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.
However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling.
On immigration, Burnham has said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.
Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from the deal on Friday.
"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.

"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.
"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."
The prime minister has said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.

Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.
The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.
Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU.
However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun, external, said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU.

He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."

items.title: Pochettino's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator
paragraphs: Manchester United fans have been given a unique and unexpected insight into Mauricio Pochettino's first training session after footage was captured by a drone flown next to the club's Carrington training ground.
Twelve minutes of the session was filmed by a drone operator and uploaded onto YouTube.
Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, are clearly visible, with the session filmed from a variety of angles and distances.
"For the people asking about legality. It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it," said the drone operator.
"The drone remained in line of sight at all times, it didn't fly over anyone or even near anyone so was a perfectly legal flight going by the CAA rules that regulates drone usage.

"The drone is correctly labelled, and I hold all the relevant licences, public liability and insurance required. As for leaking team news/tactics, it was half an hour into the managers first training session, there are many media there so certainly won't be the only footage of training released."
The session was also filmed by United's own media channel, who regularly film club training sessions.

Civil Aviation Authority guidelines include the following warning: "If you use these devices where people can expect privacy, such as inside their home or garden, you're likely to be breaking data protection laws."
Manchester United have declined to comment.
There were 10 outfield players working with Pochettino, although it seems unlikely it will be the starting line-up for Sunday's trip to Liverpool.

While Harry Maguire, Kobbie Mainoo, Amad Diallo, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo are regular starters, Ayden Heaven and Andrey Santos have had less involvement, and neither Joshua Zirkzee nor Harry Amass have started a Premier League game this season. Jaume Camacho 17, who is yet to feature at senior level, was also with the group.

On an adjoining pitch, skipper Bruno Fernandes is shown in one group playing the 'rondos' game, where two players are in the middle trying to intercept the passes of the five players in a circle on the outside. Youngster Shea Lacey and last season's FA Youth Cup-winning skipper Dan Armer are also involved, along with England youth international Bendito Mantato.
Next to that is another group which includes more experienced players in Lisandro Martinez, Matthijs de Ligt, Youri Tielemans, Mason Mount, Leny Yoro, Noussair Mazraoui and Diogo Dalot.
The identical twins Jack and Tyler Fletcher are split between the two groups, with Pochettino's assistant Jesus Perez across both.
Not all the players were identifiable and United confirmed defender Patrick Dorgu was involved.

items.title: Landmines keep civilians in Northern Syria from rebuilding
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.
One month after returning to his village near the northern Syrian town of Tel Abyad, 37-year-old Seyfo Hami stepped on a landmine that cost him one of his legs.

Hami, a father of four, said returning to his village after years of displacement caused by the Syrian civil war had raised hopes of rebuilding his life. But the incident changed everything for him and his family.

“I stepped on a landmine at the same spot where I used to walk every day before I was displaced. The explosion was so powerful that it threw me backward. My brother came and picked me up,” he told VOA, describing the incident that left him permanently disabled.

Nearly two years after the fall of the former Bashar al-Assad regime, landmines and unexploded ordnance remain a major threat to Syrians across the country. In a September report, the United Nations said that since December 2024, landmines and unexploded ordnance had killed nearly 900 people in Syria, including 269 children, and injured more than 1,600 others.

In Kurdish-populated villages in this part of northern Syria, dozens of communities that were once on the front lines of the conflict remain contaminated with landmines, preventing residents from returning to their homes.

“We live in fear. We don't dare go anywhere. If our children go out of our sight for even a moment, we clutch our hearts in fear. We cannot step out,” said Samira Said, a resident of Qiz Ali village near Tel Abyad.
“When our children go out, we walk right behind them because we don't know where the mines are,” she told VOA.
Local residents say the interim Syrian authorities have so far cleared only the main roads in the area, while landmines remain inside the villages.
Medina Ghadir, a local resident whose nephew was injured in a landmine explosion near her home, took a VOA reporter to a spot beside her house where her sons had removed a landmine themselves.
“There are so many mines,” she said. “Who is going to clear them out?”

Security officials in Tel Abyad confirmed to VOA that mine-clearance teams affiliated with the Syrian government had worked to clear major roads before leaving the area. They also said they had formally contacted international demining organizations operating in Syria, asking them to begin operations in Tel Abyad.

items.title: Sonos is taking up to 30 percent off speakers and soundbars right now
paragraphs: Sonos speakers and soundbars aren’t exactly cheap, but thankfully the company’s Black Friday sale has already begun, making everything a little easier to afford through November 30th. Most notably, you can pick up the Arc Ultra soundbar for a new low of $849 ($250 off) from Sonos, Amazon, and Best Buy, or the newfangled Sonos Play for $239 ($60 off) from the same retailers (Sonos, Amazon, Best Buy).

If you’re looking to give your home theater setup a big upgrade, the Arc Ultra is an excellent soundbar. It supports Dolby Atmos and delivers more immersive sound than the original Arc, while adding Bluetooth connectivity. Dialogue also sounds noticeably clearer, and the new Quick Tune feature automatically adjusts the soundbar’s audio to suit your room using built-in microphones, so you no longer need an iPhone to fine-tune the sound for your environment. For more powerful bass, you can also pair it with a compatible Sonos subwoofer, like the Sub 4, which is also available from Sonos as part of a discounted bundle for $1,499 ($499 off).

If you’re looking for a more affordable soundbar, the second-gen Sonos Beam has also hit a new low price at Amazon, Best Buy, and Sonos’ online storefront, where you can buy it for $339 ($160 off). The sound isn’t quite as immersive as that of the Arc Ultra, but the latest Beam can still fill a room with rich, clear audio. It also supports Dolby Atmos; however, unlike the newer Beam Ultra, it lacks side- and upward-firing speakers and instead relies on software to replicate surround sound effects. It also supports HDMI eARC, providing high-quality audio from a compatible TV.

If you’re shopping for a smart speaker instead of a soundbar, the Era 100 SL is available for an all-time low of $149 ($40 off) from Sonos, Amazon, and Best Buy (the standard Era 100 is also down to $179 at Amazon and Best Buy). The feature-packed speakers are nearly identical, but the SL model lacks a built-in mic, and thus voice controls. Both offer excellent stereo sound and rich bass, with dual tweeters and a large woofer that delivers clear, detailed audio despite its small size. They also support Bluetooth and Apple’s AirPlay 2, and you can connect a wired audio source like a turntable using an optional USB-C adapter. For a more immersive experience, you can even pair two for stereo sound or use them as rear surrounds with a compatible Sonos soundbar.

If you want a speaker you can take on the go, the newer Sonos Play is available from Sonos, Amazon, and Best Buy for $239 ($60 off), which is the first notable discount we’ve seen. The portable speaker delivers clear, detailed sound that can fill both larger rooms and outdoor spaces. It also offers up to 24 hours of battery life and an IP67 rating for water and dust resistance, making it a great companion for long days at the beach or other outdoor adventures. Plus, its removable carrying loop makes it easy to bring along, and you can even use it to top off your phone. Like other Sonos speakers, it supports both Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and you can also group it with other Sonos speakers over Bluetooth when you’re outdoors and away from Wi-Fi.

Last but not least, you can also buy the Sonos Ace for $229 ($120 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and directly from Sonos, which marks a new low price. The newer Ace Ultra offer better sound and improved noise cancellation, but the Ace is still a solid option, especially if you already own a Sonos soundbar. The gorgeous headphones deliver powerful, detailed sound, solid noise cancellation, and an exceptionally natural-sounding transparency mode, along with up to 30 hours of continuous playback on a single charge. Unlike the newer Ultra, though, they can’t transfer music from your other Sonos speakers to your headphones. However, their TV Audio Swap feature still lets you transfer audio from a compatible Sonos soundbar to your headphones, so you can watch movies or listen to music playing on your TV without disturbing anyone else.

items.title: The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife
paragraphs: Allison Aubrey has been looking into what helps keep relationships strong amid midlife transitions. Richard Drury/Getty Images hide caption
Follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.
Ever argued with your spouse in the car? NPR's Nina Totenberg can relate.

She and her husband, David Reines, have been married for 26 years, and it's on the road where they're most likely to have a spat. "The car is awful," Totenberg told me, laughing. It comes down partly to the brakes. She taps them "way before" Reines does. And when another driver cuts him off, he sometimes wants to return the favor. Totenberg's advice from the passenger seat: "Don't take the bait."

It's so relatable. And as Reines put it, "You can't not have some conflict after 26 years. I think the secret is how you deal with it." (They began our interview for this episode of Your Turn by giving each other a kiss!)

As we ask "What comes next?" in midlife, who's standing beside us matters a lot. Kids leave home, careers shift, and relationships can change, too. So what does a good partnership look like at this stage?
When people ask Reines why their marriage works, he points to four L's:

Like. Do you actually like each other? For Reines, respect is part of this. He says he has total respect for her work, and she respects his career, too. He is a retired trauma surgeon and now keeps busy as a volunteer at the Library of Congress and serves on boards. Each of them also keeps a strong sense of self. "Although we meld," Reines says. "I still have me, and she still has her."

Lust. Physical intimacy matters. They kiss every day, hold hands, "all the time," and have held off on buying a king-size bed. In hotel beds, they joke, they can't find each other if the bed is too big.
Laugh. He says she has one of the best senses of humor he knows. They laugh together every day.
NPR's Nina Totenberg and her husband, David Reines, have been married for 26 years. Kerry Thompson/NPR hide caption

I also talked with clinical psychologist Julie Schwartz Gottman who I interviewed for my book, Your Turn. She and her husband, John Gottman, co-founded the Gottman Institute and are two of the best-known names in relationship science, and co-authors of Fight Right: How Successful Couples Turn Conflict Into Connection, where they describe the "Four Horseman" which are four destructive communication patterns that can help predict the breakdown of a relationship.
Gottman points to research that shows many dual-career couples spend little time together and much of the communication can be transactional. Did you call the plumber? Did you walk the dog?

The Gottmans found that couples can improve their relationships by intentionally carving out about six hours a week together, and making changes to small, daily and weekly habits. They call it the Magic Six.

Some of these things may sound obvious, yet oftentimes these are the very things that can fall away when couples are too busy or distracted. And she says it's illuminating when couples actually track progress.
Partings (a few minutes each day). Before you leave in the morning, spend a few minutes communicating about what's happening in your partner's day.
Reunions (about 20 minutes a day). At the end of the workday, share a kiss or physical affection. Then have a 20-minute stress-reducing conversation about your day.
Admiration and appreciation (35 minutes a week). Spend about five minutes a day expressing genuine gratitude or naming a trait you admire in your partner. Or tell a story to remind each other.
Affection (35 minutes a week). That works out to about five minutes a day on physical touch, such as holding hands or cuddling before sleep.
Date night (2 hours a week). Have distraction-free time together to enjoy being together. It doesn't need to be dinner and a show. It can be a low-key hike, a museum visit or any activity you enjoy.
State of the union meeting (1 hour a week). Review what's going well as well as concerns or things that are not working, and then talk things out.
Many partners fall into the trap of trying to "fix" the other person's problems or tell them how to proceed. But the point of the daily conversation is to step away from this mentality.
"Most of us just wanna be seen," Gottman told me. "We wanna be witnessed." Jumping in with advice can cut off the conversation before your partner gets the chance to describe what's bothering them.
Instead, she suggests three simple words: "Tell me more."
It's an invitation, Gottman says. It tells your partner, "I really am interested in what you're saying." It shows them that you care.

Nina Totenberg and David Reines have their own version. Every night at dinner, they sit down and ask, "How'd your day go?" He calls Nina a good listener and she says she enjoys connecting this way and spending time together. They keep each other in check and serve as each other's confidant.

Gottman also had good news for couples who don't share every hobby. You can pursue different passions as long as you bring them back to the table and stay curious about each other. Some couples want lots of independence, and others want to do everything together. The key is to keep asking: Are you missing me? Do we need more time together, or less?

Totenberg and Reins have found their balance. They agree on watching British murder mysteries together. And when he wants a shoot-'em-up, she heads upstairs for Law & Order. Summer vacations on Cape Cod are friends-only, where they spend days doing what they each enjoy. Winter holidays are for her sisters and family.
As Totenberg put it: "If you find somebody that you really love who loves you back, you should grab that and run for all the world because it's ... an enormous gift."
So, if you'd like: give this a try: Ask your partner one open-ended question. Then say, "Tell me more."
For more, follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.

items.title: Gemini on Mac can now use your computer
paragraphs: With the new computer use feature, Google says Gemini can better help with things like filling in forms and creative workflows.
With the new computer use feature, Google says Gemini can better help with things like filling in forms and creative workflows.
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Google’s Gemini app for macOS now has computer use, meaning it can help you “get multi-step tasks done across your local files, desktop apps, and the web,” the company says. Google suggests the feature might be useful for things like speeding up workflows, filling in forms, making presentations, and listing items for sale.

Users will be able to decide which of your apps Gemini can access, and be able to follow along as Gemini works because it has its own background window that shows a live preview in your chat, Google says. The feature is rolling out now in English for users in the US.

Gemini is introducing the new feature ahead of Apple launching new restrictions for apps wanting “full disk access” on Mac due to potential risks from AI agents with computer use. A preview of the settings rolled out with this week’s macOS 27.3 beta.

items.title: Leaked images reveal Motorola’s wide foldable
paragraphs: The Razr Flex will compete with the iPhone Duo, Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, and other widescreen folding devices.
The Razr Flex will compete with the iPhone Duo, Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, and other widescreen folding devices.
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

New leaked images of Motorola’s next folding smartphone shared by SammyGuru add more credence to the theory that widescreen could be the default design for foldables moving forward. Following a single leaked shot shared to Reddit yesterday, this new crop of images reveal the Motorola Razr Flex from several angles in two finishes with its inner screen completely open and partially folded.

The photos show the Razr Flex in two finishes: coriander brown and dark botanical garden, according to SammyGuru. The brown option features a back panel with a bumpy leather-like finish, while the green has a fabric-like woven finish. The cover screen has a hole punch selfie camera centered at the top, while the Razr Flex’s inner screen pushes the camera to the upper right corner. On the back is a pill-shaped bar with two cameras and a flash.

The Flex is expected to be a smaller and more affordable alternative to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 which has a 5.5-inch cover screen and a 7.6-inch main display when unfolded. But more specific details ,including the size of the Razr Flex, its pricing, and when it’s expected to be debut, are still unknown.
