items.title: Anthropic keeps the AI party swinging, but the atmosphere is bubbly | Nils Pratley
paragraphs: Roll up, roll up, who wants to buy shares in a company whose technology “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, as the prospectus had it? Virtually everybody, as it turned out. Anthropic flew out of the blocks on its first day as a listed company.

From the point of view of the promoters, the result was as good as it gets. The final pricing for the shares at $83 apiece was meaningfully higher than the indicated range of $70 to $78, but still left room for a big initial “pop”. There were positive vibes all round – especially for the battalion of investment banks collecting $550m of underwriting fees.

And, to be fair, it wasn’t nailed-on that the show would go so swimmingly. There was a late risk that investor sentiment towards the AI universe could be jinxed – or Jensened – by the soap opera at Nvidia. More generally, there was a worry that the AI bubble, if that’s what it is, could burst when somebody tried to unload too much stock on the stock market in one go.

Anthropic, though, has set records by raising $107bn. It is an extraordinary sum, especially for a business founded five years ago. At the listing price, Anthropic was valued at $1.5tn. When shares began trading at £111.50, its market capitalisation was up to $2tn. Only 14 months ago, it raised money at a valuation of a “mere” $183bn.

The feat, though, is not wholly inexplicable. Some $26bn of the listing proceeds were virtually in the bag, thanks to the cornerstone placement to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC. That assembly of AI and AI-adjacent names fed worries about the industry’s circular financing.

But, on the other hand, every fund manager knew he or she would be betting against the crowd by saying no. Momentum can carry a stock a long way, even before the index funds and index-hugging funds are obliged to buy (Nasdaq entry will be quick; the S&P 500 will take at least a year).
Take a step back, though, and ask whether Anthropic – loss-making and with projected revenues in 2026 of $50bn-ish – can possibly be worth $1.5tn-plus.

The short, and unhelpful, answer is that virtually any valuation could be made to sound plausible if you believe, first, that AI is a generational technology that will be adopted at never-seen-before speed and, second, that “frontier” pioneering firms, of which Anthropic is the leader, will capture an outsized slice of the commercial value for years and years.

Consider the assumptions behind that thesis, however. Can Anthropic really improve from $50bn-ish of revenue this year to $600bn in 2030, which is roughly what tech analysts have pencilled in? Given the current rate of growth, perhaps it can. But sustaining the pace, or something like it, for another 16 quarters simply won’t be straightforward or mechanical.

What is the real level of demand from corporate users for frontier models? Nobody doubts that AI adoption is still in the early stage, but does everybody need the finest product from Anthropic’s Claude suite? Already executives grumble that their IT budgets are finite and that nine-month-old versions, or cheaper “open weight” models from rivals, do the job for basic work. Lasting pricing power in AI is simply unclear. “Commoditisation risk”, in the jargon, could be the next year’s valuation debate.

Then there is the investment bill to make it all happen – $900bn of spending commitments were detailed in the prospectus for computing power and infrastructure. The listing proceeds help, as does the visibility and credibility that comes with being on a public market. But debt, not just equity, will be a crucial part of this story.

“Obviously, at some point in the future we’re hoping to be investment grade,” said co-founder Dario Amodei as trading in the shares started. You bet: the price at which Anthropic borrows matters fundamentally.

Away from the party atmosphere, the European Central Bank has its eye on financial stability in the eurozone. This week, it issued one of those fuddy-duddy reminders about how much capital is being bet on the AI revolution, and how little transparency there is around the funding of hyperscalers and other suppliers to the boom.

“Big tech firms are estimated to have total off-balance-sheet commitments of more than $4tn as of the second quarter of 2026,” its report said, warning of “historical parallels with the dotcom and sub-prime bubbles”.

It is not the only one to see warning signs. Anthropic is an astonishingly successful company already and is plainly at the forefront of a significant technological shift. But it has been listed in an environment that looks – to most of us who remember the late 1990s and the subsequent bust – to have bubbly characteristics. AI technology, like the internet, is gamechanging. But it doesn’t mean today’s share prices are right.

items.title: Sid Lee Architecture references "rhythm of the vine" for curved Ontario hotel
paragraphs: Canadian studio Sid Lee Architecture has created a curved-glass hotel that takes cues from the burgeoning wine region of Ontario.
The Montreal-based studio recently unveiled The Clayfield Hotel, a 60-room hotel with a restaurant, ballroom and rooftop terrace in Niagara-on-the-Lake.
The rounded 94,000-square-foot (8,732-square metre) hotel sits on a property in the historic village that is being transformed by winemakers.

“The Clayfield was conceived as a new hub for Niagara-on-the-Lake, a place where wine culture and hospitality find a home,” Martin Leblanc, architect and co-founding partner of Sid Lee Architecture, told Dezeen.
“Its layered contours, rounded geometry and rhythmic wood elements translate the surrounding vineyard landscape into a building that celebrates the region’s contribution to Canadian winemaking.”
The hotel was conceived as a pavilion set in the emerging townscape between vineyards and the Clayfield Commons housing development on an agricultural road.
The curved form allows access and connection to its surroundings in multiple directions.
“The hotel acts as a threshold between these typologies, connecting the vineyard and the denser village-like development around it,” Leblanc said.
“Its exterior wood elements recall the rhythm of the vine rows, the layered concrete refers to the clay soil and the reflective glass registers the changing light, sky and seasons.”
The studio said that the organic, natural flow of a hotel is essential to the lasting success of the design.

Working back and forth between the architecture and the interior design, the studio laid out spaces to progress from public to private and back again, integrating moments for visitors to discover the landscape.

“As visitors approach and circulate around the building, it frames changing views of the vines, the plaza and the emerging neighbourhood,” Leblanc said. “The lobby acts as a gateway to the vineyard, while the rooftop terrace reconnects the hotel experience with its broader surroundings.”
Meanwhile, the staircase acts as a connector, transition and centrepiece between the plaza, lobby and upper levels.

“Inside, we chose a palette that speaks to the natural beauty of Niagara’s wine country: walnut panelling, concrete, dark amaranth-coloured leather, greige limestone and woven fabrics,” Leblanc said, calling out the limestone registration desk chiselled from the Niagara Escarpment and the restaurant’s curved bar that resembles the shape of the building.

With mostly Teknion furniture, each space represents a season of the vineyard, from spring in the lobby to winter in the guest rooms with more quiet, reserved furnishings that complete the rooms that fan out from the rounded concrete strata.

Founded in 2009, Sid Lee Architecture has six offices across North America and Europe. The studio previously remodelled its own offices in an I.M. Pei office building, overhauled the interiors of the iconic Fairmont Queen Elizabeth Hotel and created an artisan-inspired workplace for video game designers – all in Montreal.

items.title: Faults not fixed in 90% of homes in government insulation scheme
paragraphs: More than 90% of homes fitted with faulty insulation under energy-saving government schemes have not yet had repairs completed to fix the botched work, a minister has said.
The government found almost all homes that had external wall insulation installed as part of two of the government's ECO schemes had defects that needed repairing.
Speaking to a committee of MPs on Wednesday, Energy Minister Martin McClusky said repair works had been completed at 2,227 out of the 24,600 homes impacted.
He said he was shocked by the extent of the failures and has assured affected households they would not be asked to pay to sort out these problems.
McClusky told MPs the insulation schemes "didn't have correct oversight".
Ofgem oversees the ECO schemes and alongside TrustMark, a government-backed consumer protection service, is responsible for auditing homes to identify faulty installations.
The government and its partners have known about significant levels of defective and unsafe insulation for years, with audits finding poor work in October 2024.
Ken Palfrey, a 66-year-old retired builder from Birmingham, is among the home owners waiting for repairs.
He had external wall insulation installed through the ECO programme in 2024.
He claims the installation was "botched", causing damage to his window sills and leading to damp and mould on his walls.
He said he complained and after some months an inspection concluded the insulation had been fitted incorrectly and he was told it had to be removed immediately.
Palfrey said for two years he had been on a "merry-go-round", spending "hundreds and hundreds of hours writing emails and complaining to people".

Earlier this month, TrustMark referred his case to the National Energy Foundation (NEF), a charity that has funding from energy suppliers to put right damaged homes where the installer has gone out of business.
"It's been an absolute nightmare," Palfrey said.
"Every day of my life, every time you look at the insulation, you're worried about it."
A TrustMark spokesperson said it was working to contact affected households and to fix "the unacceptable problems left by this faulty external wall insulation scheme".
"We're sorry for what Mr Palfrey has been through and have referred him to the National Energy Foundation which should be able to get his insulation put right," the spokesperson said.
Labour MP Bill Esterson, the chair of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, told the BBC he was seeking assurances that the victims "will be supported in a timely fashion".
But he said he was concerned that Ofgem, Great Britain's energy regulator, had "failed to identify whether work had been carried out or completed to a decent standard".
When asked if he had confidence in Ofgem at the committee, McClusky did not answer the question directly.
He said: "There's clearly been failures in the system. We're designing a system now."
He added Ofgem was a "very different organisation than it was a number of years ago".
A spokesperson for Ofgem said: "It is unacceptable that households have been left with substandard ECO4 work. Ofgem was not responsible for assuring the quality of installations."

The spokesperson said the Department of Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) "is responsible for the design and overall outcomes of ECO, and that Ofgem's role did not include assessing installation quality".
"Our role, set by government, is to administer the scheme and hold suppliers to account for meeting their obligations," the Ofgem spokesperson added.
"When serious quality problems emerged, we went beyond our core role to support affected households and help establish the scale of the problem."
The two ECO schemes that have caused widespread issues are known as ECO4 and Great British Insulation Scheme (GBIS).
ECO4 was launched in 2022 and since then, more than 300,000 homes have had heat pumps, solar panels and insulation fitted under the £4bn scheme. It is closing in December.
GBIS - which opened in 2023 and has now closed - was more narrowly designed to help households lower their energy bills by installing cheap insulation.
The BBC has been reporting on the impact of faulty insulation installed under these schemes in recent years.
Fuel Poverty Action, a campaign group, argues that problems with faulty upgrades under a range of government energy efficiency schemes could be affecting as many as 100,000 homes.
"Ignoring the other defective measures is shockingly negligent, and is causing huge harm," said Jonathan Bean, policy lead at Fuel Poverty Action.
"Defective internal wall insulation causes major hidden damage, making it a ticking time bomb in homes.
"The government estimates that 29% of it is defective but chose not to include it in the Find and Fix process."
A spokesperson for DESNZ said: "We inherited the failing ECO4 scheme, which we ended after it clearly let families down.
"No household should have to pay to put the issues right and TrustMark is working to support those affected to ensure this is the case.
"Our Warm Homes Plan will overhaul the system to protect consumers and ensure failings are not repeated."

items.title: Anthony Zurcher: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance
paragraphs: So far, however, the US has been remarkably silent following the three-party meeting.

While China was quick to release a joint communique detailing the discussions and Putin expounded during an hour-long post-meeting press conference, Trump has made minimal public comments, instead promising a news conference at the White House on Friday.
On his trip to China earlier this year and following his meeting with Xi at the APEC summit in South Korea last October, Trump spoke with the press early in his flight back to Washington.

For the moment, the White House is letting the joint communique, released Thursday after the three met, do the talking. But the document is mostly a vague endorsement of efforts to ensure "strategic stability and international security".

That, along with the visuals of three powerful men sitting in the same room to amicably discuss global issues, might offer some reassurance no catastrophic conflicts are on the horizon. But pledges of further "dialogue" and an acknowledgement that nuclear war "must never be fought" provide minimal substance beyond the rhetoric.

"In general, it's good for the leaders of the major global players to come together in various formats, even if the results appear to be modest at best," David Firestein, head of the Bush Foundation for US-China Relations, told the BBC.

A line about boosting "the production and supply of refined petroleum products" seems directed at Putin, given that nation's role as a major source of fossil fuels on the international market. And it was hard to miss the condemnation of the International Criminal Court – a recent target of American ire.

If there's one thing the leaders of the three major world powers can agree on, it's that multilateral global organisations that attempt to enforce international law shouldn't have the teeth to back up those efforts.
While in China, Trump called Putin his "friend", and praised his "outstanding personal relationship" with Xi after sharing a handshake and hug with the Chinese leader.
But once Trump returns to Washington, he is likely face a political environment where views of his Asia trip range from measured concern to outright criticism.

"I am concerned by how we are characterising our relationships with geopolitical adversaries. Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends," Republican Senator John Curtis of Utah said in a statement to the BBC on Thursday.
"Diplomacy is important, but it should never come at the expense of clarity about who our adversaries are."
Democrats, for their part, did not mince words.
"American security cannot be traded away for photo opportunities or personal aggrandisement," nine senators on the foreign relations committee wrote in a letter to the White House.

Trump is hardly the first American president to seek an international diplomatic breakthrough as a salve following domestic political setbacks. Democrats Bill Clinton and Barack Obama took overseas trips as presidents shortly after their party's own midterm electoral defeats.

In those cases, any boosts to their standing proved short-lived. And while Trump may have gotten the images he wanted from his Asian summit, the lack of substantive progress accompanying them likely means this trip also will be quickly forgotten.
Brandon Drenon contributed to this report.

items.title: Attempted murder arrest after councillor stabbed in Bradford
paragraphs: Ibrar Ali was attended by emergency services on Manse Street in Bradford
A councillor has been seriously injured after being stabbed while undertaking his duties in Bradford.
Bradford Moor councillor Ibrar Ali was attacked at about 11:04 GMT on Manse Street, according to the deputy leader of Your Bradford Independent Group, councillor Ishtiaq Ahmed.
West Yorkshire Police said a 32-year-old man had been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and was being held in custody.
The force added there was "no information to suggest that this is a politically motivated incident at this time".
Ali is believed to have been injured on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to the nearby Manse Street where emergency services attended, according to police.
A force spokesperson previously said the suspect had climbed on to the roof of a property on Thornbury Avenue following the incident and was later brought down.
Councillor Ibrar Ali was stabbed while walking around Bradford Moor
Ahmed said Ali was undergoing emergency surgery at Leeds General Infirmary after being stabbed in the leg. He said Ali was in a stable condition but had lost a lot of blood.
"My thoughts are with him and his family and loved ones. It's an extremely distressing time," said Ahmed.
"We shouldn't have to fear for our personal safety because we have chosen to serve the public.
"There should be no normalisation of violence in our democratic life."
Responding to the incident in his Bradford East constituency, Labour MP Imran Hussain described the incident as "horrific" and "deeply disturbing".
"My thoughts and prayers are with councillor Ibrar Ali and his family," said Hussain.
"No elected politician should feel under threat or fear for their safety while carrying out their duties and serving their community."
Councillor Ibrar Ali was attacked on Manse Street
Ch Supt Richard Padwell urged anyone with information to contact police.
"This is a serious incident where a local councillor has been stabbed in the street and our thoughts are with him, his family and colleagues at this difficult time," he said.
"Whilst the investigation is in the early stages, there is nothing to suggest that this incident is politically motivated at this time."
Ali is a community development manager at charity The Leap.
He has worked with community organisations Bradford Moor Pass and was one of the founders of Leeds Road Festival.
He was first elected as a councillor in the May local election, replacing the previous Labour representatives.

items.title: Men guilty of abusing woman drugged and advertised for sex by husband
paragraphs: Four men have been found guilty of sexually abusing a woman whose husband drugged and secretly advertised her for sex on the internet, in the first trial of its kind in the UK.
Philip Young, 50, had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and raping his wife, Joanne Young, over a 13-year period at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire.

Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were found guilty of multiple sexual offences by a jury at Winchester Crown Court. Wilkins and Macksoni were each found guilty of one count of rape.
Joanne Young, who divorced Philip Young last year, beamed at police as she left court wiping her eyes.

James Foster, specialist Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) prosecutor, said: "This is the first time in the UK that a jury have convicted or been asked to consider a case of organised drug-facilitated sexual abuse, which has been organised by the husband."

The crimes of the former Tory councillor emerged after the highly publicised case in France of Gisèle Pelicot, whose husband, Dominique Pelicot, drugged and raped her and invited 50 other men to abuse her. Gisèle Pelicot also waived her right to anonymity in that trial.
Her husband was jailed for 20 years in France in 2024 and all the defendants were found guilty of at least one charge.
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.
Police and prosecutors building the case against Philip Young sought the expertise of the French investigators to assist them in bringing him to justice.

Detectives discovered that Philip Young, whose most recent address was in Enfield, north London, had taken 480 intimate images and videos of his wife on 200 occasions and posted images online on at least 500 occasions – with the vast majority of these taken at the family home in Swindon.
The trial of the four defendants heard the investigation into Philip Young had begun after police were alerted to the fact he had uploaded extreme pornographic images to the internet in 2023.
Wiltshire Police said it was still looking for another man wanted in connection with alleged sex offences against Joanne Young.
They described him as being of "a large build, hairy, with scarring on the back of his head, prominent lips, short or shaved hair, and a distinctive tattoo on the left side of his chest".
Wiltshire Police added the extent of drug-rape offences was unknown because victims might not know they had been targeted.

A police spokesperson said: "While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly under-reported crime type.
"Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption.
"These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging."

items.title: Anthropic begins public trading at $2tn valuation after largest-ever IPO
paragraphs: Anthropic shares soared more than a third when trading got under way on its US market debut on Thursday, valuing the company at more than $2tn in the biggest stock market flotation in history.

Shares in the AI company behind the Claude chatbot jumped 34% from its initial public offering price (IPO) of $83 a share to $111.50 when the Nasdaq opened. The gains later eased and shares were up 15% at nearly $96 by early afternoon in New York.

“Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” said Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, who rang the Nasdaq opening bell.
The artificial intelligence startup, founded in 2021, became one of the most valuable publicly traded businesses in the world with the stock market float.

Anthropic announced late Wednesday that it had sold 980m shares to underwriters, an upsized offering that raised $81.3bn, surpassing the previous record set by SpaceX’s initial $75bn fundraise in June.

The company’s listing serves as a bellwether for the multitrillion-dollar artificial intelligence boom as the first frontier lab to be publicly traded. Wall Street investors and the entire global tech industry are watching closely how it fares on the public market.
Anthropic’s stock market debut makes it the first firm focused entirely on AI “uncluttered by an ad business or a rocket business” to be publicly traded, analysts at Yorkville Ives said.

“Anthropic’s IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning,” Yorkville Ives analysts wrote in a memo.

The company has seen explosive growth in revenue every year of its existence – sometimes more than 1,000% – according to its investor prospectus, filed at the end of October. Anthropic brought in $16.2bn in the first six months of 2026, up from $4.6bn in revenue for all of 2025.

“You’ve seen an astronomical growth rate in terms of the top line,” said Evan Schlossman, a principal at Neostellar, a publicly traded venture capital firm. “The question investors are going to be looking at leading up to the IPO, and once it’s public, is what happens to that growth rate.”

Anthropic has also lost an enormous amount of money. In the first half of 2026, the company reported losses of $80bn, though that was largely due to a one-off charge. Losses grew to $104bn in the first nine months of 2026. The firm expects its costs to balloon as it works to secure more compute, which refers to the processing and computational power provided by arrays of semiconductor chips often located in datacenters. It is the resource that powers generative artificial intelligence and Anthropic’s single largest expense, about $18.8bn in the first nine months of 2026.

“The development of frontier AI models requires substantial investments of compute resources, capital, and human capital to conduct large-scale training runs that may span weeks or months and cost many millions of dollars,” the company’s executives wrote in the prospectus.

Anthropic has disclosed in great detail all the ways its AI models may pose a danger to humanity – including being used to develop bioweapons or deepen repression around the world. Amodei has called for a slowdown on the development of the most advanced AI models after employees expressed concerns that the companies were building them irresponsibility.

The company beat competitors like OpenAI to launching on the US stock market. However, the IPO comes amid uncertainty as the industry braces for any additional impact or fallout from the recent Nvidia scandal that led to the resignation of its founder and chief executive, Jensen Huang.

There is “huge volatility in the market”, and investors are going to be looking at how sustainable the company’s AI growth is, said Schlossman. Investors are also keen to see how important Anthropic will be in the larger AI ecosystem. The company has focused primarily on enterprise customers rather than individual consumers. Anthropic’s Claude code product has proved popular with software engineers.

items.title: Joanne Young was drugged and raped by strangers after her husband offered her online
paragraphs: Joanne - who waived her right to anonymity - has been called an "inspiration" by the CPS
Warning: This story discusses sexual violence and abuse
When Joanne Young awoke tied to her bed, she had no idea about the horror that had been unfolding while she was unconscious.
After hearing her then-husband Philip Young calling for someone else to "get down", she quickly realised another person was in the bedroom with them.
Unbeknown to Joanne, Young had advertised online for other men to abuse her. He then drugged her and invited a series of strangers into their bedroom to sexually assault her.
On Thursday, four men were convicted of a number of offences including raping and assaulting her. Her ex-husband had already pleaded guilty to a number of rape charges.
Young, a former Conservative councillor, and another man, Dean Hamilton, pleaded guilty to rape and sexual assault at a previous hearing.
The group came from a variety of backgrounds. One of the men worked on Ministry of Defence nuclear defence projects while another drove Red Cross trucks to Romania in the 1980s.
Speaking outside court after the verdicts earlier, Joanne said "silence is not an option if we are serious about preventing abuse" - you can read her statement in full here.
Her case has striking comparisons with the repeated rape of Gisèle Pelicot in France, with experts saying the crime was "deeply abusive".
Former councillor Philip Young secretly advertised his wife Joanne online for sex, drugged her and arranged for other men to sexually assault her

Online, Young portrayed the abuse as a shared sexual kink known as "cuckolding". The photographs used in the adverts posted on sites like Craigslist and Grindr showed Joanne inanimate and tied to the bed.

James Foster, a specialist prosecutor with the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said Young "would drug her so that he could then sexually abuse her and record that sexual abuse and also arrange for other men to attend the address to sexually abuse her".
One of the men who answered the advert was Dean Hamilton, 46, who admitted to raping Joanne and abusing her in 2015.

The other men who were convicted of sexually assaulting Joanne were Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, Richard Wilkins, 62, Norman Macksoni, 48 and Mohammed Hassan, 38 - the man Young told to "get down" when Joanne woke.
They told the court they believed they had the consent of both Joanne and Young and were told Joanne was pretending to be asleep - when in fact she was heavily sedated.
"But not once during any of this abuse did they ask Joanne Young what she wanted or show any interest in what her wishes were," Foster said.
In a statement read out in court, one of the co-offenders called Young a monster
The law states the sexual consent can only be given if the person involved "agrees by choice ... and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice".
Investigators are told to establish "what steps, if any, the suspect took to obtain the complainant's consent".
Professor Marianne Hester, emeritus professor at the University of Bristol, said Joanne "clearly" had no capacity to say no, adding a "women cannot consent if they are asleep".
"So it's the same if they are completely drugged. They cannot make the decision to agree to sex," she added.
Hester, who has researched gender-based violence for years, said those cases raise broader questions about attitudes towards women and sex.
"We have to question the men, the way men think it's okay to do sex and how they keep normalising, we keep normalising all these very abusive acts within sex and that's really problematic," she said.

Hester added: "We know that investigations have now started on certain websites and that individuals have been identified in a number of different countries who have been up to exactly the same kind of thing.
"So I think that there are potentially quite a lot more cases in the pipeline."
Gisèle Pelicot was at the centre of the largest rape trial in French history
The case has also reignited questions about the role of websites used to facilitate abuse.
Lisa Sugiura, Professor of Cyber Crime and Gender at the University of Portsmouth, argued online platforms have a responsibility to address content that normalises violence against women.
"Often these sites are accompanied by image-based abuse and deeply violent language and rhetoric about women anyway," she said.
"You think, how are these forums allowed to act with impunity without oversight and accountability?
"Before we even get to the question of whether we should simply accept the word of a man claiming to speak on behalf of himself and his wife."
Prof Hester said this case could be "a lot more cases in the pipeline"
Data shows hundreds of similar potential crimes are currently being investigated across the UK.
The National Crime Agency said there was an "urgent need" to deal with the problem as an international issue.
NCA investigators have identified more than 270 individuals linked to one online forum and successor groups.
The CPS describes this type of offending as an emerging challenge for investigators.
"This particular type of offending, where a husband is drugging and abusing his wife and arranging for other men to abuse her, does seem to be a new type of offending," said Foster.
A spokesman for Wiltshire Police explained the extent of drug-rape offences was unknown because victims might not know they had been targeted.
(Clockwise from top left) Richard Wilkins, 62, Mohammed Hassan, 38, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Norman Macksoni, 48, were convicted of sexually assaulting Joanne Young

He said: "While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly under-reported crime type.

"Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption. These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging."
Sugiura disagrees the offending itself is new.
She believes technology has made it easier to facilitate and conceal abuse that may have existed for years.

"The use of technology enables anonymity, it enables that division of identity, the protection of the respectable face offline, and these heinous deeds online," she said, adding offenders often operate within wider online communities where misogynistic attitudes are encouraged and abusive material is shared.
"These are not always isolated incidents," she said.
"They can be part of larger networks where people are swapping tips, encouraging one another and sharing material that is deeply abusive towards women."
"I think that there are potentially quite a lot more cases in the pipeline," she added.

items.title: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
paragraphs: China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.

The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.

Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.

“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.

Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.

First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”

The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.

Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”

Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce.
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.

European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.

The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.

Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.

Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.

Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

items.title: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
paragraphs: Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.

Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump, California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway.
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.

“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.

Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep. Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.
Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News.

Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health, often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

items.title: SHoP Architects designs Novak Djokovic-backed Miami supertall skyscraper
paragraphs: New York studio SHoP Architects has released designs for a ribbed supertall skyscraper in Miami, announced alongside the launch of a luxury brand for which Serbian tennis player Novak Djokovic is developing amenity facilities.

SHoP Architects, who are behind some of New York City’s tallest buildings, designed the 1,049-foot-tall (320-metre-tall) skyscraper around ATMA, a luxury brand being launched by hospitality operator Aman Group.

If completed at the stated height, it would be taller than the city’s current tallest skyscraper, and have the same projected height as the in-progress Waldorf Astoria Hotel & Residences Miami, which has been cited as the city’s future tallest.

The skyscraper will include a hotel, residences and a members’ club. According to Aman Group, ATMA’s “advanced wellness programming and world-class sport facilities” will be developed “exclusively” with Djokovic, who is credited as a global partner of the new brand.
Designs for the skyscraper itself show a ribbed form of balconied terraces organised around a central void that runs from the crown to the podium.
It is planned for Miami’s Brickell neighbourhood, and Aman Group said that the floor-to-ceiling windows of the skyscraper will merge the “futuristic architecture with the bay”.

Toronto-based interiors outfit Studio Paolo Ferrari has been chosen as the interiors lead on the project. It will include condos with one to five bedrooms, with six-bedroom penthouses pushed to the top of the skyscraper.
The structure will have setbacks at the upper floors, presumably to create more panoramic views for residences in the penthouses.
The ATMA concept is based around what Aman Group calls “performance-driven lifestyle”.
“Monolithic architecture meets biomorphic design, furniture is shaped naturally to the human form and ambience adjusts sensitively to residents’ and guests’ circadian rhythm,” said Aman Group.
Djokovic’s programme, meanwhile, will include a 120,000-square-foot spa and wellness centre.
“ATMA Miami will sit at the pinnacle of what performance living can achieve,” said Djokovic.
OKO Group and Oak Row Equities were announced as developers for the project.

SHoP Architects is no stranger to supertall luxury residences. It designed New York’s skinniest supertall skyscraper to have single-floor apartments on the city’s so-called Billionaires Row. It also designed the Brooklyn Tower, the tallest structure in the borough.

items.title: ‘In our lands the rain is made of bullets’: Palestinian artists look back in anger, melancholy and defiance
paragraphs: In 2006, Simone Fattal painted on to basalt slabs the names of places indelibly associated with massacres in the Levant since 1948: Deir Yassin; Jenin; Qana; Sabra. Through the names, in the same Arabic script, runs a line of poetry by Etel Adnan: “In our lands of drought the rain forever is made of bullets.”

Fattal’s work, which documents atrocities on a material that burst from the earth as lava before settling into stone, introduces a show that likewise combines the recording of history with anger both hot and cold.

The last named of those massacres, perpetrated by a Lebanese Christian phalangist militia during Beirut’s occupation by Israeli forces in 1982, also inspired the poem Praise for the High Shadow by Mahmoud Darwish, a line from which this show takes as its title. Writing in exile in Beirut, Darwish riffed on the sea as a symbol of Palestinian displacement and memory, connecting people dispersed around the eastern Mediterranean to each other and to their homeland. The angry, melancholy, defiant work of these (mostly) Palestinian artists also weaves a traumatic national history into the cosmopolitan culture of the Levant and the interlinked world in which we now live.

It is one lesson of their work that to live in exile is to be waiting. On the floor beside Fattal’s monument stands the suitcase that Hazem Harb carried out of Gaza in 2006; above it are two framed photocollages alluding to the international airport that was bulldozed by the IDF four years earlier. These artefacts beg the question of when, and if, the artist will be able to return to his home, and who will make that decision. That powerlessness and apprehension is etched into the faces of the people photographed by Rula Halawani at Palestinian checkpoints.

Tarek Al-Ghoussein never set foot in his own country. Born in Kuwait to Palestinian parents, he explored his fragmented identity in a troubling series of photographs displayed here on glowing lightboxes. The self in these self-portraits emerges in the unsettling combination of symbols (notably the black-and-white keffiyeh that covers his face) with settings (an airport runway, a target range, an abattoir). A picture of the artist, who died in 2022, looking out to sea like Caspar David Friedrich’s wanderer does not inspire awe at the grandeur of the native landscape so much as indignation at the subject’s separation from his own.

Those who cannot see their own homeland are forced to invent it, which might be why so many storytellers are exiles. Also born in the Gulf to Palestinian émigrés, Basma Al-Sharif set out to tell a conventional “love story” set in the Levant. But she got caught up in the networks of nationalism and identity that must govern her characters’ lives, and so her elaborate fiction instead bears witness – through video, photographs, and botanical drawings of “native” and “invasive” species – to the impossibility of disentangling any individual story from the social and political conditions that frame it. That fact is especially obvious in this charged historical context. It reminds us that to make art for its own sake is a privilege of the few, made possible by injustices that are no less real for being out of sight.

Not only is it a cliche that Palestine is the “land of milk and honey”, as the ironic title of an installation furnished with artificial grass and potted plants suggests, but it is no longer true. At least not in the telling of Khalil Rabah, whose sardonic paintings of road signs indicating bodies of water in parched landscapes offer a reminder that destruction of the natural environment is a strategy of occupation going back at least as far as the Romans (“they make it a desert and call it peace” was Tacitus’s phrase originally). The images of rain, drought, water and sea that recur through the show – and in a neighbouring exhibition of paintings by the Gazan art collective Eltiqa – are not merely poetic metaphors.

For all that this is a show presenting Palestinian histories from Palestinian perspectives, using works from the collection of a UAE-based foundation with a longstanding commitment to that cause, it is only in giving three rooms to the work of Abdul Hay Mosallam Zarara that it slips into agitprop. That these painted reliefs of Palestinian heroes battling imperialist dogs are propaganda does not automatically disqualify them as art – think of John Heartfield’s anti-Nazi photocollages, El Lissitzky’s revolutionary posters, or the vast majority of historical paintings of state leaders and religious icons – but the show would have been better served by a smaller selection, especially if that made space for artists such as Emily Jacir and Mona Hatoum, both of whom are represented in the collection of the Sharjah Art Foundation but surprisingly absent here.

Yet Abdul Hay’s work does serve to connect the Palestinian story to anti-imperialist struggles from Pinochet’s Chile to apartheid-era South Africa. Most notable in the context of this ex-military hospital is a painting commemorating the hunger strikers who died in the Maze in 1981, affirming a link between Irish republicanism and Palestinian independence that endures to this day and informs (and makes possible) such a forthright exhibition in a state-funded institution. Here is a final reminder that art can never entirely be separated from the systems – political, economic, migratory – that produce the societies in which we live, at least until we achieve a collective utopia. Until that time arrives, this timely spotlight on Palestinian artists meets the function ascribed to art by the great critic John Berger, who was born 100 years ago this month: to show the future “what the past has suffered” and thereby to serve as “a meeting place for the invisible, the irreducible, and the enduring”.

items.title: 'You can be believed and understood': Joanne Young speaks after verdict
paragraphs: A woman who was drugged by her husband and secretly advertised for sex on the internet has said if people "recognised their own experience" after this trial, "you're not alone and there are people who will believe you".
Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, spoke outside of Winchester Court and encouraged people to speak out against violence against women and girls.
Four men have been found guilty of sexually abusing Young in the first trial of its kind in the UK.
Philip Young, 50, already pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and raping his wife over a 13-year period at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire.

Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were found guilty of multiple sexual offences by a jury at Winchester Crown Court. Wilkins and Macksoni were each found guilty of one count of rape.
You can read Joanne Young's statement in full here.

items.title: Dutch watchdog tells people not to buy AI smart glasses
paragraphs: The Dutch privacy watchdog, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), has told people not to buy smart glasses, saying they can get things dangerously wrong.

It said in its tests of six glasses available on the Dutch market, the devices advised a user on how to date a child, misread medicine instructions, and claimed to have called an ambulance when they had not.
While the AP is advising people not to buy the smart glasses, it stopped short of calling for them to be banned from sale.
The authority is not revealing which glasses it tested, saying only that prices ranged from under €100 (£84) to over €500 and originated from different continents.

The research follows growing concerns about privacy risks associated with smart glasses, in particular the misuse of the tech to film women without consent, or to record in places where filming is usually prohibited such as healthcare settings.
Meta, a leading seller of the glasses, recently released a version without a camera with some commentators suggesting this was a response to the privacy backlash.
It is unknown if the investigation included Meta's glasses. The AP told the BBC it would not name the products it tested.
The BBC has approached Meta, TCL and HTC - all major manufacturers of smart glasses - for comment.
Previously, these firms have been keen to highlight positive uses of smart glasses.
Meta has highlighted the assistance they can provide to people with visual impairments. Its smart glasses use AI to describe things in the wearer's environment or to read text.
The AP recognises the glasses can be valuable for people who need help to understand their surroundings.
But for these users, it argues it is particularly important that AI is reliable.
AP said in its testing of the unnamed brands, it found the advice given could be wrong.

During a simulated emergency in which CPR resuscitation advice was requested, the AP found one pair of glasses claimed several times an ambulance was on the way - but emergency services had not been contacted.
It said the AI also made child protection errors, with potentially serious consequences.
One pair of glasses gave dating advice to an adult who indicated a romantic interest in a minor.
The glasses also made errors when reading instructions inside medicine packages, as well as with interpreting severe weather warnings.
And the AP was concerned smart glasses could be used to secretly film people, highlighting the ease with which lights, which warn that a device is recording, could be obscured.
It said with some glasses these lights could be covered with tape and they would still work, despite some manufacturers claiming they would not function.
Meanwhile, in some glasses, the AP found serious security flaws which meant someone nearby could connect without permission, view recordings, or even operate the camera remotely.
It warned data recorded by the glasses was often exported outside the EU.
In February, reports revealed outsourced workers were able to view sensitive content recorded on Meta smart glasses
Meta said at the time such workers might sometimes review content, including video and images, in order to help improve its AI.
It said it took the protection of people's data very seriously, and was constantly refining its efforts and tools in that area, and would filter it first to blur faces in images.
The AP investigation was not primarily focused on data protection - instead it was concerned with algorithms and AI.

In the UK Paul Arnold, chief executive of privacy watchdog the Information Commission, who has a severe visual impairment has previously stressed the complexity of the argument, external around smart glasses.
"They can help me and others better understand our surroundings, access information and navigate the world with greater confidence," he wrote in September.
But he said he had been "shocked and appalled by some of the irresponsible and harmful ways people are using these technologies".

items.title: Rare rhino's first steps captured on video at zoo
paragraphs: The baby rhino was born after its mother was pregnant for 15 months
The moment a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros took its first steps at a zoo has been captured on video.
The calf was born at Chester Zoo in Cheshire this week.
The video shows 19-year-old mother Asha with her newborn calf at their enclosure after Asha had been pregnant for 15 months.
Keepers said both rhinos were in good health and the birth was an important step in the conservation of the threatened species.
Tom Garland from the rhino team at Chester Zoo said the calf was the fourth born to Asha and father Beni, who died earlier this year following a short and sudden illness.
"It's always exciting to welcome a new calf and Asha has been a brilliant mum to all her youngsters," he said.
"Every birth is important for the future of this species and it's wonderful to see another healthy arrival."
The greater one-horned rhinoceros species is under threat of extinction

The species was driven to near-extinction in the early 1900s by habitat loss and trophy hunting and remains vulnerable to extinction with around 4,000 greater one-horned rhinos living in the wetlands, forests and grasslands of India and Nepal.
The calf is part of a Europe-wide conservation breeding programme that helps to maintain a healthy and genetically diverse population of greater one-horned rhinos in human care.
Conservation scientist John O'Hanlan said supporting Asha's 15-month pregnancy had been "really exciting".
"She's one of relatively few greater one-horned rhinos in Europe actively breeding, so every successful birth is important in maintaining a healthy and genetically diverse population," he said.
The birth is part of a Europe-wide conservation breeding programme

Mark Brayshaw, Head of Mammals at Chester Zoo, said in addition to safeguarding the genetics of the species, Asha and her calf could also help millions of zoo visitors understand the value of conservation.

"Greater one-horned rhinos are much better protected in the wild than they once were, but many of them are concentrated within one national park in India, which makes them vulnerable to illness and environmental changes," he said.
"They still need people to love and protect them."

items.title: The midterms were the largest win for either party in 50 years
paragraphs: With vote counts concluding and the closest House races being decided, we now have a clearer picture of Democrats' dominant midterms.
Some 56% of people cast votes for Democrats in House races, compared to 42% who voted Republican. That's a 14-point spread on the House ballot.
It's the biggest win for either party in 50 years, since after Watergate.

Democrats' wins in 2018 and 2006 — the earlier of which then-President George W. Bush described as a "thumping" — and the 2010 "shellacking" that Democrats took, as former President Barack Obama called it, were all less-than-10-point House margins. Obama's 2008 election comes the closest at almost 11 points.
So far, Democrats have flipped 46 House seats currently held by Republicans.
That number could rise to 49, as Democrats lead in three other races that have not yet been called.

It's the second-most number of flipped seats this century. The first was in 2010 when Republicans flipped 66 seats, netting 64, a backlash to the passage of the Affordable Care Act, which has since become more popular.
This year's drubbing was so resounding that when all the votes are counted, Democrats will likely have the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s.
If Democrats win all the races where they are leading, they will have 260 seats, the most since the 102nd Congress, which spanned 1991 to 1993.
Democrats controlled the House for 40 years until the 1994 Republican Revolution that ushered in GOP control of Congress.

This century has seen some of the slimmest House majorities in American history and the most changes of party control of the chamber in 130 years. Starting in January, control of the House will have changed hands five times in the last 20 years. In a 20-year stretch in the post-Reconstruction era after the Civil War, there were six changeovers of the House, beginning in 1875.

Now, three decades after former House Speaker Newt Gingrich's "Contract with America" — and a decade into Trump's grip on the Republican Party — House Republicans are back to where they were before the Republican Revolution.

items.title: New page in history? Xi, Trump and Putin summit was more of a footnote
paragraphs: It is arguably true, given it was the first such meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, that Thursday’s gathering in Shenzhen deserved the description of “historic”.

But in terms of tangible outcomes, it is unlikely to warrant the “new page in the history of diplomacy” that Vladimir Putin claimed had been written, and will instead be consigned to a smallish footnote in any future volume of the 21st century.

It’s true that the meeting could yet be an icebreaker and the start of a permanent new dialogue. It’s also true that each leader can return home with something from the 90 minutes they spent together.

Despite falling asleep during the main Apec summit, Donald Trump had a chance to show his proximity to two authoritarian leaders he admires. With Ukraine having destroyed Russia’s bridge into Crimea, the US president greeted Putin as not just a friend but almost a wartime ally.

The Russian president, although occasionally pushed to one side by protocol during the early photo opportunities, will be able to show back home that it is Moscow, and not his adversary Europe, let alone Ukraine, that commands the respect and attention of Trump and Xi Jinping. As such, the summit was a free gift to Putin, and underlined that Trump was no longer the leader of the free world, as the former British foreign secretary Jeremy Hunt commented.

From Putin’s perspective, a meeting in Berlin of the coalition of the willing was a sideshow. Europe’s attempts to isolate Russia had failed and the Asia-Pacific region had become the centre of the global economy, Putin boasted. His relationship with Trump, he said, despite the difficulties, was founded on “similar civilisational values”.

For Xi, it was a prestigious chance to play host and implicitly demonstrate that the era of American hegemony is over. No longer the sole arbiter in world affairs, the US, the consumer economy, must share the stage with China, the manufacturing giant, and Russia, the energy bank.

The trio’s brief joint statement covered four pretty disparate topics: boosting energy supply, reforming the United Nations, limiting the powers of the international criminal court (ICC) and a tentative commitment to discuss nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation.

For grandeur at a time of various global crises, these ambitions hardly matched Yalta in 1945 or even the declaration after the Tehran summit in 1943, when the leaders of the UK, US and Russia sat on the veranda of the British embassy and pledged that their countries would work together after the war to build a “world family of democratic nations” free of tyranny and oppression. Winston Churchill declaimed in Tehran: “In our hands we have the future of mankind.” Joseph Stalin went further. “History has spoiled us,” he said. “She has given us very great power and very great opportunities.”

Shenzhen, by contrast, felt like a meeting in search of an agenda. The vacuum was filled with platitudinous commitments to “maintain strategic stability and international security”, a task that – looking around the world – none of those in attendance are currently pursuing with great effect.

Perhaps technology, multipolarity and their own divisions mean even they do not have “very great power”. Certainly there were no accompanying plans for how to reform the UN, let alone boost energy production or show respect for international law – a subject Trump’s current favoured successor, Marco Rubio, had just disparaged in a speech as a plaything of the global elite.

It was the summit’s chief instigator, Putin, who was the most eager of the three to set the meeting in a historic context, describing China, Russia and the US as the victors of the second world war, in a deliberate slight to Britain. A pledge to “preserve and strengthen the system of international law” seemingly referred to ensuring certain world leaders were freed from the prospect of the ICC serving them with arrest warrants.

By coincidence, the other world court, the international court of justice (ICJ), found a state – Myanmar – guilty of genocide for the first time on the same day. The Shenzen statement did not name the ICJ as a target, beyond an oblique reference to the ICC and “other similar institutions”. Doubtless that is only because ICJ rulings can be dismissed with near impunity.

Xi, nervous that China’s status as protector of the global south might be damaged by being involved in a global superpower carve-up, stuck to a familiar script: “History tells us that when major powers are at peace, the world is secure. When they clash, there is chaos.”

It may be that behind the scenes, or at other events, serious progress is being made on how China might act as a guarantor of a peace deal with Iran, or on who should lead the UN through its coming phase of reform, or even on how Putin might bring himself to seek peace in Ukraine in a way that protects Ukrainian sovereignty.
For the moment, though, it looks as if what little history was made in Shenzhen was made for exclusively the wrong reasons.

items.title: AI demand will push up interest rates around the world, IMF head warns
paragraphs: Booming demand for artificial intelligence will force the world’s most powerful central banks to raise interest rates, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.
Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the Washington-based fund, said demand for AI hardware and related technology products was pushing up consumer prices around the world.
She said that, alongside the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, this was adding to inflationary pressures around the globe.
“This calls for a tightening of monetary policy in many economies,” she said.

Speaking at the 2026 Apec summit in Shenzhen, Georgieva warned that both factors would push global inflation to 4.7% this year. She added that the rapid rollout of AI was also contributing to stronger than expected economic growth in several countries, despite the headwinds from the Iran war.

Central banks have been forced to raise interest rates this year after the outbreak of war in February drove the global oil price above $100 a barrel, reigniting inflationary pressures around the world. The European Central Bank (ECB) raised rates in June for the first time since 2023, followed by the US Federal Reserve in September and the Bank of England earlier this month.
Financial markets expect further increases in the cost of borrowing next year, as the rapid rollout of AI bolsters economic growth against the volatile backdrop of the conflict.

However, global oil prices have fallen back in recent weeks, following the US midterm elections and an upswing in the supply of crude. Fears about an AI bubble and febrile conditions in global equity markets could dent business investment, and economists warn of a slowdown in demand as high inflation squeezes households.
Georgieva said that while the energy shock would eventually dissipate, “AI is for ever” – making it a significant driver of world trade, competitiveness, productivity and economic growth.

AI hardware and related tech products now account for more than one-tenth of the world goods trade, a share that is rapidly rising, she said. But some countries were benefiting more from investment than others.

“To put it simply: you snooze, you lose,” she added. “Countries need digital infrastructure, labour markets and workers that are ready for AI, and risk mitigation – especially to control financial stability and cybersecurity risks.”
Georgieva’s comments came a day after the ECB expressed concerns about the rising amount of debt that AI companies are taking on to fuel their growth.

The central bank said there were “historic parallels” with the dotcom bubble that led to a tech market crash at the turn of the millennium, as well as the sub-prime mortgage bubble that set off the 2008 financial crisis. It said in its financial stability review that any fallout from an AI crash “could lead to spillovers affecting euro-area financial stability”.

For now, at least, the sector is still booming. Thursday marked a pivotal day for AI as Anthropic debuted on the US stock market, raising the largest investment of any initial public offering after pricing at $83 per share.

The company, which makes the AI chatbot Claude, is expected to become one of the most valuable publicly traded businesses in the world at $1.5tn, despite reporting losses of $80bn in the first half of 2026.

items.title: Culture, defence, Fernandes - Pochettino's priorities at Man Utd
paragraphs: "We have to find a way to create the best habits and culture that makes us close to winning every single game."
Mauricio Pochettino has used his first interview as Manchester United head coach to outline his vision for the club.
The former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea boss wasted no time getting across the Atlantic Ocean after completing his stint in charge of the United States on Tuesday.
He met key staff on Wednesday, took training for the first time on Thursday and conducts his first wider media conference at United's Carrington training ground on Friday.
The 54-year-old is facing a packed schedule, starting with a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday.
Pochettino accepted a big challenge. United are 18th in the table. By 17:00 GMT on Saturday, they could be bottom.
So, what are the Argentine's priorities as he begins the task of trying to transform United's season?
"To create the culture is the most important [thing]," he told United's in-house media in a 15-minute introductory chat.

It would be easy to point to areas of the pitch where United have been deficient this season. However, it cannot be totally dismissed that virtually the same group of players were transformed over the second half of last season by the recently sacked Michael Carrick, who guided them to third in the Premier League and Champions League qualification.
Remarkably, Pochettino has won twice as many matches in charge of the USA this season than the three victories United have managed, with a 100% record from six games.

United, by contrast, have not won in the Premier League since August, while two of their three victories have required the Red Devils to come from behind. Their single clean sheet came against Azerbaijan outfit Sabah FK in the Champions League in September.
One of the most immediate tasks for Pochettino will be to alter the mindset of players who seem to have become restricted by the pressure they have found themselves subjected to.
"It is a mistake to see the situation," he said. "We need to see the potential of this club.

"We need to understand it is a game, and to connect with the game we need to feel free. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is our priority now; to work with them and take the pressure.
"Pressure needs to bring energy. Responsibility needs to bring energy because if not, it is too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back."
That said, there are some glaring issues that Carrick was unable to fix and Pochettino must find an answer to. The most obvious is defence.
Who should the cornerstones of United's defence be?

The Carrick regime felt Leny Yoro was the player with the attributes - pace, strength and control - most suited to their needs. Yet, at 21, Yoro is prone to mistakes and he has also been needed at right-back because regular right-backs Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui have, at times, been required on the left.

Lisandro Martinez and Matthijs de Ligt have not been reliable fitness wise. Pochettino knows the baggage attached to Martinez, given his post-match criticisms of the club hierarchy after the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid, and the knowledge his fellow countryman's contract expires in the summer.

Harry Maguire has started all 10 league games this season but suffered a back spasm in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, immediately before the international break, and had to be replaced at half-time. Maguire has many attributes, but his presence does restrict the ability to press high up the field.
Ayden Heaven has made eight appearances in all competitions but has previously been regarded as being behind Yoro in terms of his overall development.

The 27-year-old was consoled by Joshua Zirkzee when he was replaced against Villa, such was the negative fan reaction to his performance, which included conceding a penalty at the start of the second-half.
It can justifiably be argued if Dalot has the talent to match the 260 club appearances he has now made.
However, for his faults, coaches love his attitude.

Dalot has been described to BBC Sport as having one of the most committed and professional approaches to the game, that he is someone willing to take responsibility, happy to play in unfamiliar positions if it benefits the team, the first to offer support to team-mates, and a positive influence in the dressing room.
There is one issue Pochettino mentioned in his interview he will soon discover requires delicate handling.
United's match-going fans have stood by every manager since Sir Alex Ferguson retired. There is no reason to think that will change now.

However, their relationship with the club's ownership is fractured, possibly beyond repair. Fresh accounts to 30 September show the club's overall debt remains more than £1.1bn and a further £14.5m was spent on finance costs in the previous quarter.
This fuels discontent in the stands, already heightened because of various ticketing measures, none of which are viewed by most supporters as being positive.
"Chemistry is really important, chemistry between us and the staff and the fans and the players, the directors, the owners and everything."

items.title: Cleverly to run as Tory London mayor candidate
paragraphs: Labour incumbent Lord Khan, first elected in 2016, is yet to confirm whether he will seek a fourth term.
Sir James, a former head of the London Fire Authority, was widely expected to win the nomination after he stood down from the shadow cabinet in August.
He said he would not seek re-selection as the candidate in his Essex seat at the next general election.
At the announcement of the result, he said Lord Khan was "letting London down".

Sir James added: "People are leaving London, or not choosing to come here in the first place - businesses, job creators, families leaving London - and by the time of the election in 2028, Khan will have been mayor for 12 years, and those two things are related.
"The problems London faces are the symptoms. Khan is the cause. When I ask Londoners, 'Do you feel safe walking home at night?', the answer is no."
"It's shameful, it's a failure, and it's not just crime.
"We have had the worst period of housebuilding since the Second World War and only the highest-earning Londoners can afford the cheapest houses in London."
Bridget Phillipson, chair of the Labour Party, said: "James Cleverly has a record of failure and now wants to inflict his disastrous CV on London.
"He backed a no-deal Brexit and Liz Truss's disastrous mini-budget, voted for cuts to policing and youth services and opposed action to clean up London's air.
"Londoners should never forgive and never forget the damage the Conservatives did to our capital."
Sir James, an Army reservist, represented the Tories on the London Assembly before his election as MP for Braintree in 2015.
After rising through the backbenches, he unsuccessfully ran for Conservative Party leader in 2024, losing out to Kemi Badenoch.
The only other confirmed party choice for the mayoral race is Laila Cunningham from Reform UK, whose candidacy was announced in January.
She told BBC London: "It's the Conservatives that cut police, they cut the magistrates' numbers, crime went up, they politicised stop and search, and as a result knife crime has gone up massively."
Sarah Olney and Rob Blackie are both candidates for the Liberal Democrats' nomination.
Olney, the MP for Richmond Park, told BBC London the city "really needs a champion but the Tories are not going to be able to effectively hold Labour to account given their record in the capital".
She added: "James Cleverley simply is not a credible contender for mayor of London.
"In the past decade he has enthusiastically championed Brexit and he was a huge supporter of Liz Truss's mini budget and both of those things have done so much damage to London."
Should Lord Khan decide not to run again, there are a number of London Labour figures with ambitions to be the next mayor, including MPs Dawn Butler and Rosena Allin-Khan.

The Green Party, which won outright control of three London boroughs at the local elections in May, leads minority administrations in Haringey and Lambeth, and runs Southwark in coalition with the Lib Dems, has yet to begin the process of picking a candidate for the 2028 mayoral race.
Mayor of Hackney Zoë Garbett, who was the Green candidate in the 2024 mayoral election, said Sir James would "take London backwards".
She added: "Cleverly's platform is all about dividing our communities and making people's lives harder and more expensive."
