items.title: James Bond's favourite pen is 40% off right now
paragraphs: You've probably noticed that James Bond has been in the news a lot this week. And you probably know why: it's because then pen he uses in 1995's Goldeneye is currently £6.39 off at Amazon! What's that? The new James Bond actor has finally been announced? Oh, right. I see. Still, good news about the pen.

Yes, Yes, Robert Pattinson is James Bond, etc. etc. As a fan, I have various thoughts on the matter. But while various brands have reacted to the announcement, we can't say for sure which brands Pattinson's Bond himself will favour. Will he still wear a Tom Ford suit? Will he still wear an Omega watch? And most importantly, will he still write his Christmas cards with a Parker pen?

Pierce Brosnan did – until he clicked the end four times too many and activated the internal grenade. And if you want to make like the '90s Bond and use the same pen (with its explosive features mercifully disabled), it's currently 40% off at Amazon UK, bringing the price down from £16.37 to £9.99.
In the US, meanwhile, the discount isn't quite as generous, but it's still 28% off, down from $19.99 to $14.99.
If you're looking for more delectable writing implements, take a look at the most beautiful pens of all time

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He reports on the worlds of design, branding and lifestyle tech, and has covered several industry events including Milan Design Week, OFFF Barcelona and Adobe Max in Los Angeles. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

items.title: Australian music industry rejects ‘divide and conquer’ proposal to give musicians exemption from AI scraping
paragraphs: The music industry has declared it will not accept an AI carveout deal that leaves other creative sectors behind, rejecting a reported proposal to give musicians special treatment while allowing big tech to train on other copyrighted material – described by David Pocock as a “divide and conquer strategy”.

The trade union representing writers and creatives is “alarmed” at a proposal to let AI companies train on Australian data if they buy a permit, an idea also strongly rebuffed by the Coalition and Greens.
The Albanese government would not comment on the reported proposal but senior ministers have raised concerns about current copyright law in recent days, hinting reforms were needed.

Annabelle Herd, the chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria), and Claire Pullen, the CEO of the Australian Writers’ Guild, said the creative community – which this week launched a major AI campaign – would remain united in rejecting such changes.
“I can’t see any creative workers leaving their colleagues behind,” Pullen said.

The Australian Financial Review reported on Thursday the government was considering a copyright change under which AI companies would buy permits to train on Australian content but that music may be exempted. Such a proposal would be more in line with AI companies after Anthropic suggested a model of “conditional approval” to scrape content unless a rightsholder objected, and OpenAI told a parliamentary committee it would “potentially” support paying into a fund for creators.

Guardian Australia was not able to independently verify details of the proposal. One senior member of the creative community, involved in copyright discussions with government, said they had heard some details of such an idea – but others said they had not and doubted the Albanese government would seriously entertain it. One source in the AI industry, who declined to be named, said they would welcome such a plan.
Herd said she was unaware of the proposal before Thursday but the music industry would not desert other creatives.
“Had we been consulted, we would have advised this scheme is unnecessary, unworkable and designed to suit the commercial interests of AI companies, not protect creators,” she told Guardian Australia.
“Our position is unchanged: we stand with the rest of the creative and media industries.”

Herd and Pullen said such a scheme would be difficult to implement technically, questioning how content such as movies or TV shows – which combine copyrighted elements such as music, video and screenwriting – would be treated if just one element was exempted from AI scraping.

“This just seems like such a convoluted path, when AI companies have had an open invitation to sit down and negotiate for years,” Pullen said. “We have been working with government to come up with a model since 2024. We’ve come up with solutions and tech has steadfastly refused to even talk.”

While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has declared it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, and that artists “need to be compensated”, some AI companies have argued it is too difficult to make individual licensing deals under existing copyright law.
The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance said it would be “alarmed” at the reported proposal and demanded protections promised by Albanese “must apply to all creative sectors”.

While government MPs declined to comment on the report, senior Labor figures have recently begun more forcefully pointing to what they claim are shortfalls in copyright law in the AI age – despite major rightsholder groups rejecting the need for change. The industry minister, Tim Ayres, on Tuesday said “the status quo is no good” for creative workers, a line repeated by the acting prime minister, Richard Marles, on Thursday. Marles added on News24: “People are being ripped off”.
The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, also used newly strengthened language when contacted, promising “certainty and strong protections for Australian artists”.
“Right now, the work of Australian creatives is being used without their consent or payment,” a spokesperson for Rowland said.
“The government has long advocated for tech companies to strike commercial deals with Australian artists, and we will continue to do so.”
Potentially carving out musicians did not win support among parliamentarians, either.
The shadow attorney general, Michaelia Cash, claimed such a proposal would “divide the rightsholders”.
“This ham-fisted tactic should be strongly resisted. Everyone who owns property should have the same right for it not to be stolen.”
Pocock also described it as “some sort of divide and conquer strategy”.

“It’s hard to know what [Labor] are actually doing at the moment. The joint select committee hasn’t even given its report to the government, and we’re hearing all sorts of whispers about what the government is planning.”
The Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young urged the government not to meet copyright demands requested by big tech.

“What they’re asking Australia to do actually is to undermine copyright the world over,” she told News 24. “Australia will become known as the Cayman Islands for AI if we allow this loophole to happen.
“I say, don’t be that stupid. Stand up to them.”

items.title: An elevator, a brick wall and a bathroom: scientists use gravity to send ‘practically unblockable’ message
paragraphs: Australian scientists have used gravity as a means of communication, in a proof-of-concept experiment involving a snail-paced 1950s elevator, a brick wall and a men’s bathroom.

Physicists at the University of Queensland have used gravity to transmit a “practically unblockable” message about 70cm through a brick wall, by sending an elevator up and down between two floors and measuring changes in the gravitational field as a result of the movement.
The research, published in the journal Science Advances, involved a sensitive detection device known as a gravimeter, which was set up on the floor of a men’s bathroom adjacent to the lift.

The gravimeter was able to detect the position of the elevator’s 1.8-tonne counterweight as it moved between two levels – representing 0 and 1 in binary code – which enabled the scientists to send a message.

The researchers chose to transmit the word “gravity”, or 1000111 1110010 1100001 1110110 1101001 1110100 1111001 in binary code. At a transmission rate of one bit (digit) per minute, the single word took nearly an hour to send.

The scientists say that while gravitational communication is currently far from usable given its extremely slow speed, an advantage is that it is a “practically unblockable wireless communication scheme”.

“Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” said co-author Dr Charles Woffinden, of UQ’s school of mathematics and physics. “Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with wifi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.”

Study co-author Prof Matthew Davis told Guardian Australia: “At the moment, it’s very hard to imagine how it could be practically useful.” But he added that the experiment was “theoretically interesting enough that it was worth doing”.

To put into perspective how slow the message transmission was, Davis said that Nasa’s Voyager 1 spacecraft, which after 49 years of travel had just reached a distance of one light-day away, could “communicate with Earth at a faster data rate than our communication concept”.
According to Davis, the new method of communicating could theoretically occur at ranges of up to 500 metres and at a rate 15 times faster, if more sensitive quantum gravity sensors were used.

The idea for the elevator study arose from a project to develop a contactless weighbridge – which would use quantum sensors to detect changes in the strength of gravity due to a passing truck, allowing scientists to determine the mass of a large vehicle.

Classical gravimeters can be thought of as a mass on a spring. “If you stretch the spring, the mass bounces up and down at a certain rate, which is determined by the spring and the gravitational field,” Davis said. “If the gravitational field changes ever so slightly, the rate at which it bounces back and forth changes.
“Quantum sensors are still under development
“Sometimes doing physics leads in unexpected ways and it’s a bit of fun … you get to do quirky things on the side. It’s one of the great joys of science to have stuff like this happen.”

Other near-unblockable methods of communication – involving neutrinos or gravitational waves – have been proposed “but these approaches are somewhat hindered by the difficulty in generating a measurable signal”, the scientists note.
The physicists conducted the research in UQ’s Parnell physics building, which is also home to the world’s longest-running science experiment – the pitch drop experiment, which began in 1927.

items.title: ‘Communities are really angry’: how Australia’s datacentre opposition has gone from marginal to mainstream in five months
paragraphs: When Heather Champion raised a council motion in March opposing a massive new gas plant to power a large datacentre in the Southern Highlands of New South Wales, it failed to pass.
Five months later, when the local councillor for Wingecaribee raised a new motion calling for the federal government to implement a moratorium on new datacentres, it passed unanimously.
“I think the council’s change in perspective is a direct result of the change in sentiment in the community,” Champion says.
The shift highlights grassroots successes in pushing back on datacentre construction and how those wins are inspiring other communities to take similar action.
In May, Guardian Australia reported on three datacentre projects across the country – Hazelmere in Western Australia, West Footscray in Victoria, and Lane Cove in New South Wales.

Since the report, the project proposals have been withdrawn in WA and NSW, and NextDC’s M3 expansion in West Footscray has been stalled after Jemena, the power provider, delayed the installation of taller power poles after the community outcry.

Lane Cove Responsible Planning spokesperson, Sasha Titchkosky, says after the success of having the Goodman Group’s Mars datacentre in Lane Cove withdrawn, she is working with communities in western Sydney and the Southern Highlands on their own campaigns.
Titchkosky says by working together, the groups send a strong signal to industry and politicians that they need to do better.

As it stands, councils play a role in approving datacentres in some states, but in others, such as NSW and Victoria, fast-tracked approvals skip the local council stage. The federal government has proposed rules that would from next year set mandatory minimum requirements for large datacentres, including how projects manage energy, water, costs, community engagement, location and workforce impacts.
“Just saying they’re going to put in place regulations, but still allowing datacentres to be approved … isn’t good enough.
“They [need to] either put a pause on approvals or basically say that everyone who gets approved now will be subject to the regulations when they come in force.”
Campaigners across Australia are sharing notes and tips through WhatsApp, using the platform to organise rallies and discuss new proposals.

In Victoria, a community wiki site displays a map of locations of datacentre proposals, the community groups organising around them, and links to campaign tips from US groups that successfully lobbied against the sector in the recent midterm elections.

Titchkosky has been in contact with campaigners in the Southern Highlands, where an application refusal for one of three gas plants capable of producing 673MW of power in total is being challenged in the NSW land and environment court. The applicant, Cloud Carrier, wants to use the gas plant to power a “data campus” in Moss Vale with AI “at its core”.
“We’ve been in touch with Lane Cove for quite a long time.
“We are sharing skills, messages – it’s very lateral and it’s very informal,” Champion says of the community networks’ organic growth.
They share what works and what doesn’t work – and what might work in one area may not be suitable in another, she says.
“[Lane Cove’s] circumstances are just so completely different but in some ways that’s been really helpful … having [our] voices combined does provide some breadth.”
The groups are also working with communities in western Sydney to build their capacity to take on new centres planned for the area.

Mandy Ottaviano, a masters of sustainability student at the University of Sydney who has been researching community action against datacentres in Australia says there is a “real desire” for the groups to connect with each other, but there is no formal organisation.
“What we’re not seeing a lot of yet is [non-government organisations] stepping in and bridging that gap in terms of coordinating those groups in a meaningful way together,” she says.
“We haven’t yet seen any emergence of a national kind of coalition.”

The chief executive officer for Data Centres Australia, Belinda Dennett, acknowledges there is “more interest from the community” in datacentre development than ever before, and datacentre companies are stepping up community consultation.
“This ranges from community information sessions, door knocking, newsletters, websites, hotline phone numbers and social media updates,” Dennett says.

“Third parties delivering energy, broadband and water infrastructure are also an important part of building community support so we also encourage more coordination and information sharing between parties.”

While state and federal governments appear to be reacting to the growing community concerns over datacentres – some states are introducing new rules and the federal government is set to follow suit early next year – campaigners are concerned the changes don’t go far enough.

The New South Wales parliament’s long-running inquiry into datacentres released its report earlier this month, with the committee voting to remove two contentious recommendations: that the NSW government advocates for a moratorium on new datacentre developments until new obligations are in place; and to advocate for the new federal rules to be applied retrospectively.
The chair, Greens MP Abigail Boyd, was the only committee member to vote in support of the recommendations.
“It appears that both the Labor and Liberal parties remain in hock to the industry talking points,” Boyd said in the chair’s foreword in the report.

“I was particularly disappointed that both Labor and Liberal parties voted together against a pause on data centre approvals until sufficiently robust and legally binding obligations are in place, and similarly voted against advocating for data centres currently in the planning pipeline to have to comply with any rules that are currently being contemplated.”

Boyd said the delay to the rules coming in federally “makes clear the coordinated effort by governments and industry to avoid having to comply with even the most moderate of environmental and social obligations”.
Champion says she was “really frustrated” the recommendations were removed.
“We agreed between the group of us we would call for a moratorium, and all the community groups know that’s what’s needed.
“It feels like a real cop-out to be honest.”

Titchkosky says it is “clear as day where the two major parties” sit on datacentres – and questions whether the move may prove politically destructive, given datacentre disquiet played a pivotal role in voter sentiment in the US midterms.

“They’re ultimately prepared to sell out communities for multinational corporate interests,” she says. “I think we are going to see the same issues play out in Victoria and NSW in our upcoming elections as they were in the US midterms.
“Communities are really angry about this.”

items.title: Adobe’s democratisation of design doesn’t have to be the death of human creativity
paragraphs: A week on from my Adobe MAX 2026 experience, I'm left more conflicted than ever about the democratisation of design. While post-MAX clarity has calmed the excitement of Sneaks and new Adobe software announcements, an uncertain existentialism still lingers. Finally, everyone has the freedom to create, but in the same breath, oh dear... everyone has the freedom to create.

Add Adobe's balls to the wall AI adoption and it feels like we're snowballing into a mass slopathon. Throughout MAX, I am constantly assured AI is only there for those who want it, but I'm also hyperaware that its siren song is far too tempting for certain creatives. It all boils down to one question. In the age of democratised creativity, what defines real design?

MAX made one thing abundantly clear – Adobe is for everyone. Whether you're a novice creative looking to jazz up a poster, a seasoned influencer wanting clickworthy content or an industry vet trying to adapt to the ever-demanding creative industry, Adobe is, by its own positioning, your best friend.

This is where cracks already begin to form. Classically trained graphic designers, web developers and old-school content creators who learned through education or self-taught graft are left feeling cheated while new-gen creatives have it all at their fingertips. It's not childish to feel that things are a little unfair. There is value to the blood, sweat and tears of art created over time – something AI appears to extinguish.

And while on the surface, creativity for everyone feels like a utopian dream, the addition of AI makes me worried. Of course, jobs are sacrificed under the guise of saving time and budget, and when everyone can create, where do we find value in creativity?

Can a concept half-baked by a computer hold the same emotional nuance as human-made work? I fall in the camp of no. But art has always been subjective – who's to say an AI-generated design has less value when, at its core, it was sparked by a human idea? A better question is, where do we draw the line?

It's easy to make Adobe the fall guy for the rise in AI slop, but it's just as much a matter of how we use its tools. At Sneaks, I witnessed a number of genuinely innovative tools, like Project Deep Brush – an AI-powered lighting-aware tool for Photoshop – that proved there's a distinct difference between full-send gen AI and the odd tool to make your everyday workflow a little smoother. Adobe developers aren't sitting in front of an evil AI cauldron preying on the downfall of human design as we know it. Behind the scenes, there are glimmers of hope.

If used in a measured way, I believe AI tools can be an extension of creativity, but with no constraint other than the moral, and Adobe churning out corner-cutting AI tools with reckless abandon, it's no surprise there's slop everywhere. New creatives are hungry to push the confines of what creativity can be – AI is proposed to them as a wacky friend that can do it all. The role of 'creative' is in a state of flux, and with a new generation redefining what creativity means, artistic value has never been more abstract.

A repeated argument for Adobe's influx of AI innovations was the creative industry's increasing demand for content. A graphic designer may now be expected to be a master of motion design, web development and social media with fewer resources and even less time. These tools are merely a part of evolution – embrace them or get left behind.

But from the sidelines, I watch in horror as the creative industry eats itself over and over again. More content requires faster output. Faster output is aided by time-saving AI tools. Saved time means more space to create more content to feed the hungry attention economy. We're creating more, but as a result, we're losing a sense of quality and control. And when creativity is democratised, I worry valuable work gets lost in the shuffle.

I worry I'm a snob – that my jaded opinions are stuck in a creative world that no longer exists – but despite my discomfort, I remain hopeful. Creative democracy has its value. Accessibility is better than ever (given you can afford an Adobe subscription), and voices that may not have had the confidence to create are now empowered to do so thanks to Adobe's tools.

But what of the classic designer, like my father, who has spent decades curating their craft, only to have AI do it in seconds? It's an uncomfortable reality, but change is inevitable. To the jaded, fearful or downright nihilistic creative, I implore you to continue creating on your own terms, whether that means dipping a toe into AI tools or outright denunciation of the technology. Amidst the formulaic sea of AI, it's the quality, human-made content that will be celebrated.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

items.title: Fiona Harvey, who allegedly inspired Baby Reindeer, to appear in court on harassment charge
paragraphs: A woman who allegedly inspired the stalker character Martha in the hit Netflix drama Baby Reindeer is to appear at Harrow Crown Court on charges of racially aggravated harassment without violence.
Fiona Harvey, 61, is accused of sending several emails and three voicemails including antisemitic material to lawyer Mark Lewis, between 4 September and 9 October 2025.
During a hearing at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court on Thursday, the court heard that Lewis initially believed Harvey was a potential client.
Harvey of Camden, north London, did not indicate a plea, but elected for a Crown Court trial.
The charge is an either-way offence, which means it can be heard in either a magistrates' court or Crown Court.
She will next appear at Harrow Crown Court for a pre-trial preparation hearing on 17 December.
Harvey has previously identified herself as the woman on whom Martha is based, after the release of Richard Gadd's Emmy Award-winning series in 2024.
She is suing the streamer £128m for defamation, negligence and privacy violations, arguing that that Netflix told "brutal lies" about her to over 50 million viewers around the world.
Netflix denies the claim, which will be heard in front of a jury on May 18, 2027, at the US District Court for the Central District of California.

items.title: Wading bird called Phil tracked in epic migration to Siberia and back
paragraphs: Scientists say Phil's extraordinary travels highlight the importance of protecting the world's wetlands, which are havens for millions of migratory birds each year.

Dr Nigel Clark, of the conservation charity, The Wash Wader Research Group, said The Wash is the UK's single most important coastal wetland for migratory waders, with spectacular numbers seen in autumn and winter.
"Tracking birds like Phil the Godwit shows us how connected the Wash is with the rest of the flyway," he said.
Jeff Kew, RSPB Coastal Advisor, said many migratory bird species cross borders, depending on a whole network of wetlands along the way.
That's why it's so important to look after these special places."
Bar-tailed godwits are wading birds of similar size to pigeons, but with long bills and legs.

They are regarded as one of nature's long-distance endurance athletes, with one subspecies making the longest known non-stop migration of any bird, flying 8,425 miles (13,559km) from Alaska to New Zealand.
Phil's journey included a handful of stops to rest and refuel.
He will now spend the winter relaxing with thousands of other wading birds at the Snettisham Nature Reserve in Norfolk.

items.title: What is at stake at the EU-UK summit in Brussels?
paragraphs: The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc.
It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa.
The gathering, which follows up last year’s inaugural EU-UK summit in London, was scheduled for July but postponed when Keir Starmer resigned.
The two sides hope to announce three deals, which were initiated under Starmer’s government.

First, a food and drink agreement that will remove a lot of Brexit red tape on animal and plant products, making it easier to trade meats, cheese, wine and flowers. To secure the deal, which is not expected to take effect until 2028, the UK will align with EU standards, meaning the government, for example, must abandon a planned ban on foie gras imports.

A second agreement will link the British emissions trading system with its bigger EU cousin, restoring a link severed by Brexit. It is a significant step for industry because EU and UK businesses will be exempt from each other’s charges on high-carbon imports such as steel, cement and electricity. This agreement also requires alignment with relevant EU rules.

The third deal is the most contentious: a youth mobility scheme that will give those aged 18-30 the right to live, work, travel and study on both sides of the Channel for up to three years. The scheme may not be up and running until 2030 – bad news for anyone in their late 20s.

With less than 24 hours before the summit begins, two big issues remain open. EU negotiators want to ensure EU students pay the UK rate of university tuition, around four or five times lower than international fees. The two sides also disagree over how many people would be allowed to take part: the EU wants 100,000 visas a year, but the UK is looking at 50,000 to 80,000 to keep migration numbers down.
To maximise its leverage on tuition fees, the EU is linking the three agreements, warning they must come into force together.

Not on Friday. The UK has been pushing for inclusion in the EU’s Made in Europe plan, a protectionist scheme to favour EU companies when public money is being spent on goods such as electric cars, renewable energy and nuclear technology. Inclusion in Made in Europe is a big priority for the Burnham government, which has dangled major concessions on tuition fees to make sure British firms are not shut out.

The problem for London is that the EU lawmakers have not finalised the Made in Europe law, known as the Industrial Accelerator Act. Many EU member states want to include the UK, but France and the European parliament take a stricter position.

The EU law is not expected to be agreed until spring 2027. To help the British government, which has linked a generous offer on youth mobility with Made in Europe, the European Commission proposed delaying agreement on tuition fees by six months. But member states want precise guarantees now about equal treatment for EU students.

Another problem is that British inclusion in Made in Europe requires the UK to sign up to EU trade-defence policies. The EU, for instance, has imposed high tariffs on “unfairly subsidised” Chinese electric cars and fears the UK, which has not followed suit, could become an alternative route into the EU if Chinese companies set up in Britain and sell into the bloc. The EU is calling on the UK to align with its trade-defence policies, but the UK insists it can guard against circumvention without copying the EU.
In a sign of possible tensions, an earlier summit text proposing a trusted partnership on economic security has been downgraded to a partnership.

Beyond the headline deals, the EU-UK draft summit statement opens the door to British integration in European policies on energy, crime-fighting, educational exchange, tech and foreign policy cooperation.

The next major agreement, targeted for next year, is bringing the UK back into the EU’s internal electricity market. This is a priority for five EU member states: Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and Luxembourg. They argue that Britain’s inclusion in the EU electricity market is essential to take advantage of the nascent green power boom in the North Sea. In return for market access, the UK will be required to contribute to the EU budget to aid the development of poorer EU regions.
Beyond that, the two sides will “explore opportunities” for the UK to join the Erasmus student exchange programme after 2027; the current arrangement applies only for the 2027-8 academic year.

In a win for the UK, the EU appears ready to expand talks on the mutual recognition of professional qualifications, beyond existing negotiations on architects. The sides will sign a digital partnership, which includes joint work on AI safety, and examine how to share data on law enforcement and border management.

Far from it. A lot of diplomatic plates are spinning, but the UK remains outside the EU’s biggest economic clubs: the single market and the customs union. It also has no decision-making powers inside the EU.

Burnham says he will set out the long-term options for the future relationship after this week’s summit. “The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain,” he said on Monday in a major speech. But amid concerns among some cabinet ministers about reopening Brexit divides, the prime minister appears to be taking a more cautious approach. He said the process would take time and insisted that “at every stage the British people will be the boss”.
The EU has welcomed Britain’s interest in rejoining but is wary of a protracted negotiation that could be reversed by an anti-EU British government.
In an echo of the Brexit years, EU insiders say, once again, that it is up to Britain to define what it wants.

items.title: Parents: please don’t buy Grand Theft Auto VI for your child
paragraphs: I am haunted still by an interaction I had at my stepson’s ninth birthday party in 2014, where one of the kids asked if I could put on Grand Theft Auto V for them all. “I have it at home!”, he said, giving me the puppy-dog eyes. Mentally replaying that game in my head, flashing back to the many scenes involving such things as smoking meth, over-the-top gratuitous violence and grubby sex in one character’s trailer, I said “no way”. Later I gently mentioned to the kid’s mother that GTA V was an 18-rated game and really wasn’t suitable for kids. “Oh, but he’s really good at these games,” she told me. She was genuinely shocked to learn that an 18-rating on a video game was a flag for adult content, rather than an indication of its difficulty.

Grand Theft Auto VI is released this week. It is an incredible creative and technical feat, conjuring a realistic-looking and exhaustively detailed virtual Florida filled with every kind of filth and criminality you could imagine. It is brilliant, entertainingly observed and even sometimes unexpectedly touching, largely thanks to a central love story between the player couple, Jason and Lucia. It is lewd, violent and frequently hilarious. It is also absolutely full of stuff that I really would not want my 10 and seven-year-old boys to see or hear. I have never played a game that has more thoroughly earned its 18 rating.

Everyone knows that Grand Theft Auto is a violent game. It’s about crime and criminals, and VI’s story is about two fugitives in Vice City and the absolute dirtbags they meet along the way. You steal cars, run drugs, shoot cops and rival criminals and hold up gas stations; you kill hundreds of people over the course of the game. There are executions, brutal police raids and depictions of torture. None of that is particularly new, but it’s still pretty hardcore for, say, a nine-year-old. Plenty of millennials played Grand Theft Auto when we were underage, but video games are an awful lot more realistic now than they were 20 years ago; graphic violence on a PlayStation 2 from the 00s looks very different from graphic violence on a PlayStation 5 in 2026.

Let’s leave the violence aside for a minute, though: there is also a lot more explicit sexual content in GTA VI than any previous GTA game, or any other video game period. 2004’s Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas was briefly pulled from sale because it contained a sex minigame that you couldn’t even access without hacking the game’s code. GTA VI, meanwhile, contains a LOT of sex that is in no way hidden, including between the two main characters. On another character’s laptop, there in a browsable in-game version of OnlyFans that pulls exactly no punches. There is full-frontal nudity, male and female. One mission takes place during a porn shoot, several others in strip clubs and bars, one in a hotel where you can burst into the wrong room to find an ongoing orgy or a bunch of people eating sushi off a naked body. I don’t personally fancy explaining any of this to my kids!

Then there’s the drugs. You run drugs, you steal drugs, you sell drugs and you take drugs. Pretty much everyone in Vice City really enjoys their coke; there are copious party scenes where powder is everywhere, and the player characters can partake if you want. Chapter 3 of the game is literally titled “Tits Ass Drug Money”. You might read all of this and think, my teenager has seen worse. That’s perfectly fair – but this is not stuff a 10- or 12-year-old can really contextualise, in my opinion (and the opinion of the ratings boards). If you think your child is too young to watch Breaking Bad, they are definitely too young for Grand Theft Auto VI.

Even the in-game TV and radio is full of vulgar humour. On a phone-in show, I heard a caller and the host vamp extensively about her boyfriend’s penis’s resemblance, in size and smell, to a chicken nugget. A psychic medium considers whether people can still indulge their foot fetishes in the afterlife, in incorporeal form. One of the in-game podcasts stars two female hosts talking in explicit detail about how attracted they are to various famous murderers. Walking past random pedestrians on the street you will frequently hear people talking at length about their dicks and what they have recently done with them. This is not what you might call mature humour, but it is adult.

To be clear: I am not here to start a moral panic about adult video game content. All of the above is fair game in media for adults and, truthfully, I found a lot of it extremely funny. But believe me, as both a parent and a person who has spent over 70 hours playing this game, GTA VI is not for kids. For some reason there remains an immense knowledge gap between children and parents when it comes to the content of video games, and I think it’s in everyone’s interests for parents to make informed decisions.

items.title: This cosy Godot-made indie game makes you feel like a still life artist
paragraphs: If you're looking for an antidote to the GTA 6 noise, Glenmara: Still Life Artist is it. Think of still life art, and chances are an oil painting of fruit in a bowl or flowers in a vase. While you may be presented with those options in Glenmara, this casual, cosy game from four-person Dundee-based indie studio Bit Loom Games also lets you get creatively weird with more contemporary objects and styles.

Despite the title, it's also not a painting game like, say, Mario Paint, but rather a simulation. "It's just this small idea based on being interested in how scenes are composed," artist Caitlin Smith tells me.

Instead, it's about being given objects you can assemble and position, then choosing filters and styles with the available tools and letting the game render it for you. Artist Douglas Flinders adds, "The thinking there is you are playing the role of a competent artist, so the player has access to nice painting styles. It's like you don't need to be able to triple-jump in real life to do it in Mario. You get to feel that fantasy without necessarily needing the inherent skill yourself."

Even though you are technically painting on a canvas, the filters you have available aren't limited to painting styles. Sure, you can use traditional oil paints or watercolours, but you can also opt for mosaic or styles that resemble cel-shading or pixel art. Being free to break from conventional expectations has been an important design decision.

"The [initial] idea was that you could be scored on how well you compose a theme with traditional rules, but it changed pretty quickly after we realised it would just be much more fun to not have any rules and basically be able to do whatever you want creatively," Smith explains. "It was important to us to not have any sort of failed state. So if you want to sort of make this niche for yourself as a painter that puts eggs in all of your paintings, the game is not going to tell you you can't do that."

As the team's first game made with the open-source engine Godot, which only launched its own asset store earlier this year, all of Glenmara's shaders for its different art styles were created from scratch by programmer Henry Pullan.

"Coming to Godot from Unity, the image processing pipeline we were used to just wasn't there, and we had to come up with a different way of getting all the data to and from the GPU at the right time," Pullan explains. "Fortunately, they're not real-time effects, and being able to process the image over a few frames lets us really easily experiment."

"This led to a system where we can stack effects on top of each other to create pretty different outcomes. The majority of the effects are using the library of shaders we've built up in different combinations to create a variety of effects."

While playing as a newcomer to the fictional Scottish island of Glenmara might have you thinking of the premise of other cosy games like Animal Crossing: New Horizons, the inspiration is closer to home for Bit Loom's members, who all grew up in small places, including one from Jersey in the Channel Islands.

"We're going for the small-knit community part of Scotland where everyone kind of knows each other," says Smith. "We tried to put this in the game in various ways, including character dialects, topics of conversation, your object collection and certain events that feature in the narrative. We hope that all of these things can work together to create a comforting, homely feel for players, and even a nostalgic one for some."

This also means avoiding the trap of turning the game into a cosy capitalist sim where your still-life art is your side hustle, and you're incentivised to earn money from commissions to unlock more content.

"It would restrict creativity, and we just want people to go crazy and do loads of cool stuff in a painting," says Flinders. "Also, the story we want to tell and the feeling you get throughout is a lot more about making these pieces of artwork as gifts for members of your community that you're getting to know in a new place you've moved to. You're forming relationships with these people."
Glenmara: Still Life Artist is coming soon to PC, and you can wishlist it on Steam.

Alan Wen is a freelance journalist writing about video games in the form of features, interview, previews, reviews and op-eds. Work has appeared in print including Edge, Official Playstation Magazine, GamesMaster, Games TM, Wireframe, Stuff, and online including Kotaku UK, TechRadar, FANDOM, Rock Paper Shotgun, Digital Spy, The Guardian, and The Telegraph.

items.title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'
paragraphs: ByNick TriggleHealth correspondentChloe HaywardHealth reporter and Jim ReedHealth reporter

Early efforts to contain coronavirus "were doomed to fail" because the test, trace and isolate system in the UK could only handle a relatively small number of cases, the seventh report of the Covid inquiry says in a damning assessment.
Across 245 pages the inquiry looks at everything from border controls to how well contact tracing worked.
The report said the virus was allowed to spread virtually unchecked in the first few months after community testing and contact tracing was abandoned in mid-March 2020, costing lives.
Ministers said this was because testing capacity was being overwhelmed.
NHS Test and Trace was launched two months later and eventually became one of the biggest testing services in the world per head of population.
In the end, more than £30bn was spent across the UK during the pandemic on testing, tracing and isolating.
But in those early months the four UK nations were "effectively blind" to how quickly Covid was spreading, the inquiry said.

It criticises the government for not having a robust test, trace and isolate system in place to start with, saying this, alongside other failures, meant harsher measures, including lockdown and school closures, were needed.

Inquiry chair Baroness Hallett said the UK should have been better prepared and learnt lessons from other countries that had experience of dealing with outbreaks of other infectious diseases, such as Sars.
Unlike the UK, places such as Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan had established systems ready to go.
This was despite the fact the UK had run a series of simulation exercises in the years leading up to Covid.
They included Exercise Cygnus into a flu pandemic and Exercise Alice into Mers. Both identified problems relating to test, trace or isolation, which appear not to have been fully acted on.

The report also raises the question of whether the government could have made use of non-government testing facilities in hospitals, universities and the private sector from the start, instead of just relying on 12 government labs.
When people in the UK were told to isolate, "many felt forgotten and let down by the lack of practical or financial support when trying to follow the rules", says the report.
In the early months of the pandemic, estimates suggested less than half of people were complying with the rules around isolating if infected.
Ministers and their advisers discussed this and fines of up to £10,000 were introduced for those who did not comply, which some experts have said was counter-productive.
Changes were made to allow people to claim statutory sick pay.
But it was not until September in England – and later in Scotland and Wales – that £500 financial payments were introduced to help those on low incomes comply.
More also needed to be done to provide practical support for things such as collecting medicines and shopping for food for those who did not have people to call on.

Suspending all flights from China to the UK in February 2020 could "have provided valuable additional time to prepare healthcare systems for the impact of the pandemic", said inquiry chair Baroness Hallett. That didn't happen.
The report says the UK lacked a clear strategy for implementing border control measures early in the pandemic, which left the country in an "extremely vulnerable position".

Although the closure and restriction of borders was noted as "immensely complex", the inquiry said that border control measures could serve as an important tool "to reassure the public and increase confidence."
By April 2020, 93% of countries had put measures in place, such as flight suspensions, border closures and travel restrictions, to control their international borders.
By contrast, the UK government only requested travellers arriving from high-risk areas to self-isolate for 14 days. The UK government implemented no further border control measures until June 2020.

The report says that border controls were a "critical gap in the UK's ability to limit the spread of the virus" and recommends that in the future "international border control measures should be in place at the earliest stages of a pandemic".
The inquiry report is more positive about the use of smartphone apps, saying digital tools can have a "significant impact on reducing the spread of infection".
It quotes a mathematical modelling study from the US which estimates that, when 75% of people used a contact tracing app in the pandemic, infections were reduced by at least 50%.
Three different apps were developed during Covid - one for England and Wales, another for Scotland and a third for Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland.
The inquiry says that took up "valuable time", and it recommends developing a UK-wide digital tool to use in any future outbreak.
It says it is "fundamentally important" that apps and digital tools are as accurate as possible – and people have confidence in them.
In the summer of 2021, as Covid restrictions were relaxed, around 7% of all UK adults were told to self-isolate over a seven-day period, something dubbed by the press as the "pingdemic".
It quotes Treasury estimates suggesting that may have reduced economic growth by as much as 0.3% that month.

Zelenskyy added Ukraine was “doing everything to ensure Europe’s full participation in the negotiation process and to make these meetings productive.”
