Germany’s Merz has been out greeting foreign leaders in Berlin, here are a some of images coming through from agency photographers:
We’ve got a bit more from Putin, who says that Russia “will respond to strikes on the Crimean Bridge”.

He added that Russia’s response to attacks will be “much more painful” and claimed he had been discussing “a possible ceasefire in a number of areas” with Russia’s security council “but after the strikes on the Crimean Bridge, we will not negotiate”.
In further remarks reported by RIA Novosti, Putin lavished praise on Donald Trump, insisting the US president “sincerely strives” to settle the war in Ukraine. Of the US president, Putin said:

double quotation markI have no doubts about this, that President Trump sincerely strives both for the resolution of conflicts, including the Ukrainian one, and sincerely strives to improve bilateral relations across a whole range of areas, including – which is, of course, important for us – on the US-Russian track.
Putin criticised Kyiv and European capitals, claiming Ukraine’s leadership was stalling peace efforts.
Meanwhile, we are getting some lines from Russia’s Vladimir Putin after his meeting with Trump and Xi earlier today.
Putin said “Ukraine and Europe are not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict,” according to Reuters and Russian news agency Ria.
He also defended Russia’s “legitimate” demands on European security, Tass reported.
I will bring you the longer quotes when we have them.
First leaders are starting to arrive in Berlin, and the US peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, just got out of their car.
They are expected to brief other leaders on the Shenhzen talks between Trump, Xi and Putin, among others.

Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen has said Europe “must never accept” Putin’s demands about “European security on Russian terms,” as she urged fellow leaders to “put Ukraine in the strongest possible position.”
In a statement ahead of today’s Berlin talks, Frederiksen said:

“Putin’s demands are about much more than Ukraine. They are about European security on Russian terms. We must never accept that. That is why we must put Ukraine in the strongest possible position – both at the front and in the negotiating room.
We must strengthen Ukraine’s air defences so that they can withstand the brutal Russian attacks.
Russia is terrorising the Ukrainian population and is targeting their heat, water and electricity. Ukraine needs us in Europe to get through the winter.”
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy has now arrived in Berlin for today’s meeting of the Coalition of the Willing.

“More than 40 partners will be represented, including the team of the American President. Ukraine’s priorities are strengthening our air defence, energy and financial support, the diplomatic track, and the next steps toward ending the war and guaranteeing security,” he said.
Zelenskyy added Ukraine was “doing everything to ensure Europe’s full participation in the negotiation process and to make these meetings productive.”

“Bilateral meetings with European partners are also planned, and, of course, with chancellor Friedrich Merz. There will also be a format involving the American side and European national security advisers.”
The European Commission’s foreign affairs spokesperson Christian Wigand responded in very general terms to the trilateral meeting in China.
Speaking at the European Commission’s midday briefing, he said:
“We will continue following reports coming out of the discussions; we’ve also seen the statement that was published just a few minutes ago, so I would at this stage not go into any details here.”
Asked about Trump’s “he’s my friend” comment on Putin, the Commission’ chief spokesperson Paula Pinho said “in general, we do not comment on friendships.”
“Russia, under Vladimir Putin’s command, is continuing its relentless attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure in Ukraine, and we would support all efforts, of course, to end this.”
France’s foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot had little time for Trump’s summit with Xi and Putin, telling French media that he did not expect anything important to come out of that meeting.
“These three leaders fundamentally disagree on everything, so they cannot agree on anything,” Barrot told French broadcaster RTL, quoted by AP.

“And as for this photograph that has generated so much discussion, it isn’t quite a photograph of the world’s three greatest powers, because the world’s three greatest powers are the United States, of course, China and the European Union.”

“These three countries are meeting because they have something in common: They all border the Pacific,” Barrot said. He added: “These three leaders agree on nothing, so, in a sense, nothing is going to come out of this meeting.”
For what it’s worth, the China-US-Russia ‘peace declaration’ issued after their meeting, and published by Chinese state media, includes absolutely no mention of Ukraine or Europe whatsoever.
There is only one, rather generic, line that could be seen as close to these issues:
“The three heads of state exchanged in-depth views on the current international situation and pledged to maintain strategic stability and international security.”

The document also includes a commitment to promote UN reform, increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products, as well as the leaders’ criticism of the international criminal court and declaration of intent to work on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation.
EU ministers are also getting some questions about tomorrow’s EU-UK summit, 10 years on from Britain’s vote to leave the bloc.

Ireland’s EU minister Thomas Byrne said the main areas to be discussed on Friday “will have very significant benefits” for all parties, with the sanitary and phytosanitary agreement set to resolve “one of the biggest problems out of Brexit.”

But he was cautious talking about future relationship with the EU, saying that while he had “no doubt that the EU and Britain will want to go further on that path, we have seen how complex even dealing with the issues for tomorrow is and how long it takes.”
Sweden’s Jessica Rosencrantz stressed it is “up to the citizens of the UK to decide how close you want to work with the EU.”
But, again, asked if Britain could rejoin the bloc and keep its historical opt-outs and rebates, she dismissed it as “a highly speculative question.”

“Let’s remember how the discussion was at the time of Brexit. In that light, I think it is amazing that we now can have a big summit together, with discussions on how we can come closer together when it comes to trade and mobility,” she said.
Poland’s EU minister Ignacy Niemczycki said Warsaw’s approach “has always been very pragmatic,” as he stressed that te EU after Brexit is “weaker.”

“I would like us, wherever possible, to work out such mechanisms so it works for both of us. … This is a country that thinks similarly to us in Europe on many issues and there is no reason for us to treat each other like enemies. We are friends and let’s find the right formula for that.
“I would encourage everyone to think seriously about the benefits of being in the EU, … and I think the people of the UK see it [too], now that they are outside the union.”

Meanwhile, foreign ministers arriving for the EU foreign affairs council meeting in Brussels are heroically trying to avoid saying anything remotely interesting or controversial in response to reporters’ questions on Trump’s meetings with Xi and Putin.
Clearly, they would prefer to leave the talking to their bosses who are expected in Berlin later today.
And so, Spanish EU minister Fernando Sampedro merely said that Spain and the EU remained “strongly committed” to supporting Ukraine.
Asked specifically about his views on Trump’s comments on “his friend” Putin, he only sheepishly smiled and once again repeated his previous lines.
Sweden’s EU minister Jessica Rosencrantz said that “we don’t really know the details of this meeting, neither the agenda nor the specific issues" the leaders were planning to discuss.

“But the general principle is there should be no talks about European security without Europe; there should be no talks about Ukraine without Ukraine. That is our general attitude when it comes to issues about European security or Ukrainian security,” she said.

(For what it’s worth, her boss, Sweden’s foreign minister Maria Malmer Stenergard, was a bit more outspoken when she said early this morning that it was “worrying if we have great powers who think they should decide how the world should be governed.”)
Ireland’s EU minister Thomas Byrne struck a similar note to his Swedish counterpart, saying “nothing will be decided about Europe without Europe.”
“The only way peace can work is if Russia decides to stop its invasion.”

Meanwhile, Poland’s Europe minister Ignacy Niemczycki dismissed any comparisons between the Shenzhen meeting to the Yalta conference in 1945, saying “Europe is still very strong,” and so “the situations is very different than historically.”
“Even if some decisions were to be made, their implementation would simply be impossible without Europe’s participation,” he said.
Meanwhile in Shenzhen, the trilateral meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi is reportedly over, according to Chinese state media.
Remember that we cover that in detail on our separate Apec live blog, but don’t worry: I will pick up any lines on Europe here.

Meanwhile, Denmark’s parliament unanimously ratified a security agreement with US president Donald Trump covering Greenland, hoping to end a standoff over ⁠the Arctic island’s ⁠future that ​has rattled transatlantic relations, Reuters reported.

The US, Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September to resolve tensions after Trump repeatedly threatened to ⁠take control of the mineral-rich island, a self-governing Danish territory that is home to 57,000 people.
The deal was backed by 109 Danish ⁠lawmakers and none voted against, the parliamentary tally showed.

Meanwhile, a key bridge connecting annexed Crimea to Russia has been attacked again last night, a Russian-appointed regional governor has said, two days after Ukrainian strikes caused serious damage to it.

“Following a new attack on the Crimean Bridge, traffic has been temporarily halted. All relevant services are on site and at work. An assessment of the damage is under way,” Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of the Russian-occupied Crimea, wrote on Telegram.
The Russian transport ministry said on Thursday that no one was wounded in the attack and that train services across it had been halted.

Wednesday’s ‌attack is third this week on the highly symbolic bridge that links Russia with Crimea, which ​it seized from Ukraine in 2014. A 227-metre section of the road spanning the Kerch strait was destroyed this week, but the rail corridor appears to be operable despite sustaining some damage.
On Ukraine, Trump says at the beginning of the trilateral meeting:

“We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That’s what pretty much what the discussion was about.
I think that he and – I hope - the other side would like to see an end to that war.”
God knows what that’s supposed to mean in practice.

The trilateral meeting is now getting under way, with Trump declaring “together we are making history” with the three leaders facing “a special responsibility to maintain open, respectful and productive dialogue on issues impacting not just our people, but the entire planet.”
Our coverage of the Apec summit is here, but I will pick up any lines on Ukraine:
Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk – one of Europe’s five negotiators – does not seem to be impressed by what he saw in Shenzhen.
“God, protect us from such friends,” he said on X in an apparent reference to Trump’s enthusiastic greeting with Putin.
Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski was similarly alarmed, telling reporters:
“Indeed, it is difficult to judge, by their fruits we shall know them, but the optics of this hugging Putin, calling him a friend, causes us some concern.
Because the question arises – who is he more of a friend with, Putin or our president? And what will he possibly do if push comes to shove, which friend will he choose?”

Several European leaders from the Coalition of the Willing are meeting in Berlin today, just hours after US president Donald Trump, Russia president Vladimir Putin and China president Xi Jinping are due to meet in Shenhzen.
The trilateral meeting is due to get under way any moment now, though the tone of Trump’s earlier talks with Putin will already be worrying for Europeans.
“Who is he? He’s my friend!” said Trump, absolutely beaming, as soon as he saw Putin.
These images will send a shiver down the spine of Europe’s top leaders as they prepare to leave for Berlin to attend the “coalition of the willing”’s latest coordination meeting.

Europe’s newly appointed negotiating team of Andy Burnham, Emmanuel Macron, Giorgia Meloni, Friedrich Merz and Donald Tusk plus the EU’s Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa will be joined by several other leaders for a meeting with US peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, where they are expected to get a read out from the meeting in China.

Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte are expected to attend, as are several other key European leaders, including Finland’s Alexander Stubb, Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen, Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson, Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre, and Ireland’s Micheál Martin (and many others).
I will bring you all the latest from Berlin and reactions to Trump’s trilateral meeting.
It’s Thursday, 19 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

items.title: Top U.N. court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
paragraphs: Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling over whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 19. Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya during its 2017 military operations in northern Rakhine State.

Delivering the judgment, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said the scale and nature of the military's actions went "well beyond what would be required to punish the population" and were instead "characteristic of an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group."

This photograph shows a general view of judges of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) attending a public hearing ahead of the reading of the Court's judgment in the genocide case brought by Gambia against Myanmar, with 11 States intervening, in The Hague on November 19, 2026. JEROEN JUMELET/ANP/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
The judges estimated that around 815,000 Rohingya lived in northern Rakhine State before the operations, and concluded that around 10,000 were violently killed during the 2017 clearance campaign.

Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruling over whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on November 19, 2026. SALAHUDDIN AHMED/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

The court found that Myanmar's security forces "acted with genocidal intent." Judge Iwasawa said the operations were preceded by an atmosphere of anti-Rohingya hate speech, with the community portrayed as "sub-human" and "a violent threat."
This is a developing story that will be updated.

items.title: I dare Apple to make this delightful AirPods design a reality
paragraphs: I've been talking a lot lately about how Apple seems to have rediscovered its sense of fun. From folding iPhones to touchscreen MacBooks, via an uncharacteristically zany new TikTok presence, the company is doing a lot to persuade us it's in a more playful mode of late. But if Apple really wants to convince me it's here for a good time, it needs to make these nostalgic AirPods a reality.

The iMac G3 days have become synonymous with the halcyon days of Y2K tech design. Think bold citrus colours and translucent plastic. Those colours have made an unexpected return with the new iMac and, of course, the MacBook Neo. Apple's in-ear AirPods, however, remain available in any colour you like – as long as it's white. But wouldn't a splash of Y2K colour make them so much more fun?

Concept artist Krishnavi Anand Krishnavi has been sharing nostalgic Apple product concepts on Instagram for a while, including an iPhone SE revival I would love to see. But it's the 'AirPods G3' that are the most fun, with their noughties design sensibilities. There's a lot going on inside an AirPod, and that colourful translucent plastic tantalisingly reveals some of its secrets.

"Apple might get me if they bring back these gems," one Instagram user comments, while another adds, "If these don’t actually come out I will sue." Another rather dispiritingly chimes in, "Apple will never do something this fun and imaginative."

But we are seeing more imagination from Apple lately, at least when it comes to its phones and laptops. For now, though, if it's colourful AirPods you're after, you'll have to make do with the AirPods Max while waiting for the standard AirPods to go full retro. Alas, you might be waiting a while – perhaps even longer than it takes for the company to bring back the iPod.

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He reports on the worlds of design, branding and lifestyle tech, and has covered several industry events including Milan Design Week, OFFF Barcelona and Adobe Max in Los Angeles. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

items.title: UK joins in GTA 6 frenzy as game becomes available worldwide
paragraphs: The game, set in the fictional US state of Leonida, follows two protagonists, Lucia and Jason, through the seedy underbelly of America after an "easy score goes wrong".
It was released at midnight in all the countries it is available in, which meant New Zealanders were the first to access it.
"The graphics are great. Even from the set-up and credits, it's feeling pretty good," Aleana Fernando, who lives in Auckland, New Zealand, told BBC Newsbeat soon after she started playing.
Once the game was released at midnight UK time, gamers were equally enthralled by the game's graphics and attention to detail.
Charlie Wood from London said he had "already laughed at the dialogue before even stepping into the gameplay".
About 30 minutes into playing in Leonida, he said it was "most definitely worth the wait".
The Guardian's Keza MacDonald, external was impressed by the relationship between the main characters.
"GTA has never been particularly kind to women... there is still a lot of sexism in GTA VI's world, but now we have Lucia to react to it," she said.
"This is the first GTA in which I have felt the women are treated as people, not only Lucia but also the many other female characters in the story".

items.title: Yahoo for the loo! An ode to the commode! Dotty for the potty! It's World Toilet Day!
paragraphs: Jack Sim, the founder of World Toilet Day, travels the world promoting access to safe and clean toilets. When NPR photographed him a few years ago — on a toilet, of course — he was glad to oblige even though it was a chilly and windy November day. John Poole/Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption
Twenty-five years ago, Jack Sim was flush with excitement. (Please pardon the pun.)

The Singapore entrepreneur was looking for a meaningful project and came upon this thought from the prime minister: "He said we should measure our graciousness according to the cleanliness of our public toilets," Sim recalls.
Thus was born World Toilet Day. The goal was more than cleanliness. It was access, too — billions of people do not have a safe and sanitary toilet to use.
Enshrined as an official U.N. day in 2013, World Toilet Day aims to get people talking and thinking about a topic that maybe is a taboo in polite conversation.
A rally in India calls for decent sanitation on a past World Toilet Day demonstration. NOAH SEELAM/AFP via Getty Images/AFP hide caption

World Toilet Day is all about peeing, pooping and addressing menstrual hygiene in a clean and safe manner — followed by the "conveyance" of excreta to a sanitary disposal system, notes Kate Olive Medlicott, the sanitation and waste team leader within the WASH team at the World Health Organization. Human diseases are shed in sewage, so a top-notch sanitation system is critical, says Medlicott. Cholera is linked to sewage. Polio is, too.

This year's World Toilet Day theme is "Sanitation and Gender Equality: Safe Toilets, Equal Futures." Even though everyone suffers when they can't find a toilet, the menstrual cycle creates additional complications. If schools or offices lack a safe and sanitary place to attend to period needs and to dispose of period products, girls and women may opt to stay home.

There is another gender issue. Sofia Calltorp, the U.N. Women global head of humanitarian action, says: "When women and girls do not have access to safe toilets," they leave their home and look for a public toilet or a secluded space to do their business. "There is a huge impact in terms of being exposed to harassment or violence," Calltorp says. She points to refugee camps as a place where this issue often arises, with unlit toilets that aren't differentiated by gender.
Poo Guru is a character created by the Defeat Diarrheal Disease Initiative in its ongoing campaign to educate the world about sanitation and the need for safe toilets for all. DefeatDD hide caption

In Western Colombo, Sri Lanka, an informational sign urges users not to squat on the seat as though they were using a squat toilet, which often consists of ... a pit. Haag/ullstein bild/via Getty Images hide caption
A sign from Valencia, Spain, is a reminder of how important it is to have access to a safe toilet. Kristina Ketelsen hide caption
Now you might well ask: Has World Toilet Day made a difference?

The toilet titans we interviewed say yes, it has, just by talking about toilets in the public arena. The U.N. has stated that access to safe sanitation is a human right. And in just about every country, progress has been made in improving access to sanitary facilities. Since 2015, 1.2 billion people have become part of the world of safely managed sanitation systems.

What are the next steps? Kellogg Schwab, who specializes in water and wastewater contaminants of public health concern at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, stresses that governments should be a force for change but that it shouldn't be top down. It should also be … oh, forgive me again … bottom up. Schwab suggests giving money to communities to figure out what solutions they can come up with to improve the toilet and sanitation situation. There will be flops. But there will be successes that can be scaled up.

Sand artist Sudarsan Pattnaik created this sculpture in honor of World Toilet Day on a beach in the coastal city of Puri in India. Like the contents of a toilet connected to a sanitation system, it was ... washed away. NurPhoto/via Getty Images hide caption
So maybe one day — Medlicott of WHO thinks in 50 years or so —- Earthlings will look back and say, How curious that in a world of wealth there were not enough safe and secure toilets.
Let's end by reflecting on the present day.
"World Toilet Day is my favorite day of the year," says Medlicott. "People find it fun and funny but it's really important to celebrate and act on something we take for granted."

If you're among the population where toilets are plentiful, she suggests pausing to think of a moment — it's happened to all of us — when you needed a bathroom and couldn't find one. Maybe that incident has turned into a funny story you share with friends. Now imagine if it were to happen every day.
I am deeply thankful that all I need to do is walk down the office hallway to find a clean and private loo.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

items.title: Anthropic raises more than $100B in IPO. And, Dems nominate Jeffries for House speaker
paragraphs: Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-154344/nx-s1-mx-6047056-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has received the House Democrats' nomination to become speaker when the party regains the majority in the new year. This nomination, confirmed by a closed-door vote of 251 to 11, marks the start of the formal selection process for speaker. It will culminate in a House floor vote on Jan. 3, at the start of the new Congress. If successful, Jeffries will make history as the first Black Speaker of the House. Jeffries said after the closed door vote that he is committed to addressing cost-of-living issues, pledging to fight for lower costs in groceries, gas, housing and healthcare.
Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks during a news conference in the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 17, 2026. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images hide caption

Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping met today in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. Xi and Putin met separately the night before the trilateral meeting. Trump also had one-on-one meetings with Putin and Xi. It's the first time the three leaders have held a summit together.

Anthropic is set to debut on the Nasdaq exchange today. The company raised more than $100 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering that valued the company at around $1.5 trillion. The company sold 956 million shares at $83 each, surpassing its initial target range of $70 to $78. The seven founders sold over 23 million shares as part of the IPO, and the company's prospectus outlines plans to introduce an extra $26 billion in shares through private placements with Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
Ben Shapiro sits with NPR for a Newsmakers interview. Nickolai Hammar/NPR hide caption

Go face-to-face with the person of the moment. NPR's Newsmakers video podcast brings the biggest names in politics, business, sports, arts, and culture out of the headlines and into the interview chair to discuss the mark they're making on the world. Follow the Newsmakers podcast or subscribe to NPR's YouTube channel to get new episodes as soon as they're available.

Ben Shapiro says he remains committed to his values during Trump's turbulent presidency. The conservative podcast host voted against Trump in 2016, but actively campaigned for him in 2024. Shapiro expressed disappointment in the president's tariffs, alleged corruption and the handling of the war in Iran. He says that Trump's strict immigration policies and the "whiff of corruption" surrounding the White House contributed to the GOP's midterm losses. The co-founder of the media company The Daily Wire warns that Republicans face an "uphill road in 2028," and he doesn't see Vice President JD Vance as the right GOP presidential candidate. Shapiro argues that Vance could alienate key voter groups like Hispanics, the working class, women and the college-educated. In conversation with Morning Edition's Steve Inskeep, Shapiro discussed who he thinks could be a potential 2028 GOP candidate, his new movie, Confession, and the recent decline in his show's YouTube subscriptions.
Watch or listen to the interview or read the article about their discussion.

Israeli violist Tal Riva Theodorou (C-L) arrives for a rehearsal of the West-Eastern Divan Orchestra at the Pierre Boulez Hall at the Barenboim-Said Academy in Berlin on Nov. 9, 2026. Odd Andersen/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

The West-Eastern Divan Orchestra is an ensemble founded by Edward Said and Daniel Barenboim nearly 30 years ago in Germany to unite Middle Eastern musicians. Despite the deep personal grief and heightened tensions following the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the Gaza war, members of the orchestra strive to confront, rather than sidestep, political realities. Longtime musicians say Barenboim has helped them bridge painful cultural divides and foster enduring cross-border friendships. The space has also given some participants a safe space to discuss Gaza, allowing music to resolve the dissonance.
Abdelrahman ElGendy won the Non-fiction award at the National Book Awards for his memoir, Huna. Fadel Dawod/National Book Foundation hide caption
This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

items.title: Florence Pugh hits out at weight loss and cosmetic surgery speculation
paragraphs: Florence Pugh attended the Governors Awards in Hollywood at the weekend
Florence Pugh has said she was "disturbed" to see "thousands of people" discussing her recent appearance at the Governors Awards, and denied speculation about weight-loss drugs and facial surgery.
The actress wrote on Instagram, external how stressful" it was waking up to people "talking about you and your body in ways that you can't even comprehend".
"I have never been on Ozempic. I have never done any face surgery," she wrote. "And don't ever say that I didn't make my own nose, I've always had that beautiful ski slope. Even as a baby!"
She added: "For the first time in my entire career, I have had the opportunity to be rested, to sleep, to wake up and work out and to eat regularly and healthily."
In her eight-page statement, the Oppenheimer, Dune and East of Eden star told followers: "I'm looking after myself, and that's literally it."
Pugh has spoken out before about judgement about how women look
Pugh highlighted that losing weight had not been her goal, and she had lost "two pounds".

"The thing that's most important to me and my trainer is muscle," she said. "I think it's the most important thing a woman can do. Build muscle and be strong. I can now do six pull-ups and lift 110kg.
"Which I'm sure to many of you isn't a lot... but to me?! It's everything."
The actress said that from the moment she entered the acting industry she was "subjected to fat shaming".
"I have loved every time I get to tell someone they are being inappropriate about my weight, and I'm not changing that now just because you've all said so."
She also said she was "disturbed" that "women who now think that I'm someone I'm not, for having my body dissected and pointed at again".
"I have spent my whole career defending and protecting bodies that just grow the way they grow."
Pugh is no stranger to a striking red carpet outfit

Pugh, who was Oscar-nominated for Little Women in 2020 and played Black Widow assassin Yelena Belova in this year's Spider-Man: Brand New Day, has previously spoken out against judgement about women's looks.
In 2024, she told the Times, external she aimed to "challenge how women were perceived".
"Look, not everybody has legs that go on for days. I remember watching this industry and feeling that I wasn't represented," she said. "I've loved challenging ideas I don't like."
She also spoke about why she thinks she receives criticism about her appearance.
"I've always been aware that seeing a confident woman be happy in her skin is triggering to a lot of people and for a long time just accepted that I will receive commentary like that," she said.
"But now this...? I'm asking us all to just be mindful. We are real people, living real lives."

Pugh did not have comments turned on for her post, but it was liked by celebrities including Ashley James, who is known for speaking out about body positivity, plus Carol Vorderman, Zoe Ball, writer and actress Katy Brand and doctor and broadcaster Amir Khan.

Pugh also said she had sued several publications earlier this year, claiming they published AI-generated images appearing to show her receiving cosmetic injections that were presented as real photographs.
"I was... horrified," she wrote, claiming the articles had damaged her reputation.
The actress concluded by urging followers to think about their attitudes towards physical appearance.
"I understand that we are in a warped part of image history right now, with beauty standards changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with," she said.
"But please be gentle to yourselves and others when you go in on people's physical appearance.
"I'm not angry at you, I'm angry at the situation that's being projected onto us.
"It feels inescapable, but part of changing the tide is on you as much as us in the public eye."

items.title: Ella Langley sweeps Country Music Awards as Taylor Swift performs
paragraphs: Ella Langley said her hit Choosin' Texas was "the gift that keeps on giving"
US singer Ella Langley has swept the Country Music Association Awards (CMAs), following the huge success of her breakthrough hit Choosin' Texas.
The Alabama-born singer was named entertainer of the year at Wednesday's ceremony, weeks after the song became the longest-running number one in Billboard chart history.
"At this point, I'm sick of me," the 27-year-old joked in her acceptance speech, having spent so much of the ceremony on stage. "I could quit tomorrow and have the best career of my life."
Choosin' Texas was also named single of the year and song of the year, leading Langley to joke in an acceptance speech: "This song is the gift that keeps on giving."
Ella Langley, who won six awards on the night, performed her song Loving Life Again
Langley won six awards in total, including female vocalist of the year, music video of the year and album of the year for Dandelion.
She also performed her song Loving Life Again with a string quartet, and duetted with Miranda Lambert for a performance of Snakeskin Boots.
Choosin' Texas made history in September after spending 23 weeks at the top spot on the Billboard Hot 100 chart. It has now spent 28 weeks in total at the summit.
Following her win, Langley took to social media and said: "Hard to put this night into words and what it means.
"Thank you to my fans. Thank you for loving this record, thank you for coming to my shows, thank you for believing in my artistry.
"This year has been the most incredible journey, and I want to thank you for sharing in that with me. I love y'all."
Langley also performed Snakeskin Boots with Miranda Lambert during the ceremony
Taylor Swift also performed at the CMA Awards for the first time in 13 years.
Her performance began with Swift walking backstage and featured cameo appearances from country stars including Brad Paisley, Little Big Town, Sugarland, and Brooks & Dunn.
Swift then sang her recent hit I Knew It, I Knew You, from the Toy Story 5 soundtrack, using a blue guitar with bedazzled clouds on it, in a nod to the animated franchise.
The singer also mixed in some of her 2006 country hit Our Song, while Keith Urban joined her on the banjo.
Taylor Swift used a Toy Story-themed guitar and performed alongside Keith Urban
She also presented a lifetime achievement award to country music duo Brooks & Dunn
Swift's performance came after she was inducted into both the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame earlier this year.
Other winners on the night included Chris Stapleton who won male vocalist of the year, The Red Clay Strays who won vocal group of the year, and Brooks & Dunn with vocal duo of the year.
Meanwhile Stephen Wilson Jr won the new artist of the year award while Charlie Worsham won musician of the year.
The award ceremony began with a tribute to country music legend Dolly Parton, who died in August aged 80.
Ceremony host Lainey Wilson began the tribute by duetting with singer-songwriter Vince Gill on a rendition of Parton's I Will Always Love You.

items.title: Cricut Maker 5 review: A smaller, smarter cutting machine for serious crafters
paragraphs: The Cricut Maker 5 isn't a big leap from the Maker 4, but it's smaller, lighter, easier to set up and can cut materials up to 3mm thick. It also keeps the versatility that makes the Maker range so appealing, from intricate paper designs and vinyl stickers to engraving metal and cutting fabric.
Little reason for Maker 4 owners to upgrade
Rotary blade, knife blade and FabricGrip mat cost extra
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
Price: $349 / £349.99 machine only, $399 / £399.99 Essential Bundle, $529 / £499.99 Ultimate Bundle
Cutting speed: Up to 14.1 inches per second
Materials support: 300+ compatible materials
Maximum cutting speed: 3mm (depending on material and tool)
Compatible tools: 13, including engraving
Maximum Smart Material cut length: 3.6m (12ft)
Maximum cut area: 29.2 x 59.7cm with a large mat
Connectivity: Bluetooth Low Energy, USB-C

I've been using Cricut machines for years, mostly for quilting and personalised craft projects, and what keeps me coming back to the Maker range is how much one machine can do. The Maker 5 keeps that going. Cuts are accurate, it's quick, and Design Space makes projects easy to start, whether you work from a template or design your own.

If you own the older Maker 3, I'd seriously consider upgrading: the faster cutting and more compact body are noticeable straight away. If you already have the slightly newer Maker 4, it's a harder argument to make, because Maker 5 tidies up the older machine and makes subtle improvements rather than replacing it, and the Maker 4 is still an excellent cutter.

For anyone choosing a first Cricut, the Maker 5 is a great option, provided you'll use its extra capabilities. If you mostly make cards, stickers and vinyl decorations, the cheaper Explore range may be all you need.
In this Maker 5 review, I go into detail on what the new craft machine can do, how to use it, and how it compares with recent Cricut releases.

The first thing I noticed was the colour. The Slate Blue finish is a soft grey-blue that looks more contemporary than earlier Makers. It's also a lot smaller, with Cricut claiming a 30% reduction in size compared with earlier machines. At around 50cm wide, 19cm deep and 12cm high, it takes up noticeably less room on my desk, and at 4.9kg it's lighter than the Maker 4, so it's easy to move or put away. That's handy if you have a dedicated craft room, and even more so if, like me, you sometimes have to share your workspace with other projects.
The lid includes a storage tray to keep tools close at hand, and the overall design feels neat and considered.

Setup is straightforward. Head to the Cricut website, select the Maker 5 and follow the instructions. It tells you how much room you need in front of and behind the machine for materials and mats to feed through, and reminds you to remove the packaging before you start. Plug it in, open Design Space on your computer, and follow the prompts. The machine connects over Bluetooth; there's no separate on/off switch to worry about, and the software talks you through loading material and starting each job.

The Maker 5 comes with a 12 x 12 in LightGrip mat, a cutting tool, a scoring tool, and a dual-sided black marker, plus materials for your first project. Depending on the bundle, you may also get a portable trimmer.

If you're upgrading from an older Cricut, many of your existing tools carry over, including mats, fine-point blades, and many older Maker tools, as well as Smart Materials such as vinyl and iron-on. The new snap-in pen holder has different compatibility requirements, though, so check your pens before assuming they'll fit.

The rotary blade for cutting fabric and specialist blades such as the knife blade for thicker materials are extra purchases. They matter most if you're buying the Maker for quilting or more ambitious projects.

The Maker 5 cuts up to 14.1 inches per second, which is fast, but the Maker 4 already offered that speed, so don't expect a dramatic difference if you're upgrading from that model. Maker 3 owners will notice more: like the Maker 4, the Maker 5 cuts up to twice as fast, which really shows when you're working through multiple designs or larger projects.

It handles more than 300 compatible materials, from delicate paper and vinyl to leather, fabric and selected thicker materials. It can cut, draw, score, engrave and deboss, and it works with a home printer for full-colour Print Then Cut projects.

Smart Materials are a big part of the Cricut experience. They feed straight into the machine without a cutting mat, which makes longer designs much easier. Smart Vinyl, for example, can be loaded directly for continuous cuts of up to 12ft. Leftover vinyl doesn't have to go to waste either, as you can stick smaller pieces onto a Cricut mat.

For standard cardstock, vinyl and iron-on projects, the Maker 5 is very easy to use. Design Space tells you which material to select, which blade or tool to load and when to feed the mat into the machine, so you spend more time creating and less time worrying about settings.

This is where the Maker 5 earns its place as Cricut's flagship. The Explore range handles everyday crafting well, but I'd recommend the Maker to anyone serious about quilting, sewing or fabric projects. In fact, anything that requires more power and precision.

The rotary blade cuts fabric accurately and quickly, without endless measuring or hand-cutting shapes. You'll need to buy the rotary blade and housing separately, along with a pink FabricGrip mat, available in 12 x 12 inches and 12 x 24 inches.

For quilters, that's a huge time-saver. Design Space offers a selection of quilting blocks and templates, with components separated into shapes and colours, ready for cutting. Take the half-square triangle, a quilting staple that's surprisingly fiddly to cut by hand. You're cutting on the bias, so accuracy matters if the pieces are going to line up.

In Design Space, I create a square, add a diagonal line and change the line operation to Cut. After rotating it by 45 degrees, I position it over the square, select both elements and attach them. The result is two accurately cut triangles, ready to use. When you're making a quilt with dozens or even hundreds of identical pieces, having the machine do the repetitive cutting makes a real difference.
The Maker can also handle thicker, more demanding materials than the Explore machines, up to 3mm. Add a knife blade, another extra, and selected wood and chipboard projects open up too.

Engraving is one of my favourite things about the Maker 5. I photographed my house, uploaded it to Design Space, and used the software to prepare the image for engraving on an aluminium sheet. I was thrilled with the result. The machine picked out the lines and architectural details of the building, making a personalised piece that would suit a keepsake or gift. It's the kind of project that shows why I'd pick a Maker over an Explore if you want to experiment with different materials and techniques.
I also used the Maker 5 to engrave and colour a set of toothbrush gifts (pictured) for someone in my village. The process was challenging but fun, and the Maker 5 powered through the set with ease.

The engraving tool works with the Maker 5, but it isn't included in every bundle, so check what you're buying. You can also buy it separately, and Cricut sells suitable metal and acrylic blanks. With the right tools, the machine can also deboss, score, and perforate, leaving plenty of room to experiment beyond straightforward cutting.

Personalised vinyl lettering is one of the easiest projects to start with. I've used Design Space to make name tags for items that need a little personalisation. Select Text from the menu, type the names, and choose your font and size. When you're happy with the design, load your Smart Permanent Vinyl with the coloured side facing up. The machine cuts around the letters, leaving you to remove the unwanted vinyl.

This is where patience and a micro-weeding tool come in handy. The tiny pieces inside letters such as 'e' and 'a' can be fiddly to pick out, particularly in smaller text. Next, cut a piece of transfer tape, peel off the backing, and place it over the design. Use a scraper to make sure the lettering sticks to the tape, then lift it away and press it onto your chosen surface. Permanent vinyl is already adhesive-backed, so you don't need any extra glue.

Iron-on vinyl works similarly, with two key differences. Switch on Mirror in Design Space before cutting, and place the iron-on with its shiny side down on the mat. That way, the lettering reads correctly when you transfer it to fabric with a heat press.

Print Then Cut is one of the most useful features if you like making colourful stickers, gift labels or personalised stationery. Instead of being limited to vinyl colours and effects, you print a full-colour design on your home printer and let the Cricut cut around the individual shapes.

I use it for Christmas present labels. Create your design in Design Space, select Print Then Cut and send it to your printer. Once it's printed onto suitable printable vinyl or sticker paper, place the sheet on the Cricut mat and load it into the machine. The Maker 5 reads the registration marks and cuts around the printed designs, giving you colourful stickers with neat edges.
You'll need to buy printable vinyl or sticker paper separately, though, and the final results depend on your printer as well as the Cricut.
If you enjoy paper crafting, Design Space offers plenty to explore. You can choose pre-made templates, edit existing projects or start from scratch with your own images, shapes and text.

I've used it to make personalised Christmas gift tags, combining the machine's drawing and cutting functions. For one design, I set the machine to write a name with the pen, then switched to the fine-point blade to cut out the tag. For another, I used the blade to cut the lettering itself, which gives a different finish. Being able to write and cut in one project is useful, and Design Space makes it easy to arrange everything before you send the job to the machine.

You can also make paper flowers, boxes, cards, and Christmas decorations, with a huge range of templates you can customise in different colours, fonts, and materials. The included scoring tool helps here, giving you clean fold lines for cards and boxes.
Foil is another way to give cards, gift tags and decorations a more professional finish. The Maker 5 supports Cricut's Foil Transfer Tool, but you'll need to buy the tool and foil sheets separately.

I used the Cricut Foil Transfer Kit, which costs around £43.49 and includes the tool, foil sheets and adhesive strips. It took me three attempts to get the result I wanted, but once I'd got the hang of it, the finish was excellent.
Once it's finished, unload the mat and carefully remove your card. The metallic detail makes handmade cards and gifts look far more polished.

You control the Maker 5 through Cricut Design Space, which is available on desktop and mobile. It's easy to install and walks you through each stage of a project. There's a huge library of ready-made designs, templates, and fonts, so you don't need to be confident with graphic design to get started; you can upload your own images or build designs from scratch.
Cricut has also added AI-assisted image generation, which is handy if you have an idea but don't have the illustration skills or software to create the artwork yourself.

The basic Design Space app is free, and you don't need a Cricut Access subscription to operate the machine. Access unlocks a much larger library of images, fonts, and ready-made projects, and some features and content depend on it, so it's worth factoring the ongoing cost into your budget if you expect to use the library regularly.

What I like most is how the software guides you through the making process. Pick your project, choose your material, follow the instructions, and the machine does the hard work while you focus on the creative side.
Choosing a Cricut can be confusing with so many models around. The Maker 5 sits at the top of the range, but that doesn't mean it's right for everyone.
The Maker 4 is still very capable, and the two share much of the same cutting performance and tool compatibility.
The Maker 5 is smaller and lighter, has USB-C connectivity and a revised tool and pen-loading system, and handles compatible materials up to 3mm thick, compared with the Maker 4's 2.4mm.
Both cut at up to 14.1 inches per second, so there's no speed advantage. If you already own a Maker 4, I'd only switch if the smaller footprint, lighter body or workflow improvements matter to you.

The Explore 5 is much more affordable and ideal for everyday crafting. It handles vinyl, paper, cardstock and iron-on materials, and it's a great choice for stickers, cards, personalised gifts and decorations. It doesn't have the Maker's full range of tools, though.
If you're a quilter, want to cut fabric with a rotary blade, engrave metal, or work with more demanding materials, choose the Maker 5.
For many hobby crafters, the Explore 5 will be perfectly adequate. But if you want to grow into more ambitious projects, the Maker gives you far more flexibility.

The Cricut Maker 5 is an excellent cutting machine, and versatility remains its biggest strength. Whether you're making personalised labels, Christmas decorations, paper flowers, cards, fabric patterns, or engraved keepsakes, it can do very little with the right tool and material.

I like how easy it is to set up and use. The smaller size is welcome; the lighter body makes it easier to move around, and the software takes much of the guesswork out of creating projects. Print Then Cut is great, and the engraving shows how much potential there is beyond everyday vinyl and paper crafts.

The extras add up, though. For quilting, you'll need a rotary blade and FabricGrip mat. Engraving, foiling and other specialist projects need their own tools and materials, and printable vinyl is another cost if you plan to make stickers. The supplied cardstock is useful for getting started, but I found it stuck to the mat when I tried to remove it, so peel it away carefully.

If you're upgrading from a Maker 3, the doubled cutting speed makes a compelling case. Maker 4 owners should be more cautious, as the smaller design and extra material thickness are useful, but the cutting performance is largely the same.

For anyone buying their first serious Cricut, though, the Maker 5 is a smart buy. It's easy to use, surprisingly compact for what it can do, and it lets you experiment with a huge range of projects. If you're a quilter or someone who likes to make a little bit of everything, this is the Cricut I'd choose.

Julie Dean is a former doctor and occupational therapist by profession, which inspired her to start sewing and quilting as a therapeutic activity. She is passionate about her craft and has been quilting and using Cricut for over five years. As well as selling her own designs and products on Etsy, Julie has taken commissions for interior design agencies to create bespoke quilts, including Beata Heuman. Julie's work has appeared in Architectural Digest.
