items.title: The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next
paragraphs: "Stop Me If You Think You've Heard This One Before" sang Morrissey, as part of The Smiths in 1987, shortly before the band's acrimonious divorce.
It's a lyric Brexit veterans might be humming to themselves this week. Maybe even the prime minister, who is an avid fan of the Manchester band.
Some of the names - and arguments - that defined the Brexit period inside and outside Parliament are starting to emerge again, as the debate about the UK's relationship with the EU returns.
"It's like déjà vu with knobs on," said one veteran of the Leave campaign to us.

A new group called Stay Out has been set up, backed by figures who were part of the official Leave campaign in 2016. Boris Johnson has been back in the headlines, saying he still thinks Britons would choose to be outside the bloc.

Pro-EU groups such as the European Movement are raising their voices, pointing to the range of politicians, diplomats and academics they have supporting their argument. And a steady stream of Labour figures are now emerging to say they want to rejoin.

The former Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy made the argument on the BBC on Wednesday, saying Labour should go into the next election backing renegotiating membership of the EU and then putting that to people in another referendum.

He joins a list of cabinet ministers under Sir Keir Starmer who want to revisit EU membership; a list that includes former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, former Business Secretary Peter Kyle and former Welsh Secretary Jo Stevens. Others who served around Sir Keir's cabinet table think the same privately.
That is significant. Yes, they all backed Remain in 2016. But these are figures who were part of a government elected on a manifesto saying it was important to make Brexit work.

They set red lines in that manifesto because they thought the public had moved on. But they have now decided to say - most of them very publicly - that they think the picture has changed and the UK needs to think again.
The prime minister has opened the door to all options, from single market membership to rejoining the customs union to a referendum on full membership.

But in recent days, his language has softened a little from the clear commitment in his party conference speech that around the time of this Friday's summit he would "lay out to the country" the different options for Britain's long-term relationship with Brussels.
After some confusion about when this would take place, the government now says this will happen around the time that Burnham presents his 10-year plan, right before Parliament's Christmas break.

Burnham's allies say this will allow him to tie his EU policy more closely to his domestic agenda, arguing that a different arrangement with Europe would help with his other priorities such as the cost of living and re-industrialisation.
Others worry that the all-consuming nature of the EU debate means that it will drown out the other parts of the 10-year plan.
What remains unclear is the timeframe for the process that will follow Burnham setting out what he sees as the different Brexit options.

The prime minister has always been clear that Labour's commitments in its 2024 manifesto not to rejoin the single market or the customs union - let alone the EU altogether - still stand until the next general election.
And it was to those manifesto red lines that Burnham returned when asked about rejoining the EU at PMQs on Wednesday.
Yet those would not preclude Burnham initiating negotiations now on an arrangement breaking those red lines, which would take effect after the next general election.

Nevertheless, some on the prime minister's own side ponder that - having turned the volume up on the whole issue this autumn - he might be wise to turn it down a little in the new year, so it doesn't risk drowning out other things ministers want to talk about.

Andy Burnham is a prime minister who likes to explore things out loud. It's part of what he sees as a new way of doing politics, where he answers questions honestly and is prepared to discuss ideas while they are being formed, not just after they are a settled position.
It is a style that seeks to present a sense of a desired direction, even if some of the specifics end up being walked back from.
But even though it might be some time before the government has an official position on the future relationship, plenty of people are discussing what might happen next.
"It is all go again! My inbox is full of the same old stuff I thought I'd seen the back of years ago," one senior figure told us.
There are some nerves in the Labour Party about what might happen next. MPs who we have spoken to hold a range of views, which shows why this won't be plain-sailing.
Some are worried about re-opening the debate, calling it "toxic".
Others worry that the prime minister could disappoint pro-EU voters if he doesn't go far enough.
Others still wonder if the argument has changed enough that voters would decide differently in a new referendum.
"Both sides need fresh arguments, not the ones we all got tired of last time," said one.
"If this just looks like politicians wanting to rejoin because they never got over leaving then it's dead on arrival.

"If we can show that actually this is being led by businesses, by farmers, by different parts of society who need to rejoin because of the ways Brexit has harmed them, then it's a different matter," said another.
And what would the new EU the UK could rejoin look like?
Some Labour MPs ponder that the EU is changing – with the possibility of more right-wing leaders at the top table. They question whether they would want to be part of that.

A long standing diplomat from an EU member state said that the possibility of political change within the EU, alongside the recent offer of associate membership to Canada and at least the possibility of a potential future arrangement with Ukraine after any peace deal, could mean Brussels becomes more open to looser forms of membership that it has not been willing to consider before.
But then there is Scotland. If the government backs another EU vote, some Scottish MPs worry it adds to the argument for another vote on Scottish independence.
Despite the warnings, plenty of MPs are delighted that the Europe debate is back on the agenda.

One summed it up like this: "It doesn't really matter to me at this point where the PM is heading on this – it's all good for appealing to progressive voters. Just being seen to talk about this even without it necessarily being clear what we're going to do is a big change from before."
That seems to be a prevailing mood at the moment. Lots of Labour MPs are happy the EU debate is back. But not all of them.

Andy Burnham will on Friday sign a new deal with the EU which ministers believe will drive economic growth and cut red tape for British businesses. It will be heralded as a new moment for the relationship.
The government hasn't decided yet - but plenty of others have their own views.

items.title: Fictional Project designs home in Kerala to feel "one with the landscape"
paragraphs: Curving ceilings sweep down to frame the two small gardens that flank this home in Kerala, India, designed by local architecture studio Fictional Project.
Named Interstitial Living, the home in the village of Adoor was designed for a family of four who wanted to feel connected to the outside, in particular the lush greenery surrounding the site.
This led Fictional Project to pull the home’s built volume back to create space for two planted yards on either side, overlooked by the home’s pared-back and open interiors.
“The residence is careful not to overpower, becoming one with the landscape,” the studio told Dezeen.
Interstitial Living is organised around a bedroom at its centre, which is housed within a cubic volume finished in cement plaster.

A small window in this bedroom overlooks a potted tree within a cut-out in the floor of the adjacent living room, which faces the yard to the west through a row of full-height windows above a built-in timber bench.

On the opposite side of the home, the kitchen overlooks the eastern yard through a row of windows above its countertops. Both these spaces are defined by the curving white-plastered ceilings overhead, which sweep down from the centre of the home.

“The scale of the residence allows for intimate working spaces in the kitchen and a welcoming living room, all accentuated by the dynamic nature of the roof. The other spaces negotiate the private/public nature of the indoors,” the studio explained.
“The concavity of the roof creates a visual connection to the outdoors, becoming a marker that emerges from within the site.”
“It breaks the rigidity of a traditional sloping roof, helping create fluid indoor spaces. Nothing here is built or conceived in isolation, but rather as interconnected systems,” it added.
The smaller first floor contains a second bedroom, bathroom and a study area, which overlook the living space below from a steel-framed landing and internal windows.

While the internal finishes were kept minimal, the exterior of the home and its boundary walls were built using terracotta-toned textured blocks, which the studio described as introducing a sense of “groundedness and warmth”.

Other dwellings in Kerala recently featured on Dezeen include a home by InLe Architects framed and shaded by two large mango trees and a farmhouse by Evolving Radical Aesthetics that is built into a hillside above a carved-out, open-air temple.

items.title: Nvidia approaches Arm boss Rene Haas in search for new CEO
paragraphs: Nvidia’s headhunters have reportedly approached the chief executive of the Cambridge-based chip company Arm, in its search for a new leader after Jensen Huang’s dramatic exit.
Heidrick & Struggles, the recruiting firm hired by the company’s board, has started contacting potential candidates, according to Bloomberg.
It reported that Rene Haas, who joined Arm in 2013 and became chief executive in 2022, is among those approached.
Nvidia is searching for a replacement for Huang, one of the firm’s founders, who resigned last week after he admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman accused of spying for China.
Haas, 64, is viewed as the leading contender for the top job at Nvidia, having previously worked at the $3.6tn (£2.8tn) company for seven years as the general manager of its computing products.
Reports suggest that other potential candidates include: Ian Buck, an Nvidia vice-president; Lisa Su, AMD’s chief executive; and Johny Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer.

Arm, which is listed in New York but retains its global headquarters in Cambridge, has about 500 users of its chip designs worldwide, including Nvidia, Apple, Samsung and Qualcomm. The company employs more than 7,000 staff, including more than 3,000 in the UK. It is the biggest tech firm headquartered in Britain, now valued at $196bn.
Haas told a tech conference in Austin on Wednesday that Huang was “a legend”. “What he built at Nvidia is historic,” he said. “You don’t have many champions like that.”
Nvidia has sought to curb speculation that Huang could return to his role, after he said on Tuesday that he would be willing to come back.

He wrote in a statement: “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

It came after US president, Donald Trump, and Silicon Valley insiders – including Elon Musk, prominent venture capitalists and the disgraced Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick – called for Huang’s reinstatement.
However, the Nvidia chair, Harvey Jones, confirmed at the company’s quarterly earnings results this week that the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”.
Jones said that “while this was an unexpected transition … the board is proactively dealing with the consequences”.

Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, was named interim CEO last week and presented the financial results on Tuesday, which showed that its quarterly revenue had doubled from the same period a year ago to $115.84bn.

Huang agreed on Tuesday to appear before the House of Representatives foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party and the intelligence committee for transcribed interviews in early December. Nvidia also faces an investigation by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its business in China, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday.
Nvidia and Arm were approached for comment.

items.title: Meet Swedish Girls, Sabine Marcelis’s pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
paragraphs: Sabine Marcelis has nominated Swedish Girls as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project sponsored by Kohler. In this interview, we learn why the design duo deliberately play into stereotypes.

The steady emergence of Swedish Girls has not been lost on prolific Dutch designer Marcelis, who nominated the collective as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design over the next 20 years.
“I really like how they work with existing industrial production processes, yet the result very much speaks to the current culture,” Marcelis told Dezeen, explaining her selection.
Josefin Zachrisson and Mira Bergh run multidisciplinary studio Swedish Girls between Stockholm and Milan, creating furniture, installations and set design.

The duo met during their studies at Sweden’s Beckmans College of Design, where they graduated in 2019. They bonded over a desire to make work “without hierarchies” and maintain creative control of the studio’s output, which they prefer to call their ever-expanding “universe”.
The Big Bang for Swedish Girls was the selection of their collective’s tongue-in-cheek name, chosen after their first exhibition outing at Milan design week.
For experimental platform Alcova in 2021, Zachrisson and Bergh unveiled their ongoing metal rod Seats System project (pictured left).

Originally a single piece of modular seating without a defined front or back, the project has evolved into more metal pieces that follow the same design language, including a fruit bowl and a candle holder.

“We overheard people talking about our furniture, asking who made it, and others were like, ‘ah, it was those Swedish girls’, and we felt a bit belittled by it,” recalled Zachrisson. The duo had previously made work under their own names.

“The Swedish girl has obviously become a phenomenon,” added Bergh. “You know, blonde, sexy. But when we were talking about it, we also found it really funny because it’s so stereotypical. We thought we’d call ourselves Swedish Girls because everybody else was already calling us that.”

Humour is intrinsic to Zachrisson and Bergh’s interdisciplinary practice. Even their website, admired by Marcelis, was playfully designed as a Swedish Girls-branded Google search engine. It is meant to look like the internet itself, complete with mock web pages listing each of the collective’s projects.
“We got the idea when we launched the name Swedish Girls,” the pair explained.
“A professor from Beckmans called and said that we should change our name because when she Googled ‘Swedish Girls’, the search result was not exactly art and design,” they added.
“We thought that was so funny and decided to make Google about us instead of changing our name.”
Another of the duo’s wit-inflected projects is Only Fans, an installation presented at Gothenburg’s Röhsska design museum in 2024 during local music festival Way Out West.

Dubbed “a multidimensional art experience about fan culture” in all its forms, the installation included 25 electric fans, selected as a riff on adult content platform OnlyFans, where women are often the subject of scrutiny.
“The installation was interactive, so that visitors could stand in the middle of the fans in a hysterical storm,” said Bergh.

Alongside the fans, the collective presented seven laser-cut steel chairs emblazoned with I <3 Swedish Girls, along with a fanzine and female mannequins wearing “metal merch” designed by Zachrisson and Bergh.
“Our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things,” considered Zachrisson.

“But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life,” she continued. “It feels like a way to approach it that makes it accessible.”

“Sometimes it’s hard because we get these questions like, ‘are you a feminist?'” added the designer. “But it’s inherently political to be a woman moving through the world. Our work is just reacting to our reality.”
The pair is keen to highlight that although they make furniture, “social values are always a starting point” for their projects.
“We really want to have a practice that feels purposeful,” said Zachrisson, considering the significance of partnering with institutions like design museums.
“We’ve realised that showing work in public spaces is the most important thing,” she continued.
“Especially because the materials and processes we use have become quite expensive. So we want to put our pieces in public spaces so that everyone can take part in some way.”
“You meet all different kinds of people, and we talk to them and grow from it,” added Bergh.

Despite Swedish Girls’ various collaborations and recurring presence at Milan design week, seven years after leaving Beckmans, Bergh and Zachrisson continue to work in cafes and supermarkets to fund their design practice.
The duo are hyperaware of the difficulties faced by emerging creatives, especially those like themselves who, as they put it, “want to listen to your gut and be close to the process”.

“The hardest thing is to earn money,” said Bergh. “We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money on very quick timelines. I feel like we should have more respect.”
“You don’t get paid in a way where you as two people can survive,” added Zachrisson. “But all these years of working and keeping our creative integrity is paying off in every way except financially.”
When it comes to building their studio, the designers consider themselves to be playing the long game.

“Long term, it’s an investment to do it this way because we have now created a context where we can feel freedom and gain respect, which is why we were so happy when Sabine nominated us,” said Zachrisson.
“You can measure success in so many different ways and with this we feel respected, and that is so valuable.”
The duo said funding that they won from Sweden’s Konstnärsnämnden arts council after graduating gave them a significant leg up when they were just starting out.

Zachrisson and Bergh are concerned that scholarships like theirs have been scarcer across Sweden in recent years thanks to the country’s right-wing administration, which came into power in 2022 and has only just been voted out of office.
“All the artists we have talked to have felt an extreme difference in that time,” noted Zachrisson. “The share of the total budget allocated to culture has not been this low in 26 years.”
Still, the pair are confident and excited about what’s to come.
“It comes in handy that we have a broad practice,” said Bergh. “We have plans for the future to make it easier for ourselves to be designers.”
“I like how they surprise with their projects and feel like we have only seen chapter one of their story,” concluded Marcelis. “And I can’t wait to discover the next chapter.”

items.title: Mark Speakman resigns and says Liberals face ‘existential threat’ as NSW exodus continues
paragraphs: Former New South Wales opposition leader, Mark Speakman, will not contest his seat at the March state election, the latest in a mass exodus of MPs under the Liberal leader who replaced him, Kellie Sloane.

In a late-night speech on Thursday, the final sitting day of NSW’s legislative assembly ahead of the vote, Speakman said he would not contest his south Sydney seat of Cronulla, which he has held since 2011.

He is the eighth out of 24 current Liberal MPs to announce they will not re-contest their seat in March, following Jordan Lane, Mark Coure, Tanya Davies, Ray Williams, James Griffin, Mark Taylor and Alister Henskens.
The announcement comes almost a year to the day after Speakman resigned from the leadership of the opposition in a spill in favour of Sloane, who was elected unopposed.
In that time the Coalition has gone from commanding 28% of the primary vote in New South Wales to 23%, Sydney Morning Herald Resolve polling suggests.
Labor has gone from 37% to 30%, while One Nation, which Resolve did not start polling separately until March, is currently at 26%.

Last week, Sloane said her party would not form government with One Nation, but she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement. The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the Liberals to go into a coalition with One Nation.

In his speech in the dying minutes of the parliamentary term, Speakman, a member of the party’s moderate faction, warned the Liberals against becoming “Labor lite” or “One Nation lite”, saying they should stick to the values of “Menzian Liberalism”.
Referencing Pauline Hanson’s notion of “monoculture”, Speakman said Australia was “the most successful multicultural society on the planet” and was “so much better for it”.
“You know, we hear certain people say we want a monoculture, and that people who don’t support that monoculture somehow are enemies of Australia, hate Australia,” he said.
“I love Australia for its multiculturalism. Diversity is our strength. It is our strength, and we should build on that.”
Speakman, a barrister, served as minister for the environment between 2015 and 2017, and was attorney general between 2017 and the Perrottet government’s defeat in the 2023 election.
He was chosen as Liberal and opposition leader following Perrottet’s resignation, a position he held until November last year.

On Thursday, he said being opposition leader “is often said to be the toughest job in politics” and while it had “ultimately unravelled” for him, he had mostly led an opposition “which was competitive with, or even ahead of, the government in the polls”.

He said his record as attorney general included legislating for NSW to be the first Australian jurisdiction to criminalise coercive control, introducing affirmative consent tests in criminal sexual assault trials and reforming criminal and civil child sexual abuse cases.

Speakman’s resignation, ending speculation which bubbled up again when he spoke during question time on Thursday, is the latest blow for Sloane, who he said in his leaving speech had the “attributes to be a great premier”.
Earlier on Thursday, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, announced former Liberal councillor and parliamentary staffer Tanya Raffoul would contest the Liberal-held seat of Epping as a Labor candidate.

items.title: Incoming House majority leader Katherine Clark stresses Democratic unity
paragraphs: Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6045750/nx-s1-10011335" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Rep. Katherine Clark, D-Mass., after House Democratic leadership elections Wednesday on Capitol Hill in Washington. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images hide caption
House Democrats needed a bigger room Wednesday to accommodate their newly expanded caucus, according to Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts.
Nominated to become the first woman to serve as House majority leader next year, Clark reflected on the moment in an interview with Morning Edition on Thursday.

"It was really looking at the diversity of that caucus, people who have been sent to Congress from all walks of life, that gives me the optimism and the energy that we can really deliver for the American people," she said.

Clark, who is currently the House minority whip, was nominated for House majority leader by a unanimous voice vote. Democrats also nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker and Pete Aguilar for majority whip.
The incoming leadership faces the challenge of lowering living costs while investigating alleged corruption in the Trump administration.
"Of course we can," she said when asked whether Democrats could accomplish both. "That's our responsibility."
She also called President Trump's description of himself as "Mr. Veto" a "stunning statement," expressing hope for bipartisan cooperation on healthcare.
But Democrats face divisions within their own ranks.

Jeffries won his nomination 251-11. Opposition came from incoming progressives including Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York and Adam Hamawy of New Jersey. They have pressed for Medicare for All, immigration enforcement reforms and an end to the war in Gaza.
The two leaders have differed over U.S. aid to Israel. In July, Clark voted for a Republican amendment that would have cut aid to Israel, while Jeffries opposed it.
Despite that disagreement and concerns among other Democrats about Jeffries' leadership, she emphasized party unity when asked whether the 11 votes against him could complicate Democrats' agenda.
"We are having conversations with every part of our new caucus, and they are united behind making life better for working people," she said.
Listen to the full interview by clicking on the blue button above.
The radio interview was edited by Ally Schweitzer. The web copy was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

items.title: Top House Democrat questions what Trump accomplished in Xi-Putin summit
paragraphs: Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6046487/nx-s1-10011347" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., speaks to reporters outside a House Democratic Caucus meeting at the Longworth House Office Building in Washington on Nov. 10. Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images hide caption

Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, questioned Thursday what President Trump accomplished in his summit with the leaders of China and Russia, warning that the meeting could undermine U.S. alliances.
"I wish he had a plan and a strategy if he was going to meet with them and goals. Apparently, he does not," Meeks told Morning Edition.

His comments followed Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, which ended with few signs of progress on nuclear arms control or the war in Ukraine.

Meeks said he feared the leaders were discussing dividing the world into spheres of influence, potentially sidelining U.S. allies. He also questioned the lack of meaningful agreements on nuclear weapons and artificial intelligence safety.
Asked about the Nvidia scandal, Meeks said he would confront Xi over Chinese espionage and intellectual property theft and warn of possible retaliation.
"When it comes to our national security, that's where we draw a red line," he said.

Meeks argued that U.S. diplomats should have raised concerns about Chinese espionage and intellectual property theft before the summit to establish clear goals for the talks. In his conversation with NPR's A Martínez, Meeks also called for reducing tariffs on U.S. allies while pressing China to end its support for Russia's war in Ukraine.
Listen to the full interview by clicking the blue button above.
The radio interview was edited by J Mai and Olivia Hampton. The web version was adapted by Majd Al-Waheidi and edited by Treye Green.

items.title: Guardian Australia takes home two Walkley awards for excellence in journalism
paragraphs: Guardian Australia journalists have won two Walkley awards, one for a story about the systemic betrayal of a woman who was killed by her partner, and another for an exclusive story that revealed Pauline Hanson had travelled to the US with mining billionaire Gina Rinehart.

Investigative reporter Sarah Martin won the award for print/text news report for her exclusive story that revealed the One Nation leader and her chief of staff, James Ashby, travelled with Rinehart on the mining magnate’s Gulfstream 700 on 27 October last year.
The pair stayed at Rinehart’s Palm Beach mansion, close to US president Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort.
After Guardian Australia published details of Hanson’s flight, her office lodged an amendment to the registrar of senators’ interests declaring the sponsored travel.

Queensland correspondent Ben Smee and the Guardian team won the award for coverage of Indigenous affairs for the story of the betrayal of Kardell Lomas, who repeatedly sought help – from domestic violence support services and the police – to escape the violent and dangerous man who killed her.
Lomas had 24 interactions with various agencies – and she repeatedly disclosed fears for her safety, death threats, serious violence and other abuse.
Smee and Martin were finalists in two other categories, Martin for ‘Inside One Nation’ and Smee for his feature “‘Starting to frighten me’: the final weeks of Hannah Clarke’s life”.

Business editor Jonathan Barrett was also a finalist, in the print/text feature writing category, for his story “‘A child goes to bed and doesn’t wake up’: the families left in shock after the sudden death of their healthy children”.

The 2026 Walkley print/text award for feature writing under 4,000 words was awarded to the Australian Financial Review’s Sam Buckingham-Jones for the story “Maccas in a Rolls: inside Kyle Sandilands’ pivot to $100 tradie plans”.
For feature writing over 4,000 words, the Age and The Sydney Morning Herald’s Melissa Fyfe and Carla Hildebrandt took home the award for their story “Virginia: the Final Chapter”.
The scoop of the year was awarded to the ABC team behind “Bondi: what ASIO knew”, which included Sean Rubinsztein-Dunlop, Olivia Caisley, and Michael Workman.
Tony Wright, an associate editor and special writer for The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald, took home the award for outstanding contribution to journalism.

items.title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
paragraphs: Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.
The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.

The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.
The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.

Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”

Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.
“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.

The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.
Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.
“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”
Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.

The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”

Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.
The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.
A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

items.title: Rockstar designed GTA 6's buildings by imagining who would live in them
paragraphs: Grand Theft Auto VI is almost here, and it reminds us that a good open world needs more than a lot of buildings. It needs places that feel as though they existed before you arrived and will carry on after you've driven off. In GTA 6, Rockstar is trying to achieve that by thinking about the people behind every home, business and building in Leonida.

“For every visual design, we are getting into the heads of the people who would have inhabited that place and role-playing how the final look would have come about,” says Miriam Bellard, Vice President of Art: Visual Development. “Would they have hired an architect or DIY’d it? Are they trying to express their status and prestige, or is it all about comfort and practicalities? Are they messy or tidy? What is their taste?”

It's a wonderfully practical way to approach world-building, and after playing GTA 6 for three weeks, I can say each building feels unique yet makes sense, both to explore and to use within the game's world. Rather than designing a building as an isolated piece of architecture, the team imagines the decisions behind it. That gives each place a personality, whether it's somewhere industrial, scruffy, decadent or dangerous.

“I love that we get to do that for such a wide variety of people and places,” Bellard adds. “Everything from industrial to scruffy to decadent to dangerous. We get to design all of that – and it’s lots of fun!”

That variety matters in a world inspired by Florida, where the landscape shifts between sun-soaked beaches, retirement communities, rural enclaves, and high-end shopping districts. John Macpherson, Senior Design Director: World & Population, says reference trips and time spent with locals helped the team capture the state's “raw energy and vibrant chaos”.

The result is a world where even a building's appearance can tell you something about who lives or works there, and I found it can also help you plan heists and robberies by understanding the flow of a bank or store. Moreover, Rockstar's designers and artists have played with Vice City and the State's history, building wear and tear and architectural trends into its world. In GTA 6, architecture is another way to get to know Leonida.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

items.title: Shigeru Ban unveils proposal for tent-like church in Rome
paragraphs: A cross-shaped roof will mark the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex in Rome, Italy, which Japanese studio Shigeru Ban Architects is designing with local architect Vittorio Petrucci.
The church will occupy a currently underused site in Ostia, a coastal neighbourhood for which the project is hoped to become an architectural landmark.
The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be constructed with a frame of timber – Ban’s signature material – with a deliberately simple form that is intended to evoke a fabric tent.

According to Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci, the overarching goal is for the church to help establish a greater sense of community and place in the area, which they describe as having a “fragmented urban fabric”.
“We wanted to design a place of worship that also brings the whole community together,” said Ban.

“The timber structure expresses the idea of a tent, a simple, welcoming form that connects people with one another and with their surroundings. Through this project, we hope architecture can help create a new sense of belonging in the neighbourhood.”
Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci’s proposal was the winning entry of a competition for the church.

It is one of five winning designs selected as part of the New Churches Programme – an initiative led by the local church district, the Diocese of Rome, and the Italian Episcopal Conference, an assembly of Catholic bishops, to provide permanent homes for parish communities in the region.
As part of the project, four new churches will be built, while one existing parish complex will be extended.
The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be built on a raised public plaza, with various parish facilities, community spaces and a priest’s residence embedded below.

Its key feature will be its angular roof, which is shaped like a cross but not immediately readable as one. This is modelled on a latent cross – a feature in sacred architecture, in which a cross shape is integrated in the spatial design, without being clearly visible.

Inside, the church will have a diamond-shaped plan, with large stained-glass windows positioned in the four cardinal directions. They will be triangular in shape and feature designs modelled on neighbourhood street art.

The project will be complete with a landscaped park, as well as various recreational and sports facilities, which the studios said will “create opportunities for social interaction and everyday activities”.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex is not the first church project by Ban. Among his others is the landmark Cardboard Cathedral in New Zealand, which is formed of 98 cardboard tubes combined with wood and polycarbonate. We named it the most significant building of 2013 in our list of the 25 most significant buildings of the 21st century.
Other Italian church proposals recently featured on Dezeen include Stefano Boeri Architetti’s design for the Ambrosian Monastery in Milan, which will have a sail-like roof form.
Images courtesy of Shigeru Ban Architects

items.title: Forget Apple EarPods, these white wired earphones sound better and at $19 are 50% off
paragraphs: I've been on the hunt for the best budget wired IEMs for a while now, and though there are loads of options out there, if you're looking for that specific Gen 1 Apple EarPods look, this is by far the best deal.
You can get 50% off the Sennheiser CX 80U earphones, down from $39.95 to $19.95 over at Amazon.

As far as what you're getting for $20, the CX 80U is a fairly neutral set that has plenty of detail, but definitely doesn't pack loads of bass. There's mid bass, which will give you good thumping bass drums and the like, but they lack the deep sub-bass that make hip hop's 808 drops really shine.

Sennheiser launched the CX 80U earphones in January 2026 at a $39.95 retail price. By November 2026, US prices dropped to between $29.99 and $39.95, so this Black Friday deal price of $19 is a genuine record low price.

As far as specifications go, the CX 80U includes a 9.7mm dynamic neodymium driver and has a 28 ohm impedance, with 119dB sensitivity. What that means for you and me is the driver is a medium size to be able to generate a good range of frequencies. It's low impedance and high sensitivity means it's easy to drive. That means the CX 80U is a plug and play earphone, and you don't need to worry about it not getting loud enough for you.
They weigh 14.3 grams (very light) and feature a 1.2 metre cable (standard), a USB-C plug with a 24-bit 96kHz DAC, an inline microphone, a single button, and three ear tip sizes.

With the CX 80U you get a clear tuning, a light fit, passive isolation, and zero charging. Cons include missing volume buttons and no water resistance, so if this is going to be your gym set, consider that.

items.title: Bank your stolen cash, bring a change of clothes, go easy on the bloodshed: 15 tips for playing Grand Theft Auto VI
paragraphs: Leonida is so huge as to be overwhelming and in the opening hours, the game bombards you with tonnes of info that you will inevitably forget. But I’ve done nothing but play this game for weeks and I’m here to help. Here’s what I wished I’d known at the start

Walk faster. I found that Jason and Lucia walk incredibly slowly. If you go into the options menu, you can select “fast walk” as the default walking speed, which sped them up just a little without ruining the pace or atmosphere of the game. While you’re in there, you can also customise plenty of other things, including controls and button mapping.

Don’t worry too much about money. In the opening chapters of the game – which could take you 20 or more hours to play through – it can feel like everything is expensive and there’s never enough cash. But later on, you will have many more ways to make money and a $200 cab ride will feel like nothing. This problem will fix itself, so in the meantime, just enjoy yourself.

Bank your cash at ATMs. If you get busted by the cops or killed by anyone, you will lose a lot of your cash – and anything you had in your stash bags, too. Trouble can start at any time in Vice City, so it’s not a great idea to walk around with holdalls full of drugs and pockets full of money. Use the BuckMe app on your phone to find your nearest ATM and bank your cash, so it remains safe. And you can stash those holdalls in the trunk of your car.

Do not use your own vehicle for anything illegal. If your car is hanging around near a crime scene and the cops identify it, it’ll get impounded, which is a massive pain because you have to steal it back. Instead, just hotwire a getaway car and have it parked nearby. Then you can abandon it later with impunity.

Get your partner to fence your goods. If you cannot be bothered to drive all the way to a fence, you can hand your stash bags to your partner and ask them to do it before returning to you. You might get a little less money this way, but it saves repetitive drives and conversations. Later in the game you can also ask your fences to pick stuff up from stash boxes in your owned garages.

During missions, make liberal use of the “retry from checkpoint” option. Outside of story missions, you have to deal with the consequences of your blunders in GTA VI, whether you miss your highway exit on a long drive, pull out a gun at the wrong moment in a restaurant and start a mini gang war, or mess up a robbery and get busted. But inside the missions? You can neatly erase all your problems by pausing the game and selecting “retry checkpoint”. Take a wrong turn? Retry checkpoint. Shot the wrong person? Retry checkpoint. Accidentally run someone over? Retry checkpoint. Ended up miles from where you’re supposed to be after escaping the cops? Retry checkpoint, it usually gets you closer. This saved me a lot of time and frustration, and there was still quite enough unpredictable chaos and self-inflicted disaster to deal with outside of the story missions.

Don’t kill anyone unless you have to. Surprisingly you can get a lot of crime done in GTA VI without doing much killing at all (outside of story missions where you have to shoot a zillion bad guys/pursuing cops). On robberies and stick-ups you’re rewarded for stealth. You can sometimes sneak in unnoticed through back doors and avoid security entirely. But if that’s not an option – if a security guard starts shooting instead of surrendering when you point a gun at them, for instance – then non-lethal solutions attract less trouble from the cops. You can shoot an arm or leg to disable someone rather than killing them, or knock them out with the butt of a gun. All of this will make your getaway easier and make you feel less guilty.

Understand how heat works. Crime is a little more complex in GTA VI. Your wanted level is still indicated by stars, and this is directly related to the seriousness of your crime. Stealing a car is one star, robbing a store is three or more, killing cops always adds another star. The police response escalates with your wanted level, determining whether they send out helicopters or set up roadblocks to stop you. But now there’s also “heat”: in areas where you’ve previously committed a crime, the cops will be looking for you. They’ll have a description of your car and your outfit. A simple thing you can do is always put on a mask and a hat before you do anything that might attract the cops – then you can simply remove them afterwards. It’s also wise to change vehicles once you’re out of sight of witnesses and police. Changing outfits is more difficult: you have to store them in the trunk of your own car or buy new ones – but I found that changing cars and wearing masks was usually enough.

Watch your criminal profile. GTA VI tracks your actions as both Jason and Lucia and gives them a criminal profile. Unnecessary violence such as running people over or shooting bystanders will quickly turn you from “professional” or “hardened” to “violent” or “psycho”, which has serious repercussions for the game’s story and ending. If you go too far then either character can become “irredeemable”, and there’s no way back. You can get your criminal profile back into the professional range by being as non-lethal as possible and leaving innocent bystanders alone.

Expect people to fight back. This is Leonida: pedestrians are often packing. If you start behaving badly or insulting people on the street, someone might throw a punch or pull a gun on you. Drive into someone’s car and they might have an episode of road rage and spent the next few minutes chasing you down and trying to run you off the road. This is all extremely fun – insulting people on the street sometimes leads to some hilarious back-and-forth exchanges – but if you’re trying to stay out of trouble, don’t mess with the locals.

Prepare for big thefts. You can get away with a simple liquor store smash’n’grab by running in, waving your gun about and then getting outta there, but later in the game, if you want to rob anywhere with a real return – a bank, or a big jewellery store – then you need to have a plan for when the police inevitably turn up. Park your car somewhere quiet and fill the trunk with a change of clothes, so that you can return to it after the job, stash your loot and weapons in the trunk, and disguise yourself. If you’re clever with this you can walk or drive right past the cops after a job, safe in the knowledge that you won’t be recognised. Parking your own car in a parking garage is an especially clever option, as helicopters can’t see you in there.

Rob the criminals instead. I wasn’t far into this game before I started to feel bad about terrorising small business owners for money, but you don’t technically have to do much of this. You can make just as much money by robbing other criminals. Leonida is full of gang hangouts that you can easily infiltrate, full of drugs and cash that you can steal. The risk is that gang members will shoot you on sight if they see you skulking about, but helpfully, that also makes me feel less bad about shooting back.

Know when to cut your losses. Whether you’re robbing a store or trying to steal cocaine from under the noses of terrifying biker gangs, things can go south very fast in GTA. Sometimes the best idea is just to get outta thereand avoid losing whatever you’ve gained.

Sometimes it’s easier to get away on foot. If the cops are really chasing you down, with armoured cars and helicopters, it can be very difficult to get away in a car. Sometimes the best thing you can do is get out and run away on foot, making use of alleyways and covered parking garages in the city and tree cover out in the countryside. I once spent a good 15 minutes failing to get away from the police on the highway, crashing three cars in the process, before diving into a river and swimming desperately to the other side, ending up hiding on a golf course with $100k in stolen bills.

Take your time. This truly is an extraordinarily massive game and it will take weeks to get through even if you play for several hours a day. If you’re enjoying yourself, don’t feel like you have to rush to make progress. I found every chapter of this game to be enjoyable in its own way, and they all feel different from each other. We’ve been waiting a long time for this game – why not linger?

items.title: From training clips to thirst traps: why athletes are turning to OnlyFans
paragraphs: “I’m sick and tired of it.” Bart Swings tossed his jacket behind him. It was August 2025, the Winter Olympics were less than six months away, and the Belgian Olympic champion’s injured knee was not getting better. The clip, profanity and all, later ran on the Belgian evening news along with the weather and the football. But the injury update didn’t come from an interview – it was broadcast on the speed skater’s OnlyFans channel.

The subscription site, best known for porn dudes, cam girls and dubiously horny couples, has quietly assembled one of the stranger rosters in professional sport. The list, about 285 athletes deep, includes Olympic speed skaters and rowers, tennis players, surfers and golfers. And, despite its racy reputation, many of the athletes on OnlyFans are not putting out adult content.

Swings uploads training routines and race clips. He has no paid page at all but receives sponsorship from the site, and told Front Office Sports it is “really a meaningful part”. It helped him make it to Milan this February, where he finished ninth in the men’s mass start as he attempted to defend his Olympic title.

And while OnlyFans features athletes such as Wimbledon finalist Nick Kyrgios and former NBA star Lamar Odom, who earned millions of dollars during their careers, it is mainly the preserve of those who – like Swings – will never become rich through their sports. Many say it helps them keep their careers alive.

Avery Poppinga, a sponsored beach volleyball pro with about 144,000 Instagram followers, earns about $2,500 a month from her paid OnlyFans page alone – enough to quit her remote job and concentrate on her athletic career. Poppinga’s free page has swimsuit shots and selfies, while her paid VIP page offers “racier bikini and lingerie content.”

German Olympic champion Lisa Buckwitz estimates a bobsled season costs $59,000 to sustain. She joined OnlyFans in 2024 and while she poses provocatively, Buckwitz says she will “absolutely not” appear naked. “[OnlyFans] allows me to finance my team,” the 31-year-old told Bild. “It’s the best thing that’s ever happened to me.”

It’s easy to see why athletes can make money on OnlyFans, their careers give them the kind of bodies a lot of people want to ogle. If they are being sexualized anyway, why not make money out of it? Olympic rower Robbie Manson, who delivers what he calls “artistic nudes,” claims the platform helped double his income, with the New Zealander admitting many of his photos are “thirst traps”. Ex-UFC fighter Paige VanZant has said she made more money in 24 hours on OnlyFans than in her entire fighting career, that’s despite keeping her page “PG-13.”

Kurts Adams Rozentals, a British canoeist on an annual grant of about $21,000, says he used OnlyFans in 2025 to earn more than $130,000. He was also banned for two years over a video he posted to Instagram. “I saw a direct correlation,” he told the BBC, “of me making those type of videos and my life situation improving.” He also hinted at why many athletes turn to the internet to make extra money in the first place. “This ban would have never happened if athletes were funded properly,” he said.

The OnlyFans business model is simple, at least on paper. The site keeps 20%, and the rest goes to the athlete. With 47 permanent employees, OnlyFans is raking in $1.55bn a year in revenue. The site also actively courts athletes. Since 2023, it has tried to offset its porn image by officially sponsoring athletes. Some agree to the soft blue and white logo on a shirtsleeve or offer behind-the-scenes access and training tips. But what the athlete-turned-content-creator posts is up to them.

This intrusion into sanctioned sport has been polarizing. The UCI, the world governing body for cycling, barred mountain biker Lewis Buchanan from racing in OnlyFans kit. Likewise, National Hot Rod Association driver Summer Richardson was banned from competing as an OnlyFans sponsored athlete before the 2025 season. US college sports’ main governing body, the NCAA, supports NIL (Name, Image, and Likeness) deals but won’t allow adult content platforms. And in pro sports, contracts keep a morality clause to protect against conduct deemed “detrimental to the reputation” of the organization.

Other sports have either embraced OnlyFans or remained silent. The US team in motorcycle grand prix racing, Moto2, was an early recipient of an OnlyFans sponsorship: they now race as “OnlyFans American Racing.” Professional tennis boasts several OnlyFans athletes. Kyrgios does not post adult content but has a free page with behind-the-scenes footage “from on court to everyday life.” American Sachia Vickery uploads “suggestive” content, according to her representative but does not post full nudity or sex acts. Océane Dodin of France signed an OnlyFans sponsorship in December 2025. At Roland-Garros in May, she talked publicly about her account, yet Nike and Wilson stayed on as her sponsors. “Come discover my sexy side,” Dodin’s OnlyFans bio reads. “And if you want to see more, come message me.”

And messaging can be profitable. According to writer and analyst Ed Elson, 70% of the money that flows through OnlyFans comes through DMs, where creators communicate with their subscribers. But many creators now outsource this part of their business to third parties, a whole ecosystem of “chatting agencies” has sprung up to meet the demand. While a subscriber may think they know who they are talking to, the person on the other side could well be a worker in India or Pakistan. Or a bot.

“Loneliness is lucrative,” NYU professor Scott Galloway wrote in an essay, titled “Lonely Fans”, on Medium last year. “But that success comes at huge cost”. Galloway makes the case that sites like OnlyFans degrade both parties. Creators may abandon their careers to become a fantasy figure, while fans abandon real-life relationships for one with someone they will never truly know. A Guardian investigation this year also raised concerns about how male-run agencies seek to exploit young female creators they find on the site. Mexican diver Diego Balleza Isaias, another OnlyFans athlete, firmly believes that “no athlete does this because they like it. It’s always going to be because you need to”.

The hard truth is that only a tiny handful of OnlyFans creators will become rich. The ones who do well tend to arrive with an audience, or come with a whiff of scandal. Ultrarunner Camille Herron once held world records from 50 miles to six days. Then, in 2024, she and husband Conor Holt were implicated in doctoring the Wikipedia pages of rival runners. She lost a Lululemon sponsorship two days later. This September, she announced she was becoming an adult content creator. Odom, meanwhile, won two NBA titles during his playing career, and made more than $100m in salary. He was better known to non-NBA fans for his marriage to Khloé Kardashian, and his near-fatal overdose in a Nevada brothel.

Herron and Odom have been quick to claim success on OnlyFans. Within two weeks of her announcement, Herron posted she had “moved up to the top 0.7%” on the site (The top 1% of its earners are estimated to make at least $49,000 a year and the very top make millions). According to Odom’s representative, he made more than $50,000 in his first eight days. They appear to have varying approaches to their accounts. Odom is keeping it vaguetelling TMZ: “I’m not here to tell you what you will or won’t see.” Herron has posted explicit content on her page. She says she has no regrets. “I was freed to reinvent myself, become my own boss, and explore opportunities as a model, creator, and entrepreneur,” she told the Sydney Morning Herald.

While the money may be good, Odom, like many athletes on OnlyFans, has received backlash. When he posted a link to his account on X, the comments below were not pretty. “Who asked for this … put your tongue back in your mouth freak … how does this even happen … what are these dudes spending their money on?” wrote one user.

The end of an athletic career is a well-worn reel. The gladiator is carted off in a heap of bones. A montage plays. Scarred and sinewy, it rises from the dead for one more go. Wide-eyed spectators grin and grimace as the blows come in torrents of blood and tears and phlegm. But now there appears to be a second act for some athletes – or at least a parallel one – on OnlyFans. For some it may be crucial, for others cruel. As with everything in sports, much of how it pans out lies with the fans.

items.title: AI giant Anthropic raises more than $100 billion in record-setting IPO
paragraphs: The Anthropic website and mobile phone app are shown in this photo, in New York, Friday, July 5, 2024. Richard Drew/AP hide caption
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
Anthropic shares are about to make their market debut after the company raised more than $100 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering that valued it at around $1.5 trillion.
It's a remarkably rapid ascent for the five-year-old artificial intelligence powerhouse, and a sign of strong investor appetite despite growing concern about a possible AI bubble.
Anthropic sold 956 million shares — far more than originally planned — at an IPO price of $83 per share, it announced on Wednesday. That price exceeded its targeted range of $70 to $78 per share.

The company's seven founders also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO. On top of that, Anthropic's prospectus included plans to put an additional $26 billion worth of shares into the market through private placements with companies including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
The total haul is more than $107 billion.
Anthropic valuation could rise or fall later on Thursday, when its shares start trading publicly on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker symbol ANT.
The amount of money raised makes Anthropic's IPO the biggest in history, after Elon Musk's mega-conglomerate SpaceX landed $75 billion when it listed in June.
"We've never seen a company that's able to grow this fast [and] be this dominant," said Andrew Rocco, a stock analyst at the financial research firm Zacks.

Anthropic got its start in 2021 as a breakaway group of researchers who once worked for ChatGPT-maker OpenAI. Led by now-CEO Dario Amodei, the Anthropic founders were concerned that OpenAI, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.

Amodei and the others quickly raised hundreds of millions of dollars and set out to develop AI models in a way that the company said focused on safety and "alignment," or the idea that AI should be harmless and act in ways that jibe with human values and intent.

Anthropic launched Claude in early 2023, just months after OpenAI released ChatGPT. Ever since, the two companies have been neck-and-neck competitors in cutting-edge artificial intelligence, known as "frontier AI." The Claude family of AI models, including the Claude chatbot and Claude Code, are among the most popular and powerful in the world, and have helped transform everything from online search to software engineering.

They are also the San Francisco-based company's main source of income, according to its IPO prospectus, which said revenue in the first half of the year skyrocketed 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, versus a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.

The IPO comes at a time when shares in tech companies linked to the AI boom have been volatile. Investors have vacillated between enthusiasm for what many believe will be a revolutionary technology and concern that the vast sums of money being poured into it may be hard to justify.

"It's going to be a test of investor sentiment towards the AI trade," said Janice Quek, an equity analyst at the investment research firm CFRA. "We've seen in recent weeks that there has been a lot of pressure and really market sell-offs on the AI ecosystem just because a lot of people are worried about the AI bubble, for example, or the concerns around AI financing and whether there's a return on investment on AI."
The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down more than 11% since early October.

Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, an early Anthropic investor, told a Semafor conference on Monday the IPO is one of the best ways to invest in AI applications. He said his firm had trimmed its exposure to AI infrastructure — companies involved in things like manufacturing semiconductors and building data centers — but that Altimeter had requested an allotment of Anthropic stock worth $5 billion.
"I've been waiting for it," he said of the IPO. "We put in for the largest request in the 20-year history of our firm."

There is indirect evidence in Anthropic's prospectus that businesses, rather than individual subscribers, are its biggest source of revenue. Malik Ahmed Khan, an equity analyst at Morningstar, says the company's long-term success may hinge on those companies' pace of adoption of AI technologies, but it's unclear how fast that will be.

"Radios went from like 10% penetration to 90% penetration in the U.S. within a decade. Washing machines, to reach that level of penetration, took a multi-decade period," he said. "So when we're thinking about Anthropic and broadly AI in the enterprise setting, what does that adoption curve look like?"

Anthropic has not been without controversy. Earlier this year it became embroiled in a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used. The Pentagon wanted the military to be able to deploy Anthropic's models without restriction, but Amodei drew a line at fully autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans. The Pentagon subsequently labeled Anthropic a "supply chain risk," a designation previously reserved for foreign adversaries.

And skeptics have criticized Amodei's rapid push to develop AI despite his own dire warnings about the technology's risks. In September, Amodei wrote an essay urging his AI competitors to "pace the frontier," or to slow down development of the most cutting-edge models and make sure that safety incidents are being reported and scrutinized by third-party auditors.

That essay followed a summer when AI agents from Anthropic's lab, as well as OpenAI and other competitors, were revealed to have hacked other companies, setting off a frenzy of concern about the risks of rogue agents. This week, California sued OpenAI over its agents that hacked into Hugging Face, an open-source software platform.
Anthropic's IPO prospectus dedicated dozens of pages to potential risks, including the possibility that people could lose control of AI, or that AI could take harmful actions on its own.

The company also flagged the risk of heightened scrutiny or political backlash. Indeed, the IPO comes just weeks after midterm elections in the United States, which analysts say likely herald a period of elevated scrutiny and oversight for AI firms. Data centers became a hot-button issue this election cycle, and tech stocks sank after the election as investors anticipated that the incoming Congress would crack down on the industry.

Still, Anthropic's prospectus was bullish about the development and spread of AI. "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," it said.

OpenAI had been on track to also list shares this year, but CEO Sam Altman postponed those plans, likely to next year, after the Hugging Face incident. At the Semafor conference on Monday Altman promised: "We will go public at some point."
"The world as a whole would like exposure to this," he continued. "And I think that's, you know, directionally a good thing to do."

Meanwhile, shares in SpaceX, the first of this year's AI mega-IPOs, are trading near their initial price of $135. After the company's June listing, the stock leapt to more than $200, then slid to as low as about $108 before recovering ground.
Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.

items.title: Survivors of Uganda's deadly landslide seek justice at the UN
paragraphs: ByOndiro Oganga and Swaibu IbrahimBBC AfricaReporting fromKampala
Survivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations.
The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitution by failing to put effective disaster management measures in Bududa, a mountainous district prone to landslides.
Their case comes as heavy rains raise the risk of further landslides. They say the government relocation programme ignores their safety, land rights and livelihoods.
The UN Human Rights Committee is considering what is believed to be the first case seeking climate adaptation measures, one that could set a global precedent.
At least 33 of the 53 people who died in the 2019 landslide were children. Years later, survivors say every spell of heavy rain brings back fears of another tragedy.
William Tsama, one of the claimants, lost four members of his family.
"Victims in such situations, ignored by governments, can take them to court to compel them to help their citizens."
Uganda introduced a resettlement plan for landslide-prone areas in 2011, but progress has been limited, with relatively few people relocated.
Last month, it launched a new resettlement programme offering affected households 18m Ugandan shillings ($4,300; £3,300) to help them move to safer areas.
But some survivors have questioned whether the amount is enough to cover the cost of relocating and rebuilding their lives.

Under the programme, families can choose between receiving two acres of land, valued at 8m shillings, plus 10m shillings towards building a house, or taking the equivalent land allowance in cash, alongside the same housing grant.
The scheme is expected to benefit 1,410 households identified as living in high-risk areas.
The government has now given residents of designated high-risk areas two months, from November to December, to leave or face forced eviction.

The threat extends beyond landslides. The complainants say changing rainfall patterns and declining soil fertility have also affected farming, leaving many families struggling to secure their livelihoods.
"I want to get a new good place for my people, so even if I die, they will be okay. I am an old man, but I am doing it for my children," Tsama said.
The survivors first launched legal action in 2020 in Uganda, and received support from Ugandan environmental organisation Greenwatch three years later.
They are seeking compensation for lost family members and livelihoods, as well as emergency measures, including accessible early-warning systems in high-risk areas.
Greenwatch Executive Director Samantha Atukunda Kakuru Mwesigwa said the case is about changing how governments prepare and respond to climate-related disasters.

"Justice for claimants is not just about winning in court. It is about forcing government policy to keep pace with a changing climate, and ensuring loss and damage is no longer an afterthought in disaster management," she said.
The threat of climate-related disasters extends across East Africa.
In Kenya, floods and landslides killed at least 181 people between March and May 2024, according to the Kenya Red Cross. In Rwanda, floods and landslides killed 135 people in May 2023.

The dangers are also being felt further afield. In October 2026, a flash flood swept through Nepal's Gorkha district after a landslide blocked a river, washing away homes and infrastructure, and killing over 1,500 people.

"Disasters like the one in Bududa are only getting worse because of climate change – and they are happening all around the world, as we've seen recently and tragically in Nepal," ClientEarth lawyer Vesselina Newman said.
She said poorer countries, which have contributed relatively little to global emissions, are bearing some of the heaviest consequences of climate change and need greater financial support.
"High income countries must provide financial assistance and ensure that sufficient money goes directly to countries like Uganda, so they can roll out life-saving adaptation measures," she said.
The complainants say relocation must involve more than moving people out of danger.
They want the government to protect their livelihoods, respect their land rights, and take account of individual needs.
The case is now before the United Nations Human Rights Committee, which will ask the Ugandan government to respond within six months.

items.title: Westside Cowboy named BBC Introducing Artist of the Year 2026
paragraphs: Westside Cowboy have been announced as BBC Introducing Artist of the Year 2026.
Jimmy Bradbury, Reuben Haycocks, Aoife Anson O'Connell and Paddy Murphy formed the band in Manchester in 2023 and have since rocketed from the pub circuit to some of the UK's biggest festivals.

The award is presented to an up-and-coming artist or band who has, with the support of BBC Introducing, made a significant impact and has previously been won by Olivia Dean, Myles Smith and Tom Grennan.
Murphy, from Longridge in Lancashire, said the win put them in "good company", with Bradbury, from Shropshire, adding that it was "very flattering".

BBC Introducing supports new musical talent across the UK, providing a platform to propel new artists on to the local and national stage through 30 Introducing shows, three national radio shows and six shows across BBC Radio 1, Radio 1Xtra, Radio 2, 6Music, Radio 3 and Asian Network.
About 72,000 tracks from emerging UK artists supported by BBC Introducing make it on to the airwaves each year.

Westside Cowboy uploaded their debut single I've Never Met Anyone I Thought I Could Really Love (Until I Met You) to the Introducing platform in November 2024 and had their first play on radio within hours.

items.title: Waugh Thistleton Architects set to transform derelict bathing pavilion into Tracey Emin-backed studios and sauna
paragraphs: UK studio Waugh Thistleton Architects is set to transform the Edwardian Westbrook Pavilion in Margate, UK, into an arts centre for British artist Tracey Emin with a cafe, public sauna and changing rooms.
“The project will bring a much-loved seafront building back into use, combining its original purpose with new spaces for art, culture and the local community,” said Waugh Thistleton Architects.
The studio recently won planning permission from the local council to convert the abandoned building, which Emin purchased in 2023, into a facility run by the Tracey Emin Foundation.
The project aims to return the building to its former use as a changing room for swimmers and as a tea room, when it originally opened in 1914.
“Originally opened in 1914, the building provided public changing facilities for sea-bathing and a tea room,” said the studio.
“Following storm damage in the Great North Sea Storm of 1953, subsequent alterations detracted from its original Edwardian character,” it continued.

“The renovated pavilion will accommodate artist studios, an art gallery, clubroom, cafe, sea-bathing changing facilities, a new sauna and refurbished public toilets, restoring its original role as a place for bathing and socialising by the sea.”

Along with making the pavilion a building used by the public again, the studio aims to return the building’s core to its Edwardian look by removing later additions. It will also add glazed facades to the wings on either side of the central pavilion.
The building will be topped by a rooftop terrace, while a public toilet on the site will be renovated.

“The design draws on the proportions and character of the original building, removing later additions and reinstating lost features such as the historic belvederes which top the central tower structures,” said the studio.
“The beachfront facade will see a new glazing system and colonnade to each of the building’s wings, with a new sheltered archway forming a new seating terrace at the building’s heart,” it continued.
“The design seeks to reference the original architecture while providing contemporary needs of a public building. Where original features are references, these are distinguishable architecturally.”
Emin is one of the UK’s best-known living artists. We recently produced a video of a landmark exhibition of her work at Tate Modern.
Recent projects by Waugh Thistleton Architects include plans for the “tallest mass timber office building in the US”.
Images courtesy of Waugh Thistleton Architects

items.title: This artist's space goblins blend magical realism with classical portraiture
paragraphs: Lisa Lennon was born on the Isle of Man, a place steeped in myth and folklore. That perhaps shows in her art style, which defines as magical realism with a focus on classical portraiture. She works with watercolours, building up many layers while adding details.
Below, Lisa introduces four examples of her work. If you're inspired and need supplies for your own art, see our guides to the best watercolour paints and the best watercolour pencils.

“This science fiction piece was dreamed up while walking by the sea. Her headpiece is inspired by the pebbles there. I love wide open spaces; they give me a lot of scope to play with atmospheric scenes.”
“This is where fantasy meets science fiction. I was working with local folklore and became obsessed with goblins and elves. I developed a collection called ‘Space Goblins’.”
“Another in the ‘Space Goblins’ series. How did Tudor clothes end up in outer space? We can only speculate, but I do love a good riff, and it’s always a large technical challenge to get it right.”

“One of my classic goblins. I so enjoy painting these rather cantankerous, sassy personalities. My focus here – technique-wise – was to have a vintage look to the colour and quality, all while retaining a contemporary, whimsical feel. I love this one.”
You can see more of Lisa's work on her website.

items.title: The Specsavers GTA 6 campaign is hilariously on brand
paragraphs: GTA VI trendjacking was already everywhere, even before today's release of the most- anticipated video game in history (see our GTA VI review for our Digital Art Editor's experience playing it). A lot of the attempts to jump on the bandwagon have been lazy and half-hearted, with brands merely using AI image generators to give product shots a vaporwave makeover.
The optical chain Specsavers has turned out to be an unlikely exception. Its unusual GTA VI campaign might actually be the best brand collaboration of the year.
That's right, Specsavers has entered into its "biggest partnership of all time’. It's sponsoring GTA... just not that GTA.

The teaser post above might have raised eyebrows among gamers given that GTA VI developer and publisher Rockstar Games has very limited collaborations. There's it's deal with the Miami Heat (and with Oakley for the GTA VI Collector's Edition), but there are only parody fake brands in GTA VI itself.

But Specsavers isn't sponsoring the video game that everyone's talking about. It's hooked up with GTA Transport Ltd, a British road haulage company based in Leicester. Which sounds a bit like Leonida, right?

“It might not be the GTA partnership I originally had in mind but a deal’s a deal. I'm pleased to offer every driver at GTA Transport a free eye test,” the company's brand partnerships and sponsorships lead Neil Liddle said.

Bugz Singh from GTA Transport Ltd said: “We were surprised when Specsavers got in touch, but we’re delighted to be the GTA they’ve teamed up with. Our drivers spend all day on the road, so they’re looking forward to their eye tests.”

Specsavers' stunt rises above most of the GTA VI trendjacking that we've seen. It's funny, and it's a lot more creative and memorable than simply throwing Vice City hues onto brand imagery. Best of all, it shows that Specsavers really knows its brand and its public, maintaining consistency with the message it's been using for over 20 years.

Specsavers has been telling the same joke since 2002, and it still works. In fact, it's become even more effective. The line 'Should've gone to Specsavers', coined by then in-house creative director Graham Daldry, is now so ingrained in the public consciousness that it no longer needs to be appended onto the campaign. It's already implied.

Having already sold close to 16 million copies before today's release, GTA VI is a cultural phenomenon with a reach that extends well beyond that of most games. An AI-generated vaporwave graphic can't make an unrelated brand a part of that, but Specsavers has shown that on-brand creative thinking can forge a memorable connection to the entertainment event of the year.
