items.title: A TikTok superstar bares all: Siorna Ashby’s best shot
paragraphs: I met Meg at a nude life-drawing class. I was struck by how free she seemed and how powerfully that came through in her modelling. I asked if I could photograph her for my project Body Like Mine. This series explores the difference between how our bodies are perceived externally and how we experience them ourselves. We see a body and we bring our own judgments and assumptions on to it, but the lived experience is very different.

Rather than portraying an idealised body, the project aims to explore what it feels like to inhabit your own body, and to see it as worthy of attention without asking it to become anything else first.

My photography is collaborative. I brought some visual ideas to the shoot, and Meg brought her own ways of moving and expressing herself. The photograph developed between us. I took references from art history: Jenny Saville’s nudes and Lucian Freud’s work have inspired me, along with the sense of flesh and physical presence in Rubens’ paintings.

I lit her in a painterly way and used a canvas backdrop. As I was photographing her, I found myself getting lower down. I wanted the body to have a real presence in the photograph, to become the portrait itself. It was Meg’s idea to scrunch her belly in that way. I asked her to look away so that her face wouldn’t be the first place your eye went. I love how fleshy the image feels. Portraits often rely on the face and eyes to communicate who someone is. Here, I wanted to explore how much of Meg’s presence and personality could come through her body and gesture.

Meg loved it and was delighted when the image was selected to be displayed in the National Portrait Gallery. Her nude modelling is only a small part of what she does – most of her time and energies go into raising awareness about overconsumption and the “tat” that fills our lives and ends up in landfill. She’s a superstar on TikTok!

“Fat women’s femininity is [often] stripped from them and … I am masculinised and called brave for just existing in this body. When I am life modelling, I feel the most feminine and deeply in touch with myself. I am proud to take up space and represent people who often are not,” she says.

My commissioned work specialises in boudoir and nude photography. Coming to this has been a personal journey. I was very critical of my body – I was one of those women who couldn’t look in a mirror. For me, being behind the camera was also a way of avoiding being in photographs. I liked having that control. I started out doing headshots, but when you run your own business, you need to be visible. I became frustrated with all the negative feelings I had about myself, and one day I stripped off and I took my own photographs of my nude body. And when I looked over the images I was shocked to realise that I didn’t hate them. In fact I thought they were beautiful.

And then I noticed a change in myself. I was walking down the street taller. I wasn’t wearing cardigans to hide my arms. And I realised that maybe I can help others. I don’t think a photograph can resolve someone’s relationship with their body, but it can be one part of seeing themselves differently, feeling more connected to their body, or recognising that they are worthy of being seen.

But there is a tension in my work between beauty standards and how women want to be seen. Much of the boudoir photography I do sits in that culture that shapes how women think they should look and what makes a body beautiful or desirable. But who decides what makes a body either of these things? Women’s bodies don’t exist to meet someone else’s expectations of beauty or desirability, which change over time. There is room for wanting to feel sexy, but whose idea of sexy are we working towards?

When I make or look at a nude photograph, I ask what the pose, light, colour and composition are communicating. Whose perspective is shaping the image, and how much say does the person being photographed have in how they are seen?

With Body Like Mine, I want to give more space to people’s own accounts of living in their bodies, particularly where those experiences differ from what others assume when they look at them. The next person I’m photographing lives with endometriosis, and another participant is experiencing memory loss. I want us to explore how those experiences might be expressed in a photograph, guided by what each person wants to share.

Before we photograph, I ask each person to choose a few words that describe what they would like us to express together. Those words give us a starting point for the images. Meg’s were “real”, “joyful” and “free”.
Body Like Mine is part of the Winston Taylor photo portrait prize exhibition at the National Portrait Gallery, London, until 17 January. siornaphotography.com; @siornaphotography

Born: Blackpool, 1983 High point: Having my photograph of Meg Foster, Body Like Mine, selected for the National Portrait Gallery’s Winston Taylor photo portrait prize 2026 exhibition. Top tip: Talk through boundaries before artistic nude or boudoir photoshoots, and keep checking in as you work. Make it easy for someone to change their mind, and be ready to adapt a pose, change direction or put the camera down.

items.title: Young people lose hearing – level 1
paragraphs: Experts say that more than 1 billion young people cannot hear well.
They are between 12 and 34 years old. Young people often hear a loud continuous noise in their ears. Their hearing tests look normal. Later, their hearing test results are worse.
Experts know reasons why this situation happens. Young people listen to their headphones. They go to concerts. The music is too loud. Sometimes, music in restaurants is loud, too.
Decibels tell us how loud something is. The sound of a food mixer is 85 decibels. The sound of a train is 100 decibels. Experts say that it is safe to listen to 85 decibels at work.
Sometimes we can lose hearing when we hear something very loud only once. Loud noise kills the cells in our ears. We cannot fix the situation.
Difficult words: result (the information we get from a test or experiment), headphones (a device which people wear over their ears to listen to music), cell (the smallest part in the human body).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Young people lose hearing – level 2
paragraphs: British scientists published a study about people 12 to 34 years old; the study said that more than 1 billion of them had hearing problems.

Many young people complain about nonstop ringing in their ears. Hearing tests show no problems, but when doctors repeat the test some years later, the hearing is worse. The main reasons are headphones, concerts, and restaurants where the sounds are too loud for too long. The sound damages the cells in the inner ear, and once this damage happens, you cannot change it.

Scientists say that the safe limit for our ears is 85 decibels over a 40-hour work week. 85 decibels are the sound of a blender, while 100 decibels are the sound of a train. We can also suddenly lose our hearing when we experience a very loud noise just once.
Difficult words: cell (the smallest part in the human body), decibel (the unit which people use to measure loudness), blender (an electric mixing machine).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Young people lose hearing – level 3
paragraphs: The British Medical Journal published a study which showed that 1 billion young people were at risk of hearing loss.

Researchers shared their analysis of data from 2000 to 2021 on unsafe listening practices. If the volume is too loud for too long, headphones, a concert, or even a restaurant could cause irreversible damage. Young people are complaining about persistent ringing in their ears, although their hearing tests look normal. However, several years later, their hearing reduces.

The loud sounds damage sensory cells in the cochlea, the snail-looking part in the inner ear. Once these cells die, you can’t get them back. 85 decibels sound like a blender, 100 decibels sound like a subway train, and 120 decibels sound like a concert or a siren.

According to experts, 85 decibels during a 40-hour work week is the maximum safe limit. Just 2.5 hours of 92 decibels can damage your ears. However, only one episode of intense noise exposure can lead to lifelong hearing loss.
Difficult words: irreversible (impossible to change or return to a previous condition), persistent (continue over a long period of time), exposure (affected by something).

items.title: Seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
paragraphs: Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei are chief executive and president of Anthropic
ByTom Espiner and Lucy HookerBusiness reporters
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.
The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.
Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each.
If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each.
So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?
In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.
He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.
Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.
Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.
But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.
Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".
Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.
She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.
Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.
She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.
The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.
Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.
He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.
Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.
He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".
Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.
Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.
He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.
Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.
Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.
He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.

His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.
Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.
But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.
Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.
He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.
The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.

Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.
McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.
He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

items.title: Hacks, AI or just overdue updates - why have there been so many outages?
paragraphs: As is often the case, many outages were a result of an update or installation going wrong somewhere in a system.
A network upgrade at Microsoft caused servers to become overloaded and shut down.
It was also upgrades to a creaky old network which grounded thousands of planes in the US over the weekend.
Problems with the NSA's internal communication system and, separately, Apple's iCloud and Apple Pay were also blamed on things going wrong during system updates.
Disruption to payments in US banks has been put down to a "software bug" from JP Morgan Chase. The bank says it is not a cyber-security incident.
But some recent problems are in fact related to cyber-security vulnerabilities.
AI was used to discover flaws in Java, the third-most popular programming language in the world.
And researcher Scott Helme also discovered malicious code in Optimizely, a platform which is used by some of the world's largest companies.
Hackers were able to steal about $7,000 (£5,300) in cryptocurrency before they were discovered and kicked out.
Let's address the cyber incidents first - and the role of new AI models.
"I would be very surprised if all of these cyber-attacks and the attackers behind them were not using AI to accelerate themselves," Helme told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

Since the summer, AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have decided it's too risky to give the general public access to the most advanced models before allowing certain companies and institutions to use them.
In these cases, security professionals can use the same tech to find flaws themselves and alert others before criminals get to them.
This happened in the recent Java incident, as well as the PHP one - where there was a scramble to patch the flaws before they could be exploited.
These are not new - the world stood still in recent years as CrowdStrike and then Amazon Web Services ground many devices and systems to a halt.
Part of this may be down to technical debt - a term used when operators go for quick fixes to software instead of solving an underlying problem.
A build-up of surface-level fixes can eventually end up with more serious problems down the line.
With AI causing many companies to re-evaluate their cyber-security, they may be issuing more updates to patch flaws they have found.
Outages are often also a reminder of the physical tech our online world relies on - such as cables, servers and data centres.
In the US air traffic control incident, for example, the problem came as engineers were replacing outdated copper wires with fibre.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is adamant the recent incidents are not connected or coming from one attacker.
"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."
In cases such as PHP and Java, the "good guys" found the flaws, with the help of AI, before the bad guys - allowing them to get together some fixes before the bugs could be widely exploited.
At the same time, Anthropic, among other leading AI firms, has warned of the risks its own products pose.
Outages in particular have an impact on the physical world as they often cause disruption to healthcare, schools and people's ability to do their jobs.
Or, in the case over the weekend, planes' ability to fly.
Watch: Marco Rubio says recent tech outages are 'completely unrelated' to one another
They also shine a light on the world's heavy reliance on a small number of players.
Not just frontier AI companies, but infrastructure providers such as Microsoft and Amazon, which - along with Google - run a huge chunk of the world's computer servers.
In the PHP incident, the world was holding its breath as one programmer - working voluntarily - worked to issue patches in a form that was easily applicable.
And Java, run by another tech giant Oracle, is used by nearly all of the biggest companies on Earth.

"The Oracle Java vulnerability is a stark reminder of how dependent businesses have become on a relatively small number of critical technologies," said Sheila Pancholi, risk assurance lead at consultancy firm RSM UK.
"Organisations need to know where their critical technology dependencies sit, act quickly when vulnerabilities emerge, and test that their response has actually worked."
Meanwhile Xander Van Raemdonck, security engineer at Aikido Security, said the challenge was "knowing whether you're exposed".
"Java is bundled inside a huge amount of business software, so many companies don't have a full list of where it runs," he said.
The AI tools used to help find security flaws are still so new that they will probably continue to find vulnerabilities which have been lingering in code for decades.
"AI is accelerating discovery on both sides and speeding up how much software gets shipped," said Martin Reynolds, field CTO at software delivery company Harness.
"So the volume of what developers need to patch is going up, while the time they have to get the work done it is going down."
Tech debt will need to continue to be dealt with - which means more upgrades to systems and more potential for these to cause disruptions.
Plus there is the constant threat from hackers as they continue to get more sophisticated.
Attackers only need to find one vulnerability to exploit - whereas defenders have to protect against all potential hacks.
"Attackers can move quickly and carefree, and experiment without risk of failure so they can naturally often move a fraction faster," Helme said.
"We're currently observing that small delay between how fast the attackers can move and how fast the defenders can move."
The cat-and-mouse nature of the cyber-security game means it's unlikely to end any time soon - and the impact of AI means the stakes are getting higher.

items.title: Rugby TV pundit says sex assault 'never happened'
paragraphs: A former England rugby league player and TV pundit accused of putting her hand up a woman's skirt in a cricket club toilet has told a jury it "categorically did not happen".
Danika Priim, 42, has been charged with carrying out the alleged sexual assault in the toilets at Horsforth Cricket Club in Leeds on 22 July 2022.
Her accuser, who cannot be named for legal reasons, previously told a trial at Leeds Crown Court how Priim twice reached up her dress and grabbed her underwear.
Keighley-based Priim, who previously represented Bradford Bulls, Leeds Rhinos and England, including at the 2017 World Cup, denies one count of sexual assault. The trial continues.
Two of the complainant's friends told the court they also witnessed what happened in the toilet but, on Wednesday, Priim told the jury she was never in the toilets with the three women.
Prosecutor Chloe Hudson put it to Priim that there were only two alternatives – either she was lying or the complainant and her two friends were lying.
Priim told the jury: "It categorically did not happen."
The defendant agreed she was not suggesting that it was an accident, or the woman had invited her to touch her, or it was a joke.
Priim told the jury she was never in the toilets with the complainant, adding: "I did not touch (her) in the toilets at all."
Hudson said to her: "What you must be saying is that these three got together to make completely false allegations about you."
Priim responded: "It's the biggest question I have – it's the why."
The prosecutor asked the defendant about how the complainant demonstrated to the jury how she was grabbed.
Priim said: "She was lying. I did not do that."
She added: "I'm also a very happy heterosexual woman. I'm with a man. I live with a man."
The prosecutor said: "The truth is that you sexually assaulted (the woman), didn't you?"
Priim said: "The truth is that it never happened."
Hudson asked Priim whether she thought the complainant and her two friends had colluded in a "witch hunt against you".
Stood in the witness box wearing a chunky light brown cardigan and a cream-and-black scarf, Priim replied: "I believe they have."
On Tuesday, the complainant described how Priim "walked straight up to me and put her hand up my skirt and grabbed hold of my pants and my private parts".
The woman said she asked the defendant what she was doing, "then she did it again, grinning at me, and walked off".
One of the complainant's friends told the jury how she witnessed Priim put her hand up the woman's skirt.
She told the court: "I recall seeing her remove her hand, laughed about it and then repeated it.

Giving evidence on Wednesday, Priim said she only went to the toilet once during her time at the cricket club, and produced a photograph she took of her and two friends in there, to help the jury with timings.
She said she drove to the venue and was drinking soft drinks until later when she had one pint.
Asked about the police getting involved following the allegation, she said: "It absolutely broke me."
Since retiring from the game in 2021 Priim has appeared on BBC, Channel 4 and Sky Sports as a pundit, reporter and commentator.
Jurors were sent out to consider their verdict on Wednesday.

items.title: Logitech MX Keypad review: Can nine LCD keys take the pain out of Photoshop?
paragraphs: A smart, compact control surface with real potential, the Logitech MX Keypad has plenty of presets and context-aware functions for the best software and utilities, but you’ll only get your money’s worth if you put in the setup time.
Options+ is context-aware and offers presets for popular apps
LCD keys show a changing icon for each function
15 'pages' of custom keys is a ludicrous amount
A good alternative to native drawing tablet remotes
It’s wired only, which is disappointing at this price
Unsupported apps such as Rebelle and ArtRage need manual setup
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
Connection: Wired USB-C, 1.5m USB-C to USB-C
Features: Logi Options+, app-specific, automatically switching
Supported apps: Adobe Creative Cloud, Figma, Clip Studio Paint, CorelDRAW, VS Code, IntelliJ, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Zoom, Slack, Google (beta), and more

I’m always drawn to gadgets that promise to save time or make things easier and more accessible, whether it's the best drawing tablets, shortcut keyboards, or odd little controllers parked next to my mouse: if it claims to shave seconds off a repetitive job, I want to try it. Photoshop is my worst offender, because half the battle is remembering where Adobe has hidden things this time with each new update.

The Logitech MX Keypad is a desktop control pad with nine customisable LCD keys, each showing an icon for whatever you’ve assigned to it. Two physical buttons flip between pages, so you get more shortcuts without another huge peripheral crowding your desk. It's in the Logitech MX line, gadgets aimed as much at creatives as at everyday folk looking to make life easier.

At $99.99 / £89.99, it’s not an impulse buy but something you should consider, and after years of drilling Ctrl, Alt and Shift combos into my left hand, I wasn’t sure I needed one. I also use a drawing tablet and stylus for art, so I have just enough buttons on the pen, or I can access more on my tablet's virtual keyboard. But knowing a shortcut and having a button for the thing you hit countless times an hour, whether it's in Photoshop, calling up Google files or browser pages, is a different matter. That's where the MX keypad aims to be a decent all-rounder for everyday work and creative projects alike.

Nine square keys sit in a three-by-three grid, and because each has its own screen, the icons change based on what you’ve assigned. That beats a traditional macro pad with fixed labels: you can see what a button does instead of memorising obscure combos.

It works with the best digital art software and creative apps, including Adobe Photoshop, Illustrator, Lightroom, Premiere Pro, and Figma. Importantly, it’s context-aware, so you can select your app in Logitech Options+ and it loads presets for that software’s most common tools; from there, you can edit or set up your own actions.

Nine keys run out fast, so using up to 15 'pages' of nine preset buttons (135 total assigned actions) earns it keep as a feature. Overkill, yes, but some will want all that power at a button press. The Options+ app lets you build separate layouts for different jobs, one for Photoshop, another for Lightroom and so on. Rather than living with Adobe’s shortcuts, you build the layout around how you work, and it's as easy as going into the Options+ app and assigning keyboard shortcuts to the buttons, including combinations of buttons, and it supports different saved shortcut collections, so you can also tailor favourites to different apps.

At roughly 92 x 78 x 25mm, it sits beside a mouse and keyboard without taking over, and it's easy to hold, which matters if your desk already hosts a pen tablet or display. A kickstand and a 1.5m USB-C cable come in the box.

It’s not perfect. The keys lack the click of good mechanical keys, but they do have an old-fashioned soft-push feel, much like an old 90s dial-up digital phone, but that also means you need a little force to push one, and the stand lacks weight or 'stick', so it drifts as you press. The solution? Hold it by the top and depress with my thumb. I do like how each button has its own little digital decal icon showing its function, and you can buy sticky pads to keep it in place.
It’s also wired only, which is a little surprising at this price, but it's not the end of the world, and the cable is long enough for most setups.

For me, the MX Keypad makes the most sense with Photoshop (I've also downloaded and set it up for Clip Studio Paint, CorelDRAW, Google, and Slack), and even fast keyboard users end up wishing something were easier to reach. Favourite brushes, colour swapping and new layers all suit the MX Keypad, and you can split them across pages for selections, masking, painting, and layer management. I’m a light Photoshop user, but I found that adding shortcuts for Lasso selections, favourite brushes, and layer options sped up how I use the software.

When I’m drawing, I don’t want to look down at the keyboard or lift my hand off the tablet, so a few key actions right beside my drawing area help. For the most part, I find the custom buttons on a stylus work well alongside touch controls on a tablet, but if you are more professionally minded and need all the options all the time, a shortcut keypad is essential. While XPPen, Huion, and Xencelabs all offer good remotes, the MX Keypad is a step above, with more buttons, more configuration options, and easy-to-understand icons and button labels.

If you’re already quick on a keyboard, reaching across to press a button may not be any faster. The gain is in the visual reminders and having rarely used commands grouped on pages somewhere easy to find. With only nine keys, you’ll need to plan your pages carefully, but for serious users, once organised, you'll be able to cycle to function collections at speed.

Of course, not all apps are supported; for example, Rebelle and ArtRage aren’t here, but you can add the apps manually and set up profiles and shortcuts based on keyboard commands; it just takes more time than Logitech’s preset app library. Using presets is as simple as clicking a drop-down menu, but adding and editing a new app setup and customising each key can take around 30 minutes per 'page'.

Because profiles are set per app, the buttons change colour and icon designs as you switch software. I found this to be the MX Keypad's strength, because it becomes one device that can follow you around your creative workflow, so if you’re someone who works between software, from Blender to Photoshop, for example, the MX Keypad can follow along.

Options+, the same app used by the MX Master 4 Special Edition mouse, can configure everything, but it takes some time to get used to if you’re editing a new app that isn’t supported out of the box. If you use the most popular, most common software, it’s easy; if you use niche apps, it can feel far from plug-and-play, since you have to manually enter each keyboard command.

For artists and designers who bounce between the biggest and most common apps, it’s a compact way to build your own control pad, and LCD keys beat cryptic labels on a standard macro pad or half-remembered keyboard shortcuts.

At $99.99 / £89.99, the Logitech MX Keypad is a fair price for a quick key remote. By comparison, the Xencelabs Quick Keys cost a similar $99.99 / £95.90 and also have LCD icons, but only words and no images, while the decent XPPen Remote is $49.99 / £49.99 but more basic than both Xencelabs and the Logitech. Both are wireless remotes, unlike the MX Keypad, but as a shortcut remote, the MX Keypad is the best of the three because Options+ offers an easy setup with established software and a huge number of buttons and pages.

But the MX Keypad has more going for it than those remotes: more custom buttons, more context-aware presets, and the option to use ‘pages’, which packs a staggering number of functions onto one face. The big advantage over a traditional drawing tablet remote is two-fold: you get little icons that explain each function, plus the depth of Options+ with multiple pre-loaded shortcuts for the best graphic design software and art apps out of the box.

Do beginners and hobbyists like me need this much choice? I mostly use two to three apps, for example, and three or four functions, and I don't need speed, but if you're a pro with a library of art, design, 3D, and video editing software to pair with and move across in one project, it would be a good gadget. For pros and tinkerers, it’s essential; for everyone else, it may be overkill.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

items.title: Apec summit live: Xi welcomes Trump on China visit as Putin claims Europe in ‘humiliating decline’
paragraphs: Xi hails Shenzhen's transformation in Apec banquet speech
Trump and Putin shake hands ahead of Apec welcome banquet
Putin and Trump could meet informally during Apec summit, Russia state media reports
Xi says he hopes to build 'stable' China-US ties with Trump - state media
Xi hails ‘unshaken’ China-Russia ties after talks with Putin
Trump welcomed by Xi as he arrives for summit
Carney challenges Putin's claim that sanctions no longer work
Trump arrives in Shenzhen for Apec summit, Chinese state media reports
Trump announces new trade deal with Philippines as he heads to China
Taiwan sends representative to Apec summit
Xi Jinping calls for freer trade, greater cooperation on AI
Here is more of Xi’s speech (as per Xinhua):

double quotation markAt tomorrow’s Leaders’ Meeting, we will discuss measures to expand mutual openness, explore pathways for innovation-driven growth, broaden opportunities for pragmatic cooperation in various fields, and promote the implementation of more outcomes. I look forward to discussing the grand plan for Asia-Pacific cooperation and jointly advancing the cause of Asia-Pacific development with you all.
Now, I propose that we raise a glass together.
For the common prosperity of the Asia-Pacific region,
For the success of this informal leaders’ meeting,
For the health of all guests and their families,
China’s state news agency Xinhua has published the text of Xi Jinping’s welcome speech at tonight’s Apec banquet in Shenzhen.
In his remarks, Xi praised the city’s transformation into an international economic and innovation hub, describing it as a symbol of China’s development.
Here are a few passages from his address:

double quotation markThis evening, the shores of the South China Sea are aglow with lights, and autumn is in full swing here in Shenzhen, the City of the Phoenix. As the 33rd Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting is about to commence, I would like, on behalf of the Chinese Government and the Chinese people, to extend a warm welcome to all our distinguished guests.

I have often said that to see a thousand years of China, one should visit Xi’an; to see five hundred years of China, one should visit Beijing; and to see a hundred years of China, one should visit Shanghai. Today, I would like to say to you all: to see fifty years of China, come to Shenzhen.

Shenzhen is a place with a rich history. In 1978, when I first came to Shenzhen, it was still a small fishing village. More than 40 years have passed in the blink of an eye, and now it is filled with high-rise buildings and bustling traffic. The changes are truly remarkable.”
US president Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian president Vladimir Putin, as China’s Xi Jinping looks on, ahead of the welcome banquet at the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China:
Donald Trump has arrived at the welcome banquet with Xi Jinping:
The newswires are carrying pictures of world leaders arriving for the welcome banquet at the Apec summit, including Russia’s Vladimir Putin:
Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump could have several opportunities to speak during the Apec summit in China, according to Russia’s state news agency, Tass.
Citing Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov, Tass reported that the two leaders could exchange words informally at various points during the summit.
They will communicate “on their feet, on the steps, in chairs”, Ushakov reportedly said, suggesting their interactions need not be limited to a formal sit-down meeting.

Xi Jinping told Donald Trump he hoped their talks would help advance a “constructive, strategic and stable relationship” between China and the US, based on “respect, fairness and reciprocity”, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua.
Xi also recalled Trump’s personal welcome at the airport during his visit to the US in September, saying China’s own welcome for the US president reflected its tradition of reciprocity.
Xinhua reported the following remarks by the Chinese president:
double quotation markWhen I visited the United States in September this year, president Trump and his wife made a special trip to the airport to welcome me, and a grand welcoming ceremony was held.

China is a nation of courtesy, with a tradition of reciprocity. I welcome you back to China and look forward to exchanging in-depth views with you on major issues concerning China–US relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation and the global landscape, so as to advance a constructive, strategic and stable relationship between China and the US based on respect, fairness and reciprocity.”
Chinese state media have released a readout of Xi Jinping’s earlier meeting with Vladimir Putin.

In it, Xi is quoted as saying China-Russia relations are “unshaken by storms and steady as a mountain”, and have set “an example of a new type of major-country relationship characterised by equality, mutual respect, trustworthiness, and win-win co-operation”.
Xi also urged closer political and military ties between the two countries.

He said “the two sides should leverage the mechanisms for exchanges between the two countries’ governments, legislative bodies, militaries and political parties, ensuring that the consensus reached by the two countries’ heads of state is effectively implemented”, according to the readout.
In a notable gesture, Xi personally greeted Trump on the airport tarmac in Shenzhen, reciprocating the welcome the US president extended to the Chinese leader during his visit to the US in September.

As a reminder, Ukraine carried out a major strike on the Kerch Bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia, destroying its central road section in an operation involving two strikes over consecutive days.

The attack earlier this week dealt a significant blow to a key transport link and a symbolic project for Vladimir Putin, as the Russian president sat down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for talks at the Apec summit.
My colleague Jakub Krupa has the latest on the Ukraine conflict over on our Europe live blog here:
While we await Trump to disembark Air Force Once, we have this report from our China correspondent Rebecca Bailey in Shenzhen:
Canada’s Mark Carney has hit back at Vladimir Putin’s earlier assertion that sanctions no longer work in this day and age.

“Mr Putin can ask his financial institutions, he can ask his oligarch friends, he can ask his hockey players whether or not sanctions are a thing of the past. I think he’ll find out that they’re very real, they’re biting,” Carney told reporters.

In his address to the summit this morning, Putin had said that “the traditional tools of economic dominance and de facto coercion have largely run their course, having ⁠lost much of their intimidating power”.

Speaking at an outdoor press conference as purple clouds lingered ominously in the background, Carney said: “Not for the first time, Vladimir Putin is lying about the situation on the ground. Sanctions are very real and they’re going to continue to increase as long as this war goes on.”

Carney had previously said he would not boycott a group photo with Putin out of respect for hosts China. But he said if he were to find himself next to the Russian president, he would make Canada’s position clear.

Carney met China’s president Xi Jinping on Tuesday, with the two countries announcing remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.
The two men also discussed AI, Carney said Wednesday, adding he had taken the opportunity to share Canada’s views on a model for global governance.

“The absence of any global governance around AI is an enormous risk,” he said. “It’s an enormous economic risk but it’s a biohazard risk, and it’s a risk to democracy, human dignity, other factors... So it is past time to develop global governance frameworks for these sectors.”
Carney is due to meet Donald Trump later today, he said, where they would discuss efforts to reach a trade deal.
“We have been making progress... Two steps forward, one step back type thing,” he said.
He said he fully respected Trump’s engagement with China.

“I’m going to say something positive here about the initiative around denuclearization, the trilateral meeting that is going to happen,” he said. “Guess what? Canada’s in favor of denuclearization. If the relationship can be used towards that end, we’re very much supportive of it.”
Donald Trump has arrived in Shenzhen, China, for the Apec summit, Chinese state media reported.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 is a masterpiece, say critics
paragraphs: After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.
Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?
According to the first reviews, it's a resounding yes.
Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100, external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.
Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.
They have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN, external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".
Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building.
"The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote, external, but he added "there are also nits to pick".
For The New York Times, external one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors.
Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action.
But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.

The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian, external describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".
And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics.
"They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".
Writing for Forbes, external, Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".
The Washington Post, external said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg, external's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review.
"It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it.
"While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."
Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (£760m).

items.title: Stormont department failing to protect wild birds, oversight body finds
paragraphs: A parallel investigation is looking at the same issues involving Defra and Natural England, and they have also been issued with decision notices.

In Northern Ireland, the OEP's Chief Regulatory Officer Helen Venn acknowledged that "positive steps" had been taken, but added that delays in meeting legal obligations had played a part in the significant decline of wild birds in Northern Ireland.

"SPAs are important for achieving the Executive's commitments in relation to nature, such as the strategic outcome of thriving, resilient and connected nature and wildlife in the Environmental Improvement Plan.
"This is in addition to the Executive's international commitment to protect at least 30% of land and seas for nature's recovery by 2030.

"This is why it is important for Daera to carry out its legal responsibilities in a reasonable timeframe to deliver nature recovery and in relation to the classification and adaptation of SPAs on land."
The agriculture and environment minister Andrew Muir said there was "a moral and legal obligation" to protect wild bird habitats and welcomed continuing engagement between his officials and the OEP.

"The OEP has recognised in their investigation longstanding and concerning failures to implement recommended actions to protect wild bird habitats and populations by successive administrations both in England and Northern Ireland.
"While we have a long way to go to reverse current trends, there are signs of hope and clear examples of nature recovery in action.
"However, the scale of challenge requires greater levels of support from across government to provide the necessary resources and funding to address the nature crisis."
And he said the recently-published Nature Recovery Strategy and the Farming With Nature support package "reinforces" the department's commitment to nature restoration.
Sherwood said the group had been highlighting failing for decades.
"Today's findings from the OEP confirm what conservation organisations have been saying: action has been delayed for far too long.

"The focus must now move to delivery, with the Executive leading the way, and Daera and NIEA being resourced to take urgent action to put these protections in place and help reverse the decline of our most vulnerable bird populations.
"We hope today's OEP report will be the catalyst needed."

items.title: Annoying Trump and dodging Flock: inside MapQuest’s contrarian comeback
paragraphs: I am among the legion of former PC desk occupants with warm memories of MapQuest, the Y2K-era travel website that kept millennial drivers on course with sheaves of printed-out directions – a quantum leap over the ungainly glovebox map. But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech.

Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. Not only had it never signed off, MapQuest was reinventing itself as a plucky oppositional hero, the app most likely to uphold your geographical beliefs.

“I think the question that was posed internally was exactly that,” said MapQuest’s general manager, Doug Berger, who took over during the Gulf of America mishigas. “What if we didn’t …?” In a subsequent tweet, the company joked that it was retaining the Gulf of Mexico name “not because of politics but because we haven’t updated our maps in like 15 years and don’t remember how to do it”. The irreverence clearly resonated: MapQuest, which still attracted 35 million monthly website visitors despite having been largely supplanted by more convenient GPS options, saw a roughly 10% jump in traffic over a month. In February 2025, it doubled down, introducing a new feature allowing users to pick their own name for the gulf or let the app “surprise me” with options such as Gulf of Gumbo and Gulf of Something.

All of that was just a warmup for the executive order that came this past August, when Trump renamed Lake Ontario as Lake America – and MapQuest declared: “We’re not changing it.” While competitors scrambled to update their maps again, MapQuest said it added more than 2 million mobile users in the span of a week, a surge that temporarily made it the top free navigation app on iOS and Android. Canadians accounted for about half of the new following. “Our stance, while it can be interpreted as political, really is about giving people familiar names,” Berger said. “People who live near Lake Ontario, on either side of the US-Canada border, aren’t going to call it something else.”

MapQuest didn’t have much to lose by playing the contrarian. Spawned from the cartographic services division of printing giant RR Donnelley & Sons, it has spent the past 30 years changing hands: from AOL (which paid $1.1bn for it in 1999) to Verizon (which acquired AOL for $4.4bn in 2015) before the digital ad firm System1 snapped it up for an undisclosed but surely discounted sum in 2019.

Now a Los Angeles-based operation of about 40 people, MapQuest makes money selling banner ads and premium subscriptions instead of data. It is also licensing tools built around user engagement that other companies can put to their own mapping purposes.

The app user experience will be familiar to anyone who navigates with Apple Maps, Google Maps or Waze, just with more obvious pixeling. That’s all by design that leans hard into nostalgia, with interchangeable personal location markers called “questies” that evoke the 32-bit video game characters of yore. Berger is at pains to point out that questies are handcrafted. “Trust me, it would be very easy to create them with AI,” he said.

Since the Lake Ontario executive order, requests for new features have poured in from social media, email and even snail mail. Berger welcomes the feedback so readily that MapQuest created an online suggestion box for people to propose ideas and put them up for a vote. That’s how it wound up adding a polling places tool, which came in especially handy earlier this month. “There’s a button right here that says ‘vote’,” Berger demonstrates on our video call. “When you tap it, it shows a little unicorn in red, white and blue and tells you exactly where to go for early voting, ballot drop-off and on election day.”
But that’s not what had me booting up MapQuest again for the first time since the iPhone consigned it to the internet’s suspended animation wing alongside Go.com and LiveJournal.

Last month, as part of a Halloween-themed app update, MapQuest introduced a user-requested feature for tracking surveillance cameras on the road. Prominent in the new MapQuest layer are Flock cameras, the AI-driven, solar-powered devices that capture images of passing vehicles, logging license plates and other identifying details, often without drivers’ knowledge. The cameras are represented by blinking red eyes that beam red cones in the direction their lenses face. The real-life implications are considerably less cartoonish.

Over the past five years, Flock license-plate readers have grown into a nationwide network of 120,000 cameras spanning more than 6,000 communities, according to the company. They turn passing cars into searchable records for law enforcement agencies – and potentially others with network access – of who was where and when. Their spread has drawn criticism from civil-liberties groups concerned about the surveillance of non-suspects: research from the Electronic Frontier Foundation shows that less than 1% of vehicles scanned with automatic license plate readers, or ALPRs, are ever connected with a public safety issue or crime.

Some residents are beginning to challenge their use in communities, too. James Hayes, a community activist, frames mass surveillance as a fourth amendment issue – that it’s tantamount to unlawful search. Two years ago, he says police showed up at his house unannounced at 1am, sniffing around for a car involved in a chase. “They didn’t have the plate on the car, but they had a description through the cameras,” Hayes said. “They had no arrest warrant, no anything.”

Metro Atlanta, where I live, isn’t just where Flock Safety is headquartered. It’s a humming doomsday laboratory for surveillance, with more cameras per capita than any other city in the US and perhaps any city in the world outside China, many of them ALPRs. I never really stopped to consider this while sitting in Atlanta’s notoriously bad traffic, trying my best not to cuss out other drivers and city planners in front of my young sons. (We all fall down.) But then I spent a week using Mapquest.

My sons watched gleefully as our rainbow unicorn questie inched along the road and dissolved into laughter whenever the British grandma-voiced navigator chimed in with our next move, sounding like a Speak & Spell that had been left to drown in the Thames. But what really held their attention, and mine, were the eyes. They were everywhere – bracketing our main routes to and from home, all along the highway, boring in on the road to grandma’s house. “I feel like we could break a record for the most cameras ever seen on MapQuest in history!” my oldest said when 17 eyeballs dotted the screen on a morning school run earlier this month.

Tapping an eye in the app lets you see the type of camera, its location coordinates and the direction it’s facing. I imagine it won’t be long before there’s a feature that lets you flag a camera the app missed, like the one just yards from my kid’s school. (Could be another one for the suggestion box.) The data is drawn from OpenStreetMap, a cartographical Wikipedia of sorts that has taken to mapping surveillance cameras, which include Flock’s hardware as well as machines from Motorola Solutions, spun off from the people who gave the world the brick cellphone; and Axon Enterprises, which has experimented with using AI to marry police body cameras with facial recognition tech. “Flock has given people a name to put around them,” said Chris Fleming, a UK-based OpenStreetMap volunteer, about the recent US backlash to surveillance. “In the UK you don’t associate with a company or anything like that.”

He continued: “Personally, I think it’s important to know how prevalent these are, because if we don’t know that they exist how can we debate about what level of surveillance is taking place, what is appropriate and who has access to it? It seems that using these cameras is easier than getting a warrant for a phone, and that’s wrong to me.”

Hayes, the activist, lives just outside the Atlanta metro perimeter in Cherokee county. Last month, the county’s five-member commission board considered a 10-year, $37.3m contract with Axon to become Cherokee law enforcement’s one-stop shop for body cameras, in-car cameras, drones and license-plate readers. Over Halloween weekend, local watchdog groups ran a “trick or treat” email campaign urging concerned residents to contact commissioners before the vote. At the same time, a viral DeFlock America campaign urged Halloween revelers nationwide to cover or disable Flock cameras and the like, at their own considerable legal risk. On 3 November, while people were at the polls on election day, the Cherokee county commissioners voted unanimously to approve the measure – one in a number of worrying deals made between private surveillance firms and local governments across the country.

The timing of the Cherokee county decision, however routine – the commissioners meet on the first and third Tuesday of each month – still left a bad taste. “It’s dirty, so dirty,” said Hayes, adding that it wouldn’t be much longer before surveillance cameras become a major ballot issue. “The datacenter thing was big this past midterm, but Flock is related to it. The more datacenters, the more Flock. I’ve talked to a lot of people about this – Republican, Democrat. Nobody’s good with this.”

Cherokee county still trails in ALPR investment behind my metro Atlanta home jurisdiction. Last September, Dekalb county commissioners signed off on the nation’s largest documented surveillance contract with Flock, $18.9m over 10 years, and followed that up last week by rejecting a proposal for a civilian oversight committee to stand sentry for rights abuses. Troublingly, Flock video is shared among thousands of law enforcement agencies, giving rise to a surveillance network that makes it possible for them to build cases against protesters, abortion seekers, immigrants and others even as they cross in and out of jurisdiction.
All that is to say: you could see why someone might want to know where the Flock cameras and other ALPRs are and potentially even steer clear while they still can.

I tend to approach navigation apps like a gameshow host, calling on Apple, Google or the in-car GPS based on which one pipes up first. But after a week with MapQuest, I found it difficult to go back to the others without feeling like something was missing – those eyeballs. Surveillance state aside, it was as if I was picking up where I left off, back when MapQuest was a companion to young drivers just starting out on the road, its printouts taking pride of place on the dashboard and front seat.

These days MapQuest integrates easily enough into the CarPlay set-up, and while its maps lack the environmental textures Apple and Google offer, that matters less to me than making time. Like many Atlanta locals who yearn for light rail expansion, I spend a distressingly large chunk of my life behind the wheel, ferrying my sons to school (an hour-long commute each way, at best), extracurricular activities and a never-ending slate of playdates. Nothing irks my soul quite like the sight of red congestion lines and an ETA that climbs with every idle moment.

As a driving aid, MapQuest is as competent as any – even as it still lacks full operating system integration and freezes up on the dashboard at times. It’s also more optimistic than I would prefer. Apple tends to provide a more generous ETA, giving me the satisfaction of “beating” it. My MapQuest routes, though, often started with earlier ETAs that gradually ticked upward as the reality of gridlock set in. One afternoon school run lasted nearly 20 minutes longer until our “quest” was complete, our destination rendered on an exaggerated location pin with a big “B”, as in point B.

Sometimes on interstate journeys, which account for most of my driving these days, the app would encourage me to ramp-hop (exit and re-enter the main highway) to avoid bottlenecks. Other times, it would send me down roads where I knew more traffic miseries awaited, leaving me to wonder if I was better off going my own way. Maybe the paid versions are better, but who was I to turn down the free version, especially with MapQuest temporarily suspending ads to attract new users?

Waze showed years ago that there was space on the home screen for one more GPS app – that is, before Google swallowed it up. MapQuest would seem to have a fair shot at repositioning itself in the very lane it established, if not for its routing capabilities than for its retro stylings and cheeky contrarianism.

The politics of geography are easy enough to take for granted until a border is disputed or a landmark name is contested. I remember making the drive a few years ago to the big army base in north-west Georgia, entering through a distant back gate and doing a double take when signs for Fort Benning read Fort Moore instead. It was one of nine army bases renamed under the Biden administration to remove references to Confederate figures – a move that the Trump administration would later roll back.

The switch-around had Berger thinking about more alternate routes MapQuest can take: “Now you have my head spinning about feature requests, the concept of synonyms for familiar places,” he said. “That would be interesting.”

items.title: Cotswolds barn renovation by ConForm creates a "dialogue between old and new"
paragraphs: London studio ConForm Architects has transformed a former cattle barn into a multifunctional space for a working farm in the Cotswolds, contrasting its original red-brick and timber structure with zinc and black-timber additions.
Named Open Byre, the 124-square-metre barn has been adapted into a flexible space for meetings and gatherings, with the first floor containing a standalone apartment for guests.

ConForm Architects‘ design responds to the dual nature of the barn’s surroundings – with traditional red-brick farm structures to the east and more contemporary agricultural barns to the east – combining restoration with a new contrasting palette of stone, metal and timber.

“The design centres on a dialogue between old and new. Rather than blending the interventions into the existing fabric, we wanted each to remain legible and reinforce the other,” studio partner Ben Edgley told Dezeen.
“The building sits between two distinct parts of the farm: the older red brick buildings around the formal front farmyard and the more recent, industrial agricultural structures beyond,” he added.
“The design responds to both, retaining the brickwork and slate roof at the front while using zinc and blackened timber at the rear to reference the newer farm buildings.”

A defining feature of the barn’s new rear facade is a projecting volume wrapped by gabion walls, filled with locally-quarried stone and punctured by a large window illuminating a cross-laminated timber (CLT) staircase.

In the ground floor’s flexible office and arts spaces, the idea of material contrasts continues, with original red-brick walls and repaired timber ceilings accompanied by joinery including desks, storage and a bathroom pod in black through-coloured MDF.
Above, the guest apartment is tucked beneath the exposed beams of the barn’s roof, with its own dedicated living room, kitchen-diner and bathroom finished in matching black timber.

“The central CLT stair is the defining gesture. It brings together structure, circulation and spatial organisation, drawing the eye from the entrance through the building towards the trees beyond,” said Edgley.
“Its scale and material presence establish a clear contrast with the existing brickwork and timber frame,” he added.
“The clients were closely involved in the process, undertaking much of the timber repair alongside local craftsmen. Their commitment to retaining the original fabric was central to the project.”
ConForm Architects was founded in 2017 by Edgley alongside Eoin O’Leary.
Previous projects by the studio include a terraced home in London with perforated metal floors to filter daylight and a green-terrazzo flat extension modelled on bay windows.

items.title: Cosimo I de’Medici review – up close and personal with a Renaissance godfather
paragraphs: Mounting a “store-cupboard” exhibition – choosing items from existing collections to make a new, contained display – can be a cheap and easy way for a museum to make something out of its existing resources, without the faff of securing loans or collaborating across the industry. In the case of the Wallace Collection, however, the store cupboard is so embarrassingly rich and diverse that strong displays such as this on Cosimo I de’Medici can be drawn from only a handful of its objects.

The 19th-century collection of Sir Richard Wallace holds a notable number of medieval objects, but their display can seem – at least to contemporary eyes – like a cacophony of applied arts, armour and paintings, not to mention a ton of gilt. This Medici display is part of a new enterprise drawing out histories from the noise for singular focus, sensibly repurposing what was once the cloakroom (a previously wasted bit of prime real estate) as a new dedicated space.

The Medici family history itself is more labyrinthine than can be captured in a single exhibition, even for diehard historians (or, I dare say, bingers of the 2016 Italian-British TV series), and the Wallace eschews dense background reading here. It has a dual obligation to impart the artwork’s historical significance in relation to its existence in the Wallace Collection, which is perhaps why it omits significant details regarding Cosimo’s role in founding the Uffizi Gallery and expanding the Pitti Palace in Florence. We get the key grounding, however, in that in 1537, the 17-year-old Cosimo was elected as the new duke of Florence. This followed swiftly after the assassination of the last male heir of the senior branch of the Medici family, Alessandro, leaving a power vacuum at threat from republicanism.

And, crucially, it demonstrates that it is not necessarily the most “beautiful” works that are the most compelling. It’s always secretly thrilling to encounter a fresco that’s been hacked off the wall (removal videos are nail-biting stuff), and a 1464 fresco of the young Cicero reading taken from a Milanese branch of the Medici bank even has chunks at its base missing, the snap-lines used to mark out its design in wet plaster clearly visible up close in raking light, and somewhat hilariously mounted in an incongruous wooden frame. Among its usual Wallace location the clunky fresco medium would usually pale next to its fine art neighbours – now it shines in the spotlight.

We are told how the statesman Cicero was a model of civic virtue and morality and hence adopted as a symbol of the Florentine republic. He is envisaged here (in a commission by Cosimo the Elder, not Cosimo I as is the case for every other piece – pay attention at the back!) as a studious young figure with a sense of industry and success, implying similar connotations for the benefacting Medici family.

The varying amount of iconographic content – ie, the visual symbolism deliberately used by Cosimo I for dynastic purposes – does highlight the limitations of working within Wallace’s collection. Certainly, a parade helmet (c1550) and sword (1546-69) bear a plethora of imagery and were inventoried in the Medici armouries as alluding to Hercules, who was commonly said (by Florentines) to have founded Florence. Cosimo’s heraldry sits next to an Order of the Golden Fleece, of which Cosimo was a member, and topped by a ducal crown, despite his only becoming grand duke in 1569. In short, the iconographic picture and dynastic assertion is bright and clear.

Yet the show’s (literal) centrepiece, a 1574 earthenware wine cooler, bears only Cosimo’s personal emblem, a turtle with a sail, alluding to the motto festina lente (make haste slowly), which was itself pinched from Roman emperor Augustus. The rest of the glazed iconography is a combination of fanciful mythological whimsy, satyrs and monstrous figures. It bears a naval battle which it is noted can only with certainty be linked to its purpose for holding liquid. Unlike the armour for which its display purpose – and audience – was obvious, we can only speculate on the audience for such an object other than banqueting and revelry. Perhaps we can – only half-jokingly – look to the glaringly formidable testes of the carved monsters supporting the bowl for further declaration of dynastic strength and rigour.

Such a sparse but precise display is welcome as a contrast with the Wallace’s visual overwhelm, using close and precise old-school art historical analysis to draw out one strand of its many contained histories. Even the choice of terracotta wall colour instantly imparts a Florentine flavour – a smart touch. Its limitations remind us that the collection is based on personal, not curatorial choice, : we don’t even have a portrait of Cosimo himself in the collection, despite Bronzino having churned out dozens of them. Yet hopefully there will be more studies like this to enjoy.
