items.title: What's gone wrong at Britain's worst bathing site?
paragraphs: The official sign on the banks of the River Tone at French Weir Park in Taunton advises people not to swim.
But that hasn't stopped Jo, Jenny, Sue and a second Jo from enjoying a regular dip together.

"People think, oh you're swimming down by the supermarket, that can't be very nice, but it's gorgeous," Jenny Hillier says, as the women huddle round with their coats and hot drinks after a bracing October plunge.
People have been swimming at the spot on the River Tone in the centre of Taunton for more than a hundred years.
But it is only since 2024 that French Weir Park has been designated an official bathing site, which means from May to September the water gets tested by the Environment Agency (EA).
Those tests regularly confirm what the women's senses have been telling them for a while - the water quality is poor.

"There are times when we've come down and we haven't got in, either because of the look or the smell," says Jo Macdonald. "We don't take risks. We don't put our faces in. We don't swim with cuts or anything."
"This summer I got quite poorly," Jenny says, explaining that she'd had diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps.
"I'd swum and then within six hours I was unwell. I was poorly for probably about seven to 10 days and it was not nice. I think it was the river that day."
"There are germs everywhere, all over the place. You can catch Covid in Tesco," she says.

"The counts from just outside the treatment works in my experience were high for treated effluent", Dr Rob Morley from Index Microbiology told us at his laboratory near Bristol as he peered down at small dots of E. coli bacteria on a transparent plastic plate.
What was of particular interest to Morley were the results of the test on water samples we'd taken above and below the point where the treated wastewater enters the River Tone.
It showed 199 CFU of E. coli above, which is fine for swimming and 7,701 CFU just below, more than eight times the regulators limit.
"You can see where it's seeding the river with pollution," Morley says.
"If we were to look further down the river, we would expect the levels to get lower with the dilution effect. But that does quite clearly show the impact that treated effluent can have on the river."

We shared our findings with Dr Andrew Thompson, a fellow at the Institute of Chemical Engineers. He was involved in a 2024 report that warned high concentrations of bacteria and viruses were common, external, particularly in the summer when river levels are lower and could cause serious diseases if ingested.

Thompson told the BBC the levels of E. coli we found in the River Tone were not illegal, or even particularly unusual, because there are currently no laws or regulations about how much bacteria water companies are allowed to discharge in what the industry calls treated effluent.
We also wanted to know whether analysing the E. coli samples from the bathing site could give us clues to where it came from.

With assistance from researchers at the University of Bristol, Morley arranged for e-DNA analysis to be carried out to identify whether the E. coli bacteria were more likely to be from a human or animal gut.
The answer, as is often the case with water quality, is complex. There were lots of different types of E.coli in the samples.

"Some were from humans, some were from animals and some were just generic from the environment," Morley says. "It definitely suggests that some of the E. coli is definitely coming from human origins, therefore potentially from that treatment works."
As with all of our testing, more needs to be done to reach firm conclusions.

Both the EA and Wessex Water are investigating what's causing the water quality in Taunton to be so poor. But sources at the EA told the BBC that constant flows of treated effluent is high up the list of likely culprits.
In response to our testing Wessex Water told the BBC its treatment works at Bradford on Tone was working normally and was meeting all its permit conditions set by the EA.
So could steady flows of treated effluent loaded with bacteria be behind many of the problems at bathing sites across the UK?
"All the sewage treatment works in the UK and in England have permits to protect the ecology and the wildlife within the river," says Jim Flory, a regional manager for the EA in the south-west.
"They've not set permits for bathing water regulations, which are all about protecting people who may want to be swimming, canoeing or using the water."

That has led to a system where a popular bathing site gets officially designated – the testing regime discovers it has high levels of faecal bacteria – and then a lengthy process begins to try to work out where the sources are and whether it's affordable to fix them.

items.title: How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
paragraphs: Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.
That partnership has now ended following Huang's resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which is alleged to have been with a Chinese spy.
The company has been rocked by the scandal, with hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value and questions swirling about the extent of the impact of Huang's departure.
While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.
The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.
Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.
It is now one the most valuable firms, worth $3.8 trillion (£2.9 trillion), and on Tuesday said its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.

But there's now an air of uncertainty over Nvidia's future direction. Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on the company, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at investment firm AJ Bell, says because Huang was also a key figure in "flying the flag" to drum up enthusiasm and investment for the wider AI industry, his departure posed a "real risk" that Nvidia could now decide to change its current strategy and rein in spending.
Such a move could spell a wider slowdown in AI investment, which would have an economic impact. How big? That's "unknown", Coatsworth says.

"If they decide to go with the much more cautious route... there could be a knock-on effect in that you have got various companies in the AI infrastructure space suddenly finding they don't have a key source of finance," he says.

Kunjan Sobhani, senior technology industry analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, expects the impact of Huang leaving to be "limited" for now as Nvidia has strong commitments and a deep order book. But he said this picture could change in the long run.
That is because Nvidia, on its journey to the top of the AI industry, has created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?
That risk is perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, have called for Huang's reinstatement.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, which has also prompted a campaign by shareholders and supporters to "Bring Jensen Back".
Huang himself has said he is open to a return, just days after resigning.

Coatsworth says he has never seen circular financing used at this scale before, but admits there are competitive rivals around, which could insulate the wider AI industry from any potential slowdown at the firm.
When Nvidia's share price plunged in the wake of the affair revelations, the stock of its rival semiconductor makers including AMD, Broadcom and Marvell Technology jumped.
"I don't think all AI activity grinds to a halt if Nvidia slows down what it's doing and if it pulls some financing, but it does change how people would look at the whole situation," Coatsworth adds.
The risk of a slowdown has already rattled stock markets. Investors took fright at Democrat gains in the midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms.
Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will actually pay off.

Investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, who said the technology would remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.
Nvidia's interim boss Colette Kress said it was "business as usual" without Huang at the helm as the company's rapid growth remains on track.
The value of the shares in Big Tech companies have cushioned the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, buoying investments and pensions for people worldwide.
Despite Huang saying he would be "honoured" to return, Nvidia's board has said it is not considering bringing him back.
And while Coatsworth thinks "no CEO is irreplaceable", he admits the pressure is on for whoever succeeds him.

items.title: Prince Harry speaks about social media – level 1
paragraphs: Prince Harry visited Brussels. He speaks in the European Parliament about children and online world.

Harry says that social media apps are dangerous for children. They cause bad problems like bullying. He tells leaders that looking at phones all day is bad for kids. Some leaders are looking into their phones while he is speaking. Harry wants social media companies to follow strict rules to keep young people safe.
Meghan comes with Harry. They meet families of children who die because of social media. EU leaders say that Harry is right. They want to make the internet safer for all children.
Difficult words: dangerous (not safe), bullying (hurting someone again and again), because of (as a result of something).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Carolina Zimbalist pours bioplastic over silk for Emma Watson's LACMA Gala dress
paragraphs: Artist Carolina Zimbalist has co-created a biomaterial dress with actress Emma Watson, who wore it at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art’s 15th annual Art+Film Gala.

Zimbalist, a graduate of the Parsons School of Design, employed a homemade bioplastic she frequently uses in her artistic works in order to create the one-of-a-kind garment, which comprises a longline bodice and floor-length skirt rendered in shades of red.
The petroleum-free poured-and-dried material, containing vegetable glycerin alongside naturally derived proteins such as pea powder, is layered over silk – a natural biopolymer itself.
“The formulation draws on naturally derived proteins and other ingredients, with the exact composition varying depending on what I’m making,” Zimbalist told Dezeen.
“Very often I favour the usage of byproducts.”
The material’s technical makeup lends itself to a distinctive aesthetic once poured and dried.
“My biomaterial creates sculptural forms and flexible surfaces that move with the body,” said Zimbalist.
“The visual qualities are meant to draw greater interest in sustainable materials while remaining fundamentally artistic.”
Zimbalist has variously referred to her recipe as a bioplastic, a biomaterial or a biopolymer, but now favours the latter to avoid negative associations with the term “plastic”.
“For years, I described my formulas as bioplastics, but about three seasons ago, I switched to ‘biomaterials’; when people hear ‘bioplastic’, they tend to focus on the plastic,” Zimbalist continued.

“‘Biomaterial’ opens up a different conversation about what the material is and what it can become. All three terms apply, but they bring different associations – although biopolymer is the most technically accurate.”
Zimbalist hopes that by experimenting with these natural materials, they can become a mainstream and accessible means of constructing garments beyond one-off pieces.

“The environmental benefits are something I’m developing along with the growing wave of biomaterial artists now assembling – I like to think we are presenting sustainable fashion in a way that inspires more interest beyond the fringes.”
Zimbalist is no stranger to clothing celebrities: 2024 saw musician Chapelle Roan wear a hand-painted, garden-inspired dress that the artist made partially using seaweed.
As well as garments, the artist also creates ethereal and sculptural homeware, including lighting and vases.
Biomaterials are sweeping the fashion world, opening up opportunities for aesthetic and sustainable progress in a sector not historically known for its eco-friendliness.
Designers are increasingly finding ways to derive materials, fabrics and ornamentation from pioneering sources, including mycelium, tree cellulose and soil.

items.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
paragraphs: The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.

Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.

The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.

Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.

In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.

If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).

According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.

In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.

“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”
Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.
The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.

The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.
One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.
In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.

The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.

In order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers shows that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.

On this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU announced the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.
The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.
During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.

Timothy Kaldas, the deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, said the commission had generally “done a poor job of leveraging the funds of European taxpayers to support genuine stabilisation” on the other side of the Mediterranean. “The strategic interest of Europe is seeing a more economically stable Egypt with a population that is less precarious,” he said.

Sandra Gómez López, a Spanish socialist MEP who recently visited Cairo to assess human rights in Egypt, said the data presented by the Guardian raised important questions. “The commission must explain transparently why it considers these commitments to have been fulfilled and demonstrate that European funding is genuinely contributing to improving social protection for the Egyptian population,” she said.
She stressed that the EU should not withdraw support, “but neither can we allow the country’s strategic importance to lead us to lower our standards when it comes to human rights”.

For critics, the questions about the EU’s willingness to hold Egypt accountable on very precise socioeconomic targets do not bode well for the broader but less defined goals for democracy and human rights.

Strik said: “The fact that Egypt and the commission even seem to ignore the crystal-clear socioeconomic conditions doesn’t increase my expectation that they adhere to the vague precondition on democracy and the rule of law.”
Claudio Francavilla, an associate EU director at Human Rights Watch, said: “Without benchmarks, the EU has turned a human rights conditionality into a blank cheque for Egypt’s authoritarianism.”

In a statement to the Guardian, the European Commission said the policy target on Takaful and Karama referred to new beneficiary families “and not to its net increase”. The spokesperson said there was “no contradiction” between this statement and that in a confidential document that said Egypt was required to “further expand cash transfer programmes”.

Asked about the release of the remaining €1.5bn in promised loans, the commission said it “will be made once all conditions have been met”, referring to 24 economic policy conditions, keeping an IMF programme on track and “taking concrete and credible steps towards respecting effective democratic mechanisms, including a multiparty parliamentary system, and the rule of law, and guaranteeing respect for human rights”.
It added: “Compliance with the conditionality is examined thoroughly” by EU officials and diplomats based on “information provided by the Egyptian authorities and other relevant sources”.
Egypt’s mission to the EU in Brussels did not respond to a request for comment.

items.title: Waymo temporarily pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways
paragraphs: Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said.
The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless taxis from state freeways following a series of recent traffic incidents.

California's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) cited an "imminent hazard to public safety" for the ban, noting an incident this month in which several driverless Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101.

Waymo said it was working with state officials "diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations", adding that no injuries or collisions were reported following the incident on US Route 101 south of San Francisco.

California's DMV said Waymo's driverless taxis presented a risk "due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present".

In another incident earlier this month, footage widely seen on social media appeared to show a Waymo car trying to overtake patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing the pace of traffic on a San Francisco highway.

The California ban, which came into effect on 11 November, would remain in place until Waymo "demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions".
A Waymo spokesperson said: "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance."
Data on Waymo's website suggests that its cars, compared to human drivers, are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury.
Waymo currently operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, but only offered freeway rides in a handful of those locations, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami.
The company's driverless taxis can continue to operate on regular city streets.
In May, Waymo recalled thousands of its self-driving cars in the US over a software issue that could allow vehicles to drive into flooded roads.
In the same month, multiple Waymo cars were spotted driving around a cul-de-sac in Atlanta, Georgia, in the early hours of the morning.

items.title: Jeff Bezos says he was 'heavily involved' in casting Robert Pattinson as new 007
paragraphs: "There was something special about Rob", Bezos said at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World Event on Tuesday.
Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday, taking over from actor Daniel Craig. He will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.
In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."
The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.
The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.
Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.
But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.
"We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday," Bezos said.
There were five finalists who went through "real, old-fashioned screen tests", acting out three different scenes in full costume, with real sets and other actors, he said.

"By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance," Bezos added. "It was immediately undebated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director … we all gravitated toward Rob."
The pick comes amid widespread Hollywood cuts and consolidation, with studios struggling to get people into cinemas.
Hollywood insiders have said Pattinson was viewed as a safe pick to bring audiences in, rather than taking a risk on a new actor who could grow with the franchise.

"Maybe he's boring. Maybe Hollywood would be passing up a chance to anoint a badly needed new star. But with so much at stake for everyone involved, that all makes him the obvious pick," Hollywood journalist Matthew Belloni, who predicted the pick, wrote in his newsletter.
The BBC's Regan Morris contributed to this report.

items.title: Government risks missing climate targets if EV rules weakened, adviser warns
paragraphs: The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Change Committee (CCC) has warned.

In a letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, the CCC argues that weakening the targets would result in "economic and energy security costs" and leave households "more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices".
The CCC says that switching to an electric vehicle can save a typical household around £800 a year, with fewer people benefiting if the targets were watered down.
The warning comes after weeks of speculation that the government plans to announce changes to the EV targets. Government sources insist no decision has been made.

Under the current rules, a "zero emission vehicle" (ZEV) mandate requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be zero emission by 2030 and all new cars to meet that standard by 2035. Companies that fail to meet their ZEV mandate face a potential fine of £12,000 per car, although there are exemptions.
Industry groups have long complained the current rules impose too heavy a burden, calling instead for a "sustainable transition".
Latest data from trade body the Society of Motor Manufacturing and Traders (SMMT) shows that EVs, as well as plug-in hybrids, are driving growth in new car sales.
In the year so far, 26.6% of all new car registrations have been fully electric, the SMMT says, which is below the headline target of 33% for 2026.

But the industry as a whole appears on course to comply with this year's mandate once flexibilities are accounted for, according to analysis by New AutoMotive, a transport research organisation which supports the transition to electric cars
SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes accused the CCC of ignoring the costs of the targets it was defending.
"The industry cannot subsidise the transition indefinitely, which is why it is unified in seeking change," he said.
The CCC analysis also argued that weakening the targets would lead to a hole in the government's carbon savings that need to be made in order to meet its legally binding climate targets.

The CCC said the ZEV mandate "underpins the largest share of emissions reduction to 2037" in the government's net-zero plan. The climate targets set for 2033-2037 will be missed "without alternative action at the same scale", the CCC argued.
CCC analysis shows surface transport - which includes cars, vans and trucks - remains the country's highest carbon-emitting sector and one of the slowest to decarbonise.
Lord Deben, former CCC chairman, said going against CCC advice would "not be sensible" as it would "cost people money".
He said climate targets were "not random targets" and "if you don't reach them then you put yourselves in really serious danger of having climate change, which we can't handle".

A government spokesperson said: "We remain committed to the phase out of all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and to all new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, as well as to our legally binding net zero targets. Our consultation on the Mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition."

items.title: Pakistan's solar revolution has been so successful the national grid is crumbling
paragraphs: Jewellery, glimmering silverware, sofas and an air-conditioning unit. Three months after his wedding, Faisal Shahzad's home in rural Punjab is bursting with gifts from his bride's family, as part of the dowry.
But the most prized possession is tucked under the bed: a 340W solar panel.
"In the summer we ran it from 08:00 in the morning until the evening," he says, adding they didn't need to use grid power at all during the day. "We ran our air cooler on it all day."
Pakistan has seen a boom in imported solar panels, which glisten from the rooftops of homes and hospitals; from farmers' fields to industrial complexes.

From 2018 to 2025, the share of electricity generated from solar energy in the country rose from 1% to 28%, according to Pakistan-based think tank Renewables First, with some seven million households now owning panels.
People used to gift motorbikes or other household items at weddings, Shahzad says. "Now they give a solar panel and an air cooler. It has almost become a must."

Alongside the solar panel he still uses the national grid to meet his energy needs, particularly as he lives in a house with his family and brothers' families, who often use multiple appliances simultaneously. But in a country where the average wage is just under 40,000 Pakistani rupees (£110; $145) per month, bills are becoming unaffordable, rising to 15,000-18,000 rupees.

This year, COP31 is pushing the world to move away from fossil-powered vehicles, boilers and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment. And while Pakistan has become a poster child for solarisation, the national grid system is experiencing knock-on eﬀects.

The big pivot to solar wasn't driven by government policy but by individual Pakistani households. Most people we spoke to said they installed panels to escape soaring electricity prices from an often unreliable national grid.
Electricity tariffs have more than doubled in a few years, says Muhammad Hassan Dajana, industry liaison at Renewables First, while the cost of Chinese solar panels has "decreased by 93%".

"People have just found another way to be able to survive," says Energy Minister Awais Ahmad Leghari. "It's a very healthy thing. We have adapted to the situation. The people have reacted and responded in a very economically viable and efficient manner."
While the solar boom brings clear benefits, particularly for a country that imports huge amounts of fuel, there are worries too.
Pakistan needs to avoid the so-called utility death spiral.

When people buy less energy from the national grid, fewer customers are left to cover the fixed costs of maintaining it. That can force prices up - which in turn encourages even more people to switch to solar.
Over time, this can lead to a two-tier system in which those who can't afford to buy panels face ever-rising bills, while the national grid becomes an increasing burden on the state.
"You'll have a white elephant in the form of a state-owned enterprise that requires a lot of public funding to just stay afloat," says Dajana.
But as the government tries to improve the grid, solar is still expanding with widespread adoption in industry.

Kohinoor Textiles Mills in Islamabad, which is powered by a sea of huge blue solar panels, is one example. Utilities manager Sabawoon Khan describes them as his "baby", pointing at construction work levelling the ground for more panels.
When the sun shines, the mills' hundreds of machines are powered entirely by solar energy, Khan says. The heavy-furnace-oil engines they once relied on sit mothballed in a warehouse.

But there are limits. When it's too cloudy or polluted, and during the night, the company takes more energy from the national grid. In the coming weeks, like other firms, it will start using industrial batteries which can store excess solar energy.
"We needed to reduce our energy costs and this was one way to do it," says Taufique Sayeed Saigol, the mills' CEO, who adds the plan is not to disconnect from the grid altogether.
"The state unfortunately doesn't have the resources so we can't really say that we blame everything on the state. We do some of the things ourselves."

Despite admitting that the first wave of solar adoption was a "surprise" to the government, Leghari says he has no fear that solar could outrun their plans, saying it has been incorporated into their 10-year forecasts and the numbers leaving the grid have slowed.
Pakistan has big ambitions for solar; there are plans to open solar battery factories around the country and encourage more electric vehicles.

"There are two paths ahead," Dajana says. One is a future where solar and the grid work in parallel, demonstrating how a gradual energy transition can succeed. The other is where Pakistan becomes a cautionary tale, burdened with a costly, declining grid.
Shahzad's solar ambitions for his home in rural Punjab certainly have not slowed.
"We plan to get another 10-15 panels and install them on the roof, then connect a full system with batteries and back up.
"The plan is to be fully self-sufficient."

items.title: Apple outage: iPhone apps suffer disruption days after major Microsoft issues
paragraphs: Thousands reported disruptions to Google’s Gmail and Apple’s iPhone apps, such as Apple Pay and iCloud, on Tuesday, according to Downdetector. Apple confirmed the outages in a statement but said it had resolved them, while Google said it had not seen internal signs of outages.
Apple’s own system status page as of 2.30pmET showed problems with services such as the App Store, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps and AppleCare.

“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” an Apple spokesperson said.

A Google spokesperson said: “We’re not currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption. Our teams monitor service health closely, and real-time status updates are always available on the Google Workspace Status Dashboard.”
The outage reports come on the heels of major disruptions in technological infrastructure, particularly in the US but also worldwide, that range from air traffic control systems to email accounts.
The outages began in earnest last week when Microsoft Outlook users across the globe could not access their email accounts or other critical Microsoft Office applications.
The day after that outage began, the US Department of Transportation grounded all flights in the US in response to a communication system malfunction.
On Monday, United Airlines experienced service outages, and thousands of Chase Bank customers also reported they had trouble using their accounts.

In a statement on Monday, JPMorganChase said it had “experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems” and said it wass “taking longer than usual to service some customers”.
The bank said there was “no evidence this is cyber-related”. As of Monday evening, a Chase spokesperson told NBC News that transactions were being processed normally again.

Before the news of the Apple and Gmail disruptions on Tuesday, reports of an outage involving the US National Security Agency (NSA) made headlines. CNN reported that a highly classified network the NSA uses for its internal communications, known as NSANet, was down.

A US official told CBS News that the NSA experienced a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance”. They said that “while some internal systems were affected, mission/critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues”.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told NewsMax on Tuesday of the outage of NSANet: “We see no evidence that this was a cyber-attack.” She added that “there is no crisis, or anything like that, for Americans to be worried about”.
Also on Tuesday, Charles Schwab said its website suffered a “brief webpage loading issue” but said that by noon ET it had been resolved.

Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, appeared on Fox News this week where he said that artificial intelligence, which Trump and members of his administration call “super-intelligence”, or “SI”, could be behind the recent outages.

“I talked to one guy in the tech industry, he asked not to mention his name, it’s not Elon, I asked, what could be causing these outages? He said I believe it’s the SI, he said because these programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is,” he said.
And when asked about the flurry of recent outages on Tuesday, Donald Trump said: “No, it’s life.”
“When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen,” the president added. “It’s fine.”

items.title: US moves to restrict China's remote access to advanced SI chips
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

The U.S. Commerce Department announced new restrictions Monday on remote access to advanced super intelligence (commonly referred to as artificial intelligence), chips and servers, technology. The new restrictions are meant mainly to stop Chinese companies that are getting around U.S. limits on chip sales by using or renting computer time in other countries.
The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule developed at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council.

Under the new rule, U.S. chip suppliers will need government permission before selling advanced chips to data centers that let Chinese companies rent or use large amounts of that computing power. The limit is roughly equal to the power of about 330 of Nvidia’s more advanced chips.
It also requires licenses for chip exports to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, which Commerce says pose a higher risk that chips will be diverted.

The rule requires data centers, overseas chip manufacturers and chip exporters to conduct enhanced due diligence on customers, including determining whether they are directly or indirectly owned or controlled by Chinese state-owned enterprises or entities in Macau.
In addition to China, the restrictions cover Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Russia.

The Commerce Department said the rule is intended to bring safeguards governing remote access to advanced computing capabilities into closer alignment with existing controls on the physical shipment of sensitive American technology.

The department said the United States remains the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the legitimate commercial use of American technology worldwide. But it warned that rapid advances in cloud computing and super intelligence infrastructure have made it increasingly possible to access advanced U.S. computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers in countries not subject to U.S. export restrictions.

China's Foreign Ministry criticized the new restrictions, accusing Washington of interfering in China's trade and technology cooperation with other countries. Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said Tuesday that the United States was "overstretching the concept of national security."
He added that the measures violated understandings reached between the two countries, warning that "China will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its legitimate rights and interests."
Chairman of the House Select Committee on China and Republican Representative John Moolenaar of Michigan, welcomed the announcement of restrictive measures by the U.S. government.
In a statement Monday, Moolenaar said the rule “sends a message to the CCP that America is serious about closing dangerous export control loopholes China has been exploiting for years.”

Moolenaar called the measure an important step toward preventing sensitive chips from falling into the wrong hands, strengthening U.S. national security laws and protecting America's leadership in the race for super intelligence.

In January, the House passed the Remote Access Security Act, which seeks to restrict foreign adversaries, including the Chinese Communist Party, from obtaining access to U.S. technology through cloud computing services.

Rush Doshi, who served as director for China affairs on the National Security Council during the Biden administration, said in a post on X that the Trump administration's new remote-access rule was driven by the controversy surrounding Jensen Huang. The former Nvidia CEO resigned last week after admitting to an extramarital affair with a businesswoman who U.S. authorities believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, according to The New York Times. China rejects the report.
The announcement also comes amid differences within the Trump administration over how to approach Megaspeed.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC last week that the Treasury, State and War departments, along with the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, had favored placing Singapore-based Megaspeed on the Commerce Department's Entity List for months.

The list identifies foreign individuals and entities considered to pose risks to U.S. national security or foreign policy interests. U.S. companies generally need a license to export certain items to listed entities, with the licensing policy varying by entity and product.
Bessent said the Commerce Department controlled the decision, adding that it was up to the department to explain its internal process.

President Donald Trump told reporters Monday that there were "two different views" on how to approach the issue. He described one as favoring a friendlier approach and the other as being willing to risk a confrontation. Trump said both positions were acceptable and that he understood both sides.

Trump departed Monday for the Philippines to attend a special U.S.-ASEAN summit in Manila. He is also scheduled to travel to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' informal meeting and hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.

items.title: US Congressman-elect Dan Koh has a message for North Korea
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.
President Donald Trump will be in China this week for an Asia-Pacific summit, and he has floated possibility of meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
An incoming Korean American congressman says he is open to engaging adversaries, if it serves the interests of the United States and South Korea.
In an interview with VOA, newly elected Democratic Representative Dan Koh had his own message for the people of North Korea.
“I am thinking of you, and I hope that one day we will be able to work side by side," he said.
Koh, who won Massachusetts’ 6th Congressional District in the November 3 midterm elections, spoke with VOA on November 12.

On the possibility of resuming U.S.-North Korea summit talks, Koh said he does not “oppose meeting with adversaries or those with whom the United States disagrees." However, he stressed that any such engagement should serve the national interests of both the United States and South Korea.

"This is something I will hold very close to my heart and prioritize during my time in Congress," he told VOA. "I will work to ensure that the relationship between South Korea and the United States remains very strong.”

While outlining plans to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, President Trump said he might also meet North Korean leader Kim, adding that such a meeting would be welcome.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told VOA during an October 31 press briefing in Atltanta that he believes Trump would be willing to engage in talks again “if there’s something productive that can come out of it.””
Rubio also discussed North Korea during a question-and-answer session with reporters on November 13 at the Federalist Society’s National Lawyers Convention in Washington.

While stressing that he was not defending atrocities committed in North Korea, Rubio said Kim Jong Un, unlike Iran’s leadership, seeks regime survival rather than expansion and is not seeking to invade Japan or China.
Incoming Democratic Representative Koh also underscored South Korea’s importance as a U.S. ally and expressed opposition to tariffs on South Korean products.

“Of course, I think there are certain critical technology sectors where tariffs may be appropriate to protect the United States,” Koh told VOA. “But South Korea is not our enemy, and what we’re doing right now is destabilizing all of our allies around the world.”

In an April executive order on tariffs, President Donald Trump "declared that foreign trade and economic practices have created a national emergency" and the "order imposes responsive tariffs to strengthen the international economic position of the United States and protect American workers."

Koh also addressed report of discrimination against U.S. companies operating in South Korea, including against Coupang, South Korea’s biggest online retailer, often called “the Amazon of South Korea."
The information comes from a July report by the House Judiciary Committee. Koh said it was important to ensure that American companies are treated fairly in South Korea.

The report, titled “Closed for Competition: South Korea’s Discriminatory Attacks on American-owned Businesses,” says that the Korea Fair Trade Commission aggressively targeted U.S.-owned companies through early-morning raids and threats of criminal charges.
It also says that South Korea’s Personal Information Protection Commission discriminated against Coupang by imposing a fine of more than $410 million, in June over a personal data breach.
South Korea’s Foreign Ministry rejected the report, saying it reflected only Coupang’s arguments.
About his Korean heritage, the fresh congressman expressed deep pride in his family heritage and Korean American identity.

“It is a tremendous honor to be able to give a little bit of pride back to the hometown and family of my grandfather, who came to America against all odds,” Koh said.“I think this is such an exciting time for Korean American culture, and I am incredibly proud to be a part of it."

items.title: Taliban ban cricket broadcasts in Afghanistan's Kandahar province
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.
The Taliban have ordered local radio stations in the southern Afghan province of Kandahar to stop airing news and information about cricket, the country’s most popular sport.
The Taliban’s provincial Department of Information and Culture issued the order on Saturday.
“Both commentary and news coverage, or even reporting about their winning results, is also banned,” the source in the department told AFP, requesting anonymity for security purposes.

Three chief editors and managers of private radio stations in Kandahar told Radio Azadi on Monday that they have received verbal instructions from the Taliban’s provincial authorities prohibiting all cricket-related broadcasts.

An official in Afghanistan’s Cricket Board, who requested anonymity as he was not authorized to speak to the media, told VOA that the board was aware of the development but said the “restrictions are limited to the Kandahar province,” and that the board is currently in discussion with the provincial authorities.
Cricket is the most popular sport in Afghanistan, particularly among younger people.
Afghans, who had been living in refugee camps in Pakistan, are credited with bringing the game to their impoverished South Asian nation.

Cricket flourished in Afghanistan after the U.S.-led coalition toppled the Taliban in 2001, when the country became an associate member of the International Cricket Council, the world’s cricketing body.
Afghanistan became a full member of the ICC’s elite club of 12 countries in 2017, and it enjoys the status of a test-playing nation.
Since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, the national team has mostly trained and played outside the country.
The Afghan team won widespread admiration during the 2023 Cricket World Cup, defeating three former champions: Pakistan, England and Sri Lanka.

The international community has not formally recognized the Taliban government mainly for restricting Afghan women’s access to education, employment, sports, and public life at large. The curbs have prompted some countries to boycott bilateral cricket competitions with Afghanistan.
The Afghan men's team, however, has become increasingly competitive internationally, reaching the semifinals of the 2024 Men's T20 World Cup for the first time.
Afghan players have also become prominent figures on international cricket teams.

items.title: Iran continues crackdown on women: teacher’s retrial denied, Baha’i citizen sentenced
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

Iran has rejected a request for a retrial by Kokab Bodaghi Pegah, a teacher's union advocate living in Izeh, for a second time, and referred her case for enforcement of her one-year prison sentence, the Coordinating Council of Iranian Teachers’ Trade Associations reported Sunday.
Bodaghi Pegah was convicted of “propaganda against the regime” over her union activism.

According to the council, the Supreme Court upheld the teacher’s one-year prison sentence after the Khuzestan Province Court of Appeals fully affirmed the initial one-year sentence issued by Branch 101 of the Ahvaz Criminal Court in late July of this year.
In September 2025, Bodaghi Pegah was also sentenced to a three-month suspension from service by the Administrative Violations Appeals Board of the Khuzestan Province Department of Education.

Also on Sunday, the U.S.-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) reported that Nazanin Abedini Kafshgari, a Baha’i resident of Qaem Shahr, was sentenced by the Sari Revolutionary Court to three years in prison and an eight-year ban on social rights, such as holding public sector jobs.

According to HRANA, the sentences were issued on November 9 by Branch 1 of the Sari Revolutionary Court, presided over by Judge Ammar Ramezani. The court charged the Baha’i citizen with "propaganda against the Islamic Republic system" and "propaganda in favor of groups or organizations opposed to the Islamic Republic system."
HRANA stated that the court cited her educational and religious activities—including teaching Baha’i beliefs to children and her social media activity—as the basis for her conviction.
HRANA further reported that Fariba Asadi, a social activist detained in connection with the 2025–2026 protests, has been sentenced to six years in prison along with supplementary punishments.

According to HRANA, the Islamic Republic charged the female protester with "assembly and collusion, acting against national security, and participating in protests." In addition to the prison term, she was sentenced to a two-year travel ban, a two-year ban on membership in social groups and organizations, and dismissal from government and public service jobs.

Her verdict was issued by Branch 2 of the Karaj Revolutionary Court, presided over by Judge Sabzevari. Asadi, a resident of Karaj, was arrested by Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Intelligence agents on January 26, 2026.

Separately, the Hengaw Organization for Human Rights announced that Golaleh (Nazanin) Elyasi, a resident of Mahabad, was arrested on Saturday, November 14, after being summoned to the city’s Sentence Execution Unit, and was transferred to the women's ward of Urmia Central Prison to begin serving her two-year sentence.

According to Hengaw, Elyasi was sentenced to two years of imprisonment in August 2026 by Branch 1 of the Mahabad Revolutionary Court, presided over by Judge Ahad Siami, on the alleged charge of "assembly and collusion to commit crimes against national security."

In its reports on religious freedom in Iran, the U.S. Department of State has specifically documented the persecution of Baha’is, Iran's largest non-Muslim religious minority. According to the State Department, they face arrest, imprisonment, and social restrictions for peaceful religious activities, including teaching their beliefs.

The State Department has repeatedly designated Iran as a "Country of Particular Concern" for "particularly severe violations of religious freedom," emphasizing that Baha’is in Iran face systematic discrimination in areas including education and employment. The United States has consistently called for the release of prisoners of conscience and the dropping of charges that violate the universal right to freedom of religion or belief.

items.title: Caribbean nations fear economic impact of shuttering citizenship program after EU threats
paragraphs: The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned.

On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis.

Mark Brantley, the premier of Nevis, which has autonomous self-governance in some aspects, said he understood that the “country was given very little choice”, but did not “support the winding down of the program”.

The 42-year-old CBI programme, which St Kitts and Nevis pioneered, allows wealthy foreigners to obtain citizenship and ultimately a passport by investing in infrastructure and other development projects. It has brought billions of dollars into the country and in some years accounted for the largest share of government revenue.

In June, the European Commission wrote to the five Caribbean nations that currently operate CBI programmes: St Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and St Lucia. It warned that countries may lose visa-free access to its 29-country Schengen area if they did not phase out CBI.

In Friday’s statement, Drew blamed concerns over the programme on mismanagement by previous administrations, including years of underselling to undercut other countries, a controversial prison project, weak escrow protections and investment sums not being properly paid into the citizenship unit.

He said his government had led major reforms to the Caribbean’s programmes with international partners, including the US treasury, but argued that continuing the programme risked visa-free travel to parts of Europe and access to international banking. That could disrupt services allowing visitors to use overseas cards and families abroad to send money home.
Brantley, however, argued it was unfair for the EU to force St Kitts and Nevis to make a move without offering assistance to navigate the transition to other industries.

“I have not yet seen from the EU any corresponding suggestions of assistance. And we have to realise that these citizenship-by-investment programs, not only in St Kitts and Nevis, but … smaller countries of the Caribbean, have contributed significantly to our gross domestic product and also to ensuring that our people … can get adequate access to water and to education, to healthcare and the like,” he said.
Brantley described the 1 June 2028 deadline the EU gave the country to phase out the lucrative programme as “frankly ludicrous”.
In his statement, Drew said the CBI programme “did a lot of good, but it also created a danger”.
“When one source pays for half or more of everything, you are at its mercy. If it stops, everything stops. That is putting all of your eggs in one basket,” he added.

The prime minister said the government aimed to diversify its economy by strengthening tourism, yachting, and digital and creative industries, among others. He added that the sale of clean, geothermal energy was “at the heart of it” with drilling and exploration already planned.

“I will not pretend that the road is easy. Less CBI money means we must spend wisely and plan carefully. We will. Our plan is to make this change by growing our economy. Raising taxes is not part of that plan,” Drew said.

Antigua and Barbuda has also expressed willingness to end the programme, though it is trying to negotiate a longer transition period. The five Caribbean governments have taken differing positions on the EU demand. According to local media, Grenada has indicated it wants its programme to continue until 2032, while Dominica and St Lucia have responded to Brussels without publicly committing to ending their programmes.
Jermine Abel in Basseterre contributed reporting

items.title: Isolated Brazilian tribe emerges amid alarm over threats to group’s way of life
paragraphs: About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest, several organizations reported on Tuesday, raising the alarm about increased invasions into the tribe’s territory.

According to the NGO Survival International, members of the Awá people, who live in voluntary isolation, arrived on Monday in a village and made contact with a government team in a “historic encounter”.
The village they entered was within the Arariboia Indigenous territory in the north-eastern state of Maranhão, home to the Guajajara ethnic group.
Local community leaders said the villagers offered food to the group.
“They asked for yams and took them back into their forest,” said Survival International.
The NGO explained that the Awá typically subsist on hunting and gathering. However, they have faced increased incursions from illegal loggers, hunters and cattle ranchers.
A video of the encounter, filmed by Guajajara villagers and released by Survival International, shows a group of men, women and children at the edge of the forest.
Partially concealed by vegetation, they appear naked and are wearing necklaces. The men carry bows and long arrows.

“The physical condition of some members, particularly the children and the elderly, caused concern among the villagers, who noted clear signs of severe emaciation,” warned Coapima, an organization representing Indigenous groups in Maranhão.
Coapima highlighted the risks that unplanned contact poses to such groups, noting that they are particularly “exposed to diseases” against which they have little to no immunity.

Funai, the public agency responsible for Indigenous affairs, said in a statement sent to AFP that its technical teams were closely monitoring the situation and analyzing available information regarding the group’s health.

Survival International’s director, Caroline Pearce, said the group’s choice to emerge from isolation was a “troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger”.
She said the Awá were being driven into “an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction”.
According to the NGO, about 196 “uncontacted” peoples and groups, who choose to live in isolation, have been identified across 10 countries.
More than 90% of such groups live in the Amazon rainforest, primarily in Brazil, with others in Indonesia and India.

The Forest Guardians – a group of Guajajara people who have battled illegal invasions for years – warned in comments in the Survival International statement that “climate change, fires, deforestation and land encroachment” were affecting the Awá’s way of life.
According to Survival International, many of the guardians have lost their lives trying to protect the territory they share with the Awá.

items.title: Air travel, Microsoft, banking: Why are our IT systems failing?
paragraphs: NPR's Sacha Pfeiffer speaks with cybersecurity expert Dmitri Alperovitch about the coincidence of several major technical failures in IT infrastructure — and how best to understand it.

Say that last Thursday, you were trying to email your boss about a business trip this week. But Microsoft Outlook was down, so you had to wait to send that email till Friday. But on Friday, a fiber-optic cable replacement crashed the routers that deal with air traffic, and that held up nearly all departing flights nationwide. When that finally sorted out, and you rebooked a flight on Monday, United Airlines had a brief system outage that further delayed your takeoff, at which point you went to your banking app to see how much all this was costing you, but that was briefly down yesterday too.
UNIDENTIFIED REPORTER: AI, United, Chase bank.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: It's life. It's life. When you're big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine.

PFEIFFER: President Trump downplayed all the outages today. Although, speaking of being big and powerful, NPR has confirmed that the classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its own internal communications has been having issues today. We have so many questions about all of this, which is why we have called Dmitri Alperovitch. He's cofounder of the cybersecurity technology company CrowdStrike, and he's founder of the Alperovitch Institute for Cybersecurity Studies at Johns Hopkins University. Thank you for coming on the program.
DMITRI ALPEROVITCH: Thanks for having me.
PFEIFFER: At this point, is there any evidence that all these incidents are connected in any way or maybe are tied to cybercrime?

ALPEROVITCH: No. And I understand that people are very suspicious. Obviously, all of these events happening almost every day is very strange. But these things happen. And, you know, one of Murphy's laws, of course, is that never attribute anything to malice that which is adequately explained by incompetence. I think a lot of these things happening because people are actually in the midst of a lot of upgrading right now.

There is, of course, the AI threat. A lot of vulnerabilities are being found by these AI models. And as a result, a lot of companies, a lot of organizations across the world, are trying to patch these vulnerabilities as quickly as possible. So we're going through this patch apocalypse right now. And sometimes when you're updating systems, we all know things can go wrong, and I think that's partly what's happening here.

PFEIFFER: So are we having this collision of our extreme reliance on technology, overtaxed, often aging systems that, as you said, periodically need updating. We know that cyberattacks are common. We know that rogue AI is a fear. Are we seeing the fragility of the system all coming together?

ALPEROVITCH: Well, these are all different systems. So there's no question that we're much more reliant on technology. So when things go down now, it causes much more inconvenience for us. You know, in the old days, it was easier to get into, perhaps, your bank and - physically and withdraw money, and now we're relying much more on online banking and those sorts of things. So the impact to us is much greater, but these things have always happened. But I do think there's something to the idea that, right now, it's happening more because everyone is trying to update their systems before they can get hacked by these AI models.
PFEIFFER: I was going to say updates are a fact of life, but you're saying particular updates happening now because of the risks of AI that are becoming apparent - people trying to get ahead of that.

ALPEROVITCH: That's right. More vulnerabilities have been discovered this year than the last 30 years combined. So that's as a result of AI looking at these software packages, identifying new vulnerabilities. So enterprises, government agencies are, right now, completely flooded with reports that you need to update your systems because there's another critical vulnerability that has just been discovered.
PFEIFFER: Could that mean that we're going through a rough patch right now, but it will be temporary, or is this going to be an ongoing symptom of our modern age?

ALPEROVITCH: I think the next 12 to 18 months are going to be very rough, not just because of the update cycles, but also because some people will not upgrade in time, and, of course, there will be more hacks as a result. But I think we'll come out on the other end in a much safer way because a lot of the software - your Microsoft Office, your, you know, infrastructure software - will all get much more secure.

PFEIFFER: It's a bit of a cat and mouse game in terms of technology and upgrades and bad actors looking for vulnerabilities. So does that suggest that this is just going to be the ongoing game of cat and mouse that lasts forever?

ALPEROVITCH: Well, this has been the life in cybersecurity for the last 40 years, and I don't think that's going away. As long as there are people out there with malicious intentions, whether it's nation states or criminals or hacktivists, we're going to have problems. And, of course, the biggest vulnerability remains the user, not your computer system, because people fall for social engineering attacks, for phishing scams, and that I expect will continue to be the case.

PFEIFFER: And people have weak passwords, and they might not use two-factor authentication. What - to give some practical advice for people, are we all just helpless victims of this, or what basic things should people be doing to try to protect themselves?

ALPEROVITCH: Well, in terms of your own systems, yes, update it automatically. Make sure that you're fully patched whenever a vulnerability comes out. Make sure, as you said, you have two-factor authentication and strong passwords. But when it comes to this infrastructure going down, you know, we're all observers here and unfortunately sometimes victims because if your bank goes down, there's not a lot you can do.

PFEIFFER: When you looked at the FAA national ground stop on Friday, which we now know appears to have been related to a upgrade happening in Arkansas where something didn't go well and, suddenly, the whole system goes down, is there, in general, not a way to prevent small mistakes happening in isolated areas from crashing an entire system?

ALPEROVITCH: Well, usually, there is, and this was a surprise that there's sort of this one weakness in the system that could take the whole thing down. Usually, there's redundancies. Now, the problem is that a lot of these systems have gotten so complex, with so many layers to them over the years, that it's very, very difficult to understand where those points of failure might be. And hopefully, this is one area where AI might actually help us to identify these problems ahead of time.

PFEIFFER: Oh, that's interesting. Many people are so focused on the negatives of AI and the fear that it will go rogue and cause chaos. But you're saying here's a reminder that it could help us in this situation.
ALPEROVITCH: Absolutely. I think it's going to do some amazing things for us in lots of different areas, but there's no question, like, every technology, it comes with downsides.
PFEIFFER: It sounds to me like your industry has work for infinity, basically.
ALPEROVITCH: There's a lot of job security in cybersecurity.

PFEIFFER: (Laughter) In terms of an overall parting thought, is there any way that we as individuals can be trying to minimize the impact of this on our lives, whether it's reducing our dependency on tech, increasing our protections? What's your advice for those who want to throw their hands up in the air?

ALPEROVITCH: Everyone should focus on resiliency in their daily life. Always have some cash lying around just in case you can't get your money withdrawn from an ATM for a period of time. You know, stockpile some water, stockpile some groceries. I think those are prudent things to do in any scenario. Of course, there could be other catastrophes, weather-related, terrorism, etc. that you want to be prepared for. So that's always a good thing to do.
PFEIFFER: That is Dmitri Alperovitch, a cybersecurity expert and CEO of the Silverado Policy Accelerator. Thank you.

items.title: US Army seeks faster access to emerging defense technology
paragraphs: At the annual Association of the United States Army (AUSA) exposition in Washington on October 12 - 14, 2026, Army leaders called for faster access to new technologies as defense companies showcased systems designed for the modern battlefield. VOA's Julie Taboh reports.

items.title: Campaigners take claim 'regulatory gap' risks poultry farms polluting rivers to High Court
paragraphs: The legal action against Natural Resources Wales landed in the High Court
River campaigners are taking on Wales' environmental regulator in the High Court over what they believe is a "regulatory gap" that risks pollution from poultry farms in two rivers.

River Action UK has accused Natural Resources Wales (NRW) of not doing enough to assess or address any risk to local rivers and and other water bodies when plans for three farms in Powys were approved last year.
It follows years of debate over the alleged impact of chicken farming on rivers such as the Wye and Severn - in an area dubbed the UK's "poultry capital".
NRW said it would be inappropriate to comment ahead of the court case, but that it would "participate fully in the legal process".
The case is about plans to increase the capacity of three Powys farms by a combined 336,900 chickens, bringing the total to 522,000.
The three farms are Neuadd Isaf, Rhosddu and Llanshay.
Two of the farms, Rhosddu and Llanshay, are in the River Severn catchment while Neuadd Isaf is in the River Wye catchment.
Campaigners said the Severn was showing "signs of strain" with regular algal blooms, brown algae smothering the riverbed.
The three poultry units in Powys are located within river catchments including the River Wye
Campaigners' concerns have centred around the birds' manure becoming a pollutant when it is spread on fields and leaches into rivers.
Nutrient-rich agricultural run-off can contribute to algal blooms, turning rivers green and smothering wildlife.
Following a consultation, NRW approved permit variations in November 2025, allowing the three poultry units to expand.
Rather than keep and spread the manure on site, the farms' operators said they would export it for use or processing elsewhere.

River Action argued NRW wrongly concluded it had no legal power under the Environmental Permitting Regulations 2016 to assess the potential environmental impacts of this off-site manure management, or to take action to prevent or mitigate pollution arising from it.
Emma Dearnaley, head of legal at River Action, argues there is a "regulatory gap" in the management of off-site manure
Campaigners set up a chicken-themed protest outside the High Court hearing in Llandrindod Wells on Tuesday.

"River Action will argue that Natural Resources Wales has the power to address and assess the impact of that manure on the environment and, as the specialist regulator, should be lawfully deciding how to use that power when operating the permitting regime," said Julia Eriksen, of solicitors Leigh Day, representing River Action.
The organisation insisted NRW could put controls on the farm's permit to reduce or remove the risk of manure causing pollution.
Campaigners believe the birds' manure will spread on fields and into rivers, causing harm

Emma Dearnaley, head of legal at River Action, said NRW "decided that it didn't have the power to look at what would happen when a lot of the manure would go offsite" when the plans were approved last year.
"That matters because more chickens means more muck, and that needs to go somewhere and someone has to deal with it," she said.
"So this case is all about making NRW realise that it does have the power to deal with it."

An NRW spokesperson said: "As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment on matters that are before the court. We will continue to participate fully in the legal process and await the court's determination."

items.title: Eight-year-old Haitian boy returns home after release from ICE custody
paragraphs: An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by immigration agents in San Diego on 4 November and transferred to a facility in Texas has been reunited with his family in California.

Representative Juan Vargas shared a photograph of the boy and his family in a social media post on Monda, writing: “11 days ago, an 8-year-old in San Diego was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in. He was separated from his loved ones and held in a facility in Texas. Today, he’s finally home.”
The Haitian Bridge Alliance, an immigration advocacy group, confirmed that the third-grader had been released from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody.

“An eight-year-old child belongs in a classroom, on a playground, and surrounded by love – not in immigration detention. We welcome his release, but his freedom should never have required a public outcry,” Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said in a statement.

The third-grader at Fay elementary school was put in restraints and taken into custody by federal immigration officers at a check-in earlier in the month, according to video obtained by NBC News and an oversight letter Democratic lawmakers sent to the Departments of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services.
A spokesperson for the homeland security department said ICE took the child into custody “out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety”.

The uncle, the spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian, was unable to prove legal guardianship – and that officials were obliged by federal anti-trafficking laws to take the boy into care as an “unaccompanied alien child”.
The Haitian Bridge Alliance said the boy was in the care of his uncle and cousins after his father was deported last year.

“I’m so grateful that he’s home, but this should have never happened in the first place,” Vargas said in a second social media post, adding that he would be asking the Trump administration for answers. While he was detained, the child was “held in a facility in Texas, far away from his home in San Diego”, Vargas said.

Celebrating the boy’s return, Jozef of the Haitian Bridge Alliance told NBC News: “The aunt was literally crying, and she said: ‘I have not eaten since the Wednesday they took my baby.’ They haven’t been able to sleep because of that.” She added: “The cousins were there when they took him, and wondering: will they ever see him again? But today [Monday] they are able to see him again. They are able to hug him.”

Millions of us play on consoles, laptops and phones - it's big business. Grand Theft Auto 6 is the latest blockbuster release. But is gaming having an impact on the environment?
