items.title: Iranian satirist Saeed Shakiba gets five years for Khamenei impersonation
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

Saeed Shakiba, an Iranian blogger and satirist who was arrested after posting a satirical video impersonating late Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei’s voice, has been sentenced to five years in prison by a Tehran Revolutionary Court.

The Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) reported on Friday that Branch 28 of the Tehran Revolutionary Court issued the sentence on the alleged charge of “assembly and collusion against national security.” Shakiba is being held at Greater Tehran Penitentiary.
The Hengaw Organization for Human Rights also confirmed the report, saying that Shakiba’s hearing took place last week and that the verdict was delivered to him in prison.

Saeed Shakiba was arrested in mid-October after posting a satirical video on social media in which he imitated the voice of Ali Khamenei, the Iranian Supreme Leader who was killed during the joint U.S.-Israeli military operation against the regime.

Following the video's publication, Mizan News Agency, which is affiliated with Iran’s judiciary, announced that a case had been opened against a blogger, describing the published content as “insulting and abusive.”

On October 25, the agency also reported that an indictment had been issued in the case. A statement from the judiciary cited several alleged charges during the proceedings, including insulting officials, propaganda against the state, and supporting Israel.
According to HRANA, however, Shakiba’s five-year prison sentence was issued on the alleged charge of “assembly and collusion against national security.”

The satirist’s conviction comes after the U.S. State Department documented severe restrictions on freedom of expression and the prosecution of critics of the Islamic Republic in its 2023 annual human rights report on Iran.
The report said Iranian authorities use criminal laws to intimidate and prosecute people who criticize the government, the Islamic Republic’s leader, or official policies.

The State Department also noted that Iran’s security and judicial institutions have, in some cases, used citizens’ remarks and social media posts as grounds for bringing national security charges against them.

The report further cited the arrest and punishment of government critics, restrictions on media activity, and censorship of online content among the violations of freedom of expression in the Islamic Republic.

items.title: Trump–Xi talks to test progress on trade, SI and strategic stability
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are preparing to meet in Shenzhen next week, testing whether their personal diplomacy can deliver progress on trade and super intelligence (commonly referred to as artificial intelligence or AI) risk management.

Preparations continued on November 11, when Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi about Trump’s visit to the November 18–19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and Xi’s planned attendance at December’s G20 summit in Florida.

The State Department said the call, requested by China, covered the importance of substantive leader-level conversations on peace and denuclearization, including at a potential meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
China described the call as positive and constructive. Its account emphasized policy continuity and managing differences but did not mention denuclearization or a trilateral summit.
The Shenzhen encounter would be Trump and Xi’s third meeting this year, following reciprocal visits in May and September.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who said he would accompany Trump, outlined plans on November 10 for the bilateral dialogue on super intelligence.

In prepared remarks to the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations, he described exchanges on evaluating advanced models before release, preserving human control, and creating a direct channel for reporting serious incidents.

Those plans follow September’s agreement to establish a technology dialogue and an incident communication channel. His remarks did not say whether that channel was operational, leaving implementation as a concrete measure of progress.
China this week extended the suspension of an additional 24% tariff on U.S. goods for two months from November 10, while retaining an additional 10% tariff.
It also continued suspensions of restrictions affecting American entities, subject to licensing and review requirements.

Washington is pressing for implementation of trade commitments agreed upon last year. In a November 6 call with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer discussed economic ties. Greer emphasized agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals, according to his office.
Beijing has linked expanded farm purchases to implementation of reciprocal tariff reductions covering $30 billion of goods in each direction.

Yun Sun, director of the Stimson Center’s China Program, told VOA that changes in U.S. Congress ushered in by the midterm elections would not automatically produce a fundamental shift in Beijing’s approach.
“I do not think China’s assessment of the United States or its policy will undergo major changes,” she told VOA.
Congress can complicate administration policy through hearings, investigations and oversight, she said, but Trump’s preferences and White House decisions would remain influential.
“Beijing will certainly face more uncertainty, but that uncertainty is not unlimited,” Sun said.
Taiwan, trade, Chinese investment and human rights could all become sources of congressional pressure.
A possible Trump–Xi–Putin meeting could broaden the agenda, but the Rubio–Wang call did not confirm such a meeting.
Trump has said potential discussions could cover denuclearization and ending the Iran war.

Sun questioned whether Beijing could offer consequential concessions on Iran, saying a substantial reduction in Chinese oil purchases was unlikely. Uncertainty over Washington’s next steps also made it premature to assess the conflict’s impact on China policy. Regardless, she says there will be little impact on current U.S.-China ties.

items.title: Amnesty International calls on Aussie government to recognize ‘gender apartheid’ in Afghanistan
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.

Amnesty International Australia has called on the Australian government to support international recognition of "gender apartheid" and back efforts to hold the Taliban accountable for what it describes as systematic violations of the rights of Afghan women and girls.

In an open letter, the rights group urged Canberra “to support recognition of gender apartheid under international law and follow through on accountability for the Taliban's crimes against women and girls.”

The appeal is part of Amnesty Australia's campaign, "16 Days of Activism Against Gender Violence and Persecution in Afghanistan," launched alongside the global 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence initiative observed annually from November 25 to December 10.

Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have barred women from secondary and higher education, restricted most employment opportunities, and imposed limits on freedom of movement. Human rights organizations and Afghan women's groups increasingly describe these policies as "gender apartheid," arguing they amount to a system of institutionalized gender-based oppression. While gender apartheid is not currently recognized as a distinct crime under international law, advocates are pushing for its formal recognition.
Amnesty also encouraged the public to sign the open letter and amplify the voices of Afghan women and girls through advocacy and social media campaigns.

Recent findings by U.N. Women have highlighted the worsening situation for women in Afghanistan. The agency reported in August that the Taliban have issued more than 100 decrees affecting women and girls since 2021, restricting access to education, employment, justice, freedom of movement, and public life.

The United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) has also documented enforcement of the restrictions. In an October report, the mission expressed concern over arrests and detentions of women in Kabul and Herat for alleged violations of dress-code regulations, saying the measures undermine women's rights to freedom of movement, expression, and personal autonomy.

Amnesty International Australia said the campaign seeks to ensure Afghan women and girls are not forgotten amid competing global crises and to maintain international pressure for accountability and the restoration of their rights.

items.title: All-female Kurdish force in Syria to join Interior Ministry
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.

The Women’s Protection Units (YPJ) has announced that Syria’s Ministry of Interior has agreed to integrate two special battalions of the all-female Kurdish force. The announcement comes after months of negotiations between Syrian government officials and Kurdish leaders over the future of the force, following an agreement to integrate northeast Syria into state institutions.

Ruksen Mohamed, a spokesperson for the Kurdish group, said Thursday that the interim Syrian government has agreed to integrate 800 YPJ fighters into two special battalions under the Ministry of Interior. The Syrian government has yet to confirm the announcement.

The YPJ was a major component of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), once a U.S. partner in the fight against the Islamic State terror group in Syria. The SDF formally announced its dissolution in August 2026, after government forces took control of the region it had administered in northeast Syria.
The Kurdish group said it had also submitted the names of nearly 1,500 other personnel but had received no response from Syrian authorities regarding their status.
VOA contacted the Syrian government for comment but had not received a response.

Since negotiations over the integration of Kurdish-led forces and institutions into the Syrian state officially began more than a year ago, the status of Kurdish female fighters has been a major point of contention. The Islamist-led Syrian government has opposed integrating Kurdish female fighters into the country's military but has shown some flexibility toward incorporating them into police forces and other local security structures.
Political observers say a lack of transparency surrounding the integration process has further complicated negotiations between the two sides.

“When the specific method for integrating these forces has not been officially announced, it implies that negotiations are still underway and have not yet concluded,” said Abdulhalim Sulaiman, a political observer based in Qamishli, Syria.

“I believe there are ongoing discussions over the specifics and details, determining exactly how the YPJ will be incorporated into Syria’s security structure, particularly within the Kurdish regions,” he told VOA.

Gulistan Gulo, a spokesperson for the Star Congress, an umbrella organization for women’s groups in northeast Syria, said any attempt to marginalize the YPJ or strip it of its military identity would likely face opposition within the Kurdish community, where the female fighters are widely respected for their sacrifices in the fight against terrorism.

“We do not agree with the interim government’s position that the YPJ cannot be accepted as a military force within the army,” she told VOA. “The YPJ belongs to the Ministry of Defense and the army, given its years of military experience.”

items.title: SpaceX to attempt double catch of huge Starship rocket
paragraphs: The 124m-tall rocket is scheduled to blast off from the Starbase launchpad in Texas at 1645 local time (2245 GMT) with a 75-minute-long launch window.
After six and a half minutes, the first planned catch will be attempted when the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - returns to the launch tower.

The top part of the rocket, called the Ship, will continue its journey to space and deploy 26 satellites. These will form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high speed internet from space.
The Ship is then due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning for the second catch attempt about 22 and a half hours after taking off.
Until now, SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.
But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the chopsticks. Instead it's splashed down in the ocean.
SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it's in space.
If any problems are detected there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean.
After SpaceX went public earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will the US Space Agency.
The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline.
SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface.

But it's not the only company working with the US Space Agency. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touch down.
Both companies will also play a key role in Artemis III, which is currently planned for summer 2027- another challenging schedule.
This mission will see four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers.
Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended.
But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida.
Blue Origin had said they would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027.

Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said America is in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.

items.title: Political divide threatens Kurdish autonomy; US urges unity
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.
Last week's withdrawal of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan from the Iraqi Kurdistan’s regional government has deepened the political standoff between the region's two main ruling parties.
The rise in tensions came after a disputed parliamentary session prompted the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) to announce its withdrawal from the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG).

The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), led by the Barzani family, and the PUK, led by the Talabani family, have dominated Kurdish politics for decades. Their rivalry led to a brutal armed conflict and separate administrations in the 1990s.
Some regional analysts warn that the latest tensions could lead to a renewed division of the Kurdistan region.

"If we divide this region ourselves, the entire world will abandon us,” Kamil Omar, a university professor in Sulaimaniyah, told VOA. “How long can they continue worrying about us when we cannot protect our own region, our people’s future and our nation’s strategic interests?”
The Kurdistan Region gained de facto autonomy following the 1991 Gulf War, with its federal status recognized in Iraq’s 2005 constitution.
“We have received political and military support and protection from international allies for the past 35 years," he added.

Speaking at Chatham House in London on Wednesday, U.S. special envoy for Syria and Iraq Tom Barrack urged Kurdish leaders to overcome their “family” and “tribal” divisions and strengthen cooperation with Baghdad.
“This is an Iraqi issue. This is an Iraqi decision. This is not an American decision,” Barrack said. “My advice, the president’s advice, is: Get over it.”
Masoud Haider, a KDP member and former Iraqi deputy finance minister, described Barrack’s remarks as a clear political message urging both parties to agree on forming a government.

“A strong Kurdistan Region with unified institutions contributes to Iraq’s strength and stability,” Haider told VOA. “This message calls on Kurdish political forces to put their differences aside and form a government based on cooperation and responsibility.”
Mahmoud Khoshnaw, a PUK member, described Barrack’s remarks as both a reflection of political realities and a warning.

“Any step that promotes stability and development strengthens the region, while any step that undermines stability, creates political divisions or marginalizes a political party weakens it,” Khoshnaw told VOA.
Speaking Thursday at the Sulaimani Forum, PUK leader Bafel Talabani described the dispute as “the single largest political crisis in the history of the Kurdistan Region.”
He rejected the legitimacy of the disputed parliamentary process and warned against further unilateral moves.
“We effectively have two administrations,” Talabani said, although he cautioned that discussing two separate governments was premature.
“Every escalation will be met with a well-planned escalation,” he warned, adding that dialogue remained possible.
Talabani rejected characterizing the dispute as a family feud, describing it instead as a longstanding rivalry between two political forces.
On Monday, KDP leader Masoud Barzani called for negotiations.
“I call on our brothers in the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan to sit down with the KDP, resolve the problems and bring an end to the Kurdistan Region’s political crisis,” Barzani said in a statement.
The KRG Council of Ministers, meeting Wednesday without PUK ministers, also urged them to return and address their concerns through cabinet discussions.
Talabani dismissed those appeals as political rhetoric intended to shift blame for the divisions onto the PUK.

items.title: Ukraine looks to international partners to cover growing financing needs
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Ukrainian article.

More than 40 leaders of European countries gathered in Ireland for a summit Thursday, with discussions centering around European security and the need to support Ukraine amid increased attacks by Russia on its infrastructure and businesses.

Funding for Ukraine was a top issue in Europe in the run up to the two-day European Pollical Community and the informal European Council summit. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz urged the European Union to find the money to meet request from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine for an additional $77 billion for the next year.

In his letter to European Council President António Costa, earlier this week, Merz called the new aid an "essential prerequisite" for approving the next EU budget. The content of the letter was first reported by the Financial Times.

The leaders of Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria have already voiced their opposition to linking approval of the EU’s budget to any new funding for Ukraine, which may delay the approval of the money.

Following the meeting with Zelenskyy on Thursday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen assured the Ukrainian leader of the EU's support, covering immediate survival this winter and funds needed through 2027. She announced the European Council will review the Commission's proposal for Ukraine's financing needs by the end of the month.

To alleviate immediate financial pressure, Ukraine hopes to obtain $1.67 billion in fresh funding from the International Monetary Fund by the end of the year. IMF's Director of the Communications Department, Julie Kozack told reporters on October 29 that the money will be released once the IMF completes assessment of its program in Ukraine. The IMF has started the review of the program for Ukraine on Monday.

The U.S., as the most powerful member of the IMF, supports the current Fund's program for Ukraine, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced earlier this year (in April) when met he with Ukrainian Prime Minister Yulia Svyrydenko.

"Secretary Bessent underscored President Trump’s efforts for a lasting peace for Ukraine, and highlighted the United States’ support for Ukraine’s new IMF program and for the progress that Ukraine has made on its reforms," a Treasury Department statement said.
An analyst told VOA staying on track with the IMF program is an important anchor for Ukraine to secure support from other international partners.

“There are other partners who support us much more,” Yuliya Markuts, head of the Center for Public Finance and Governance at the Kyiv School of Economics, said. “But the IMF is an anchor that demonstrates to our partners that Ukraine is indeed a country they can work with, they can trust and treat as a reliable partner. Therefore, Ukraine is very much dependent on having an IMF program.”

Over the past several months, Ukraine's parliament has approved several laws envisaged by the program. Markuts says she is “cautiously optimistic” that Ukraine will obtain the favorable review from the IMF.
If Ukraine does not get the fresh funding, the situation could be dire, said Markuts, as Ukraine has virtually no room to cut spending.

“This is actually a very difficult situation. Because shelling is taking place constantly. There are ongoing problems with critical infrastructure, particularly energy infrastructure,” Markuts said. “We have to provide the people living in this country with heating, water, electricity, and so on.”
Markuts stated that Ukraine's current investment is geared towards endurance and providing basic services to its people through the war.
Timothy Ash, chief strategist of BlueBay Asset Management, believes that the IMF supports maintaining the program.

“But the IMF operates in a certain way - the program has to be sustainable," he told VOA. He highlighted that this would require financing assurances from Ukraine’s allies “that those gaps will be met."
Ash says he is confident that Ukraine will be able to secure funding from European partners, despite the opposition from some EU members.

“The big economies in Europe totally get it. Europe has figured out that Ukraine is central to its security in its long-term defense," he said. "Europe needs time to build autonomous defense capability, and the longer Ukraine survives in this war, the longer Europe has to build that autonomous defense capability. So, Europe has an interest now in helping Ukraine defend itself and Europe,” he adds.

items.title: US-based Russian activist sentenced to 6 years in absentia for "military fakes"
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Russian article.

A court in Ulan-Ude, Russia, has sentenced U.S.-based activist and researcher Maria Vyushkova in absentia to six years in prison on a charge of allegedly “spreading knowingly false information” about the Russian armed forces.
"The kind of persecution in absentia and then attempts to put pressure on relatives who remained in Russia" are now becoming more widespread, Vyushkova VOA's Russian service.

The case stemmed from her research on the killings of hundreds of civilians in Bucha, Ukraine, in March of 2022. Russia has consistently denied any involvement in the killings and has called the evidence staged.
Some media accounts at the time singled out Buryat soldiers in the Russian army as being responsible. Buryats are an Indigenous people who live mainly in southern Siberia near the Mongolian border.

Vyushkova, herself a Buryat, argued that Russian paratroopers from Pskov were in Bucha at the time of the killings. The court said it found her statements were motivated by political hatred, according to the independent outlet Glasnaya.

Vyushkova, a citizen of the Russian Federation and the United States, is one of the co-founders of the Free Buryatia Foundation, which has been recognized in Russia as an "undesirable", "terrorist" and "extremist" organization.
In April 2026, the Russian authorities put Vyushkova on the register of foreign agents, and in July, the Ministry of Internal Affairs put her on the wanted list.
Vyushkova, who lives in the United States and has not traveled to Russia for many years, says she is surprised by the attention of the Russian authorities to her activities.

She says she believes that "this is part of a large, coordinated campaign against activists from regional ethnic groups, because this case was opened against me in the summer of 2026 for an interview that I gave in the summer of 2023."
Vyushkova says she plans to completely ignore the sentencing. "I do not recognize any right of the Russian authorities to put me on trial, to accuse me of something and to judge me," she told VOA.

items.title: Explainer: From undercover employment to corporate data breaches: the "Combating Foreign Threats to Main Street Act"
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

A bipartisan bill that could help U.S. small businesses recognize threats from foreign adversaries, including the risk posed by North Korean workers posing as job candidates, was debated and passed in the House of Representatives on Wednesday. It now moves on to the Senate.

The core provision requires the Small Business Administration to develop and distribute educational materials so that businesses can recognize the risks identified by the U.S. government and learn how to respond.

Its official title is the “Combating Foreign Threats to Main Street Act of 2026." It requires the Small Business Administration to guide businesses on how to identify, prevent, and respond to threats. The bill requires the SBA to develop materials in collaboration with relevant agencies and distribute them through regional offices and existing support programs. The SBA would be expected to use its existing budget to produce new materials.

Rep. Roger Williams, a Republican from Texas’s 25th Congressional District and chairman of the House Small Business Committee, is leading the effort. Williams has specifically identified China, Russia and North Korea as foreign threats the legislation seeks to address. Explaining the need for the bill, he said that “while many small businesses are exposed to foreign threats, they lack the resources and expertise to respond.”
Rep. Derek Tran, a Democrat representing California’s 45th Congressional District, is also involved in the effort. He serves on the House Small Business and Armed Services committees.
Why Is This Important for Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises?
“Even small companies have technology and information that needs to be protected”, according to the proposed bill.

For example, even a small software company may have programs it developed in-house. “If a manufacturer’s blueprints or customer and business partner information are leaked, it could harm the business”.
Chairman Williams’ office explained that “many small businesses lack the resources or expertise to identify and respond to increasingly sophisticated threats”.
The bill goes beyond simply alerting businesses to risk; it also provides guidance on prevention methods and where to seek assistance.
It includes guidelines to ensure that while risks are assessed when conducting business or receiving investments overseas, legitimate commercial activities are not unnecessarily restricted.

The bill relies on the Commerce Department’s definition of “foreign adversary,” which includes North Korea. While it does not specifically address North Korea’s use of covert IT workers in U.S. companies, its coverage of cyber intrusions and its catch-all provision for emerging threats could allow the SBA to include such schemes.
During hiring: North Korean IT workers misrepresent their identities and actual work locations to secure remote work positions.
Once hired: They gain access to the company’s computer networks and the data necessary to perform their duties.
If that access is abused: It can lead to the theft of corporate information or extortion.

Last January, the FBI warned of a case in which North Korean IT personnel stole sensitive corporate data and program source code from a company and, after being discovered, used this as leverage to demand money.
In July of the same year, the FBI stated that companies that outsource IT work to third-party vendors may face additional vulnerabilities because they cannot directly manage the hiring process.
This alert is directed at U.S. companies in general. It does not mean that all affected companies are small and medium-sized enterprises.
What kind of assistance will companies receive?
The bill requires the SBA to guide companies on how to protect intellectual property, trade secrets, sensitive corporate information, and supply chains.
The proposed bill covers not only cybersecurity but also the import of goods produced through forced labor, counterfeit goods and illicit trade, and predatory investment practices.
The bill now moves to the Senate. There is currently no Senate version of the bill, and this session of Congress ends in early January.
- September 10: The bill was introduced by Rep. Roger Williams (R-Texas), with Rep. Derek Tran (D-Calif.) as the Democratic co-sponsor.
- September 16: The House Small Business Committee voted 22–0 to recommend the bill to the full House.
- October 9: The committee’s official report was submitted.
- November 11: Passed by a voice vote. The Senate must approve it with the same wording, and the President must sign it.

items.title: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go | Nils Pratley
paragraphs: Half the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.
It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability.

An extramarital affair is not usually a resigning matter in itself – saintliness is not an absolute requirement of the job. But the circumstances here were different. A relationship with the Chinese boss of a Singapore-based firm suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China? That displayed recklessness on top of mere unfaithfulness.

Did he know the Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang (no relation), was regarded as a Chinese spy by US officials? It hardly matters. In the ultra-political world of in-demand AI computer chips, there were enough reasons for him to be careful in the extreme. The conflict of interest, and the risk of landing Nvidia in a quagmire of national security inquiries in Washington, would have been obvious.

Reports of a second affair with a senior Nvidia employee compounded matters – US companies tend to be sensitive about such relationships. But the company’s directors might also have wondered what else could be revealed in coming weeks. Rule number one in these situations is to get all the bad news out on day one.

The kneejerk reaction to Jensen Huang’s resignation was 13% off the share price. That was understandable – some investors truly believed the “irreplaceable” thesis. However, sitting in Nvidia’s boardroom, the job was not to worry about the initial stock market response but about what was best for the business. For multiple reasons, it was time to “rip off the Band-Aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter”, as Dan Ives, a senior tech analyst, put it.

First, the congressional investigations will happen anyway. Democratic senators have asked administration officials to preserve all documents and communications related to the sale of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China. At heart, that issue is wider than Nvidia – it’s about whether US officials have themselves jeopardised the country’s lead over China in AI. But, one way or another, the company’s activities, and ties to the Trump administration, will come under scrutiny like never before. Nvidia is better placed to defend itself without Huang in the top job.

Second, his personal lobbying clout on export policy had evaporated. After this week’s revelations, he had no credibility as an advocate of looser restrictions. The political demand will be entirely in the other direction – for loopholes to be closed.

Third, there is the issue Nvidia’s underpowered board has dodged for too long: over-reliance on one individual. Never mind the risk of scandal, there is always a danger in concentrating too much day-to-day power in the hands of one individual. Nobody doubts Huang’s commercial talents, but even “godfathers of AI” in leather jackets don’t go on forever. Better to have a setup that can cope with change at the top.

Colette Kress, the chief financial officer who will stand in as chief executive, is well regarded on Wall Street. Nvidia will not be short of outside applicants on a permanent basis. And the board has heard the governance criticism that a multitrillion-dollar company ought to have an independent chair: Harvey Jones, a former chief executive at semiconductor company Synopsys and a member of the current crew of directors, has got the gig. Then comes the task of creating some proper governance checks and balances, which may require fresh faces among the independent directors.

Within a couple of hours, the fall in the share price had narrowed to 5% as investors remembered that Nvidia still has the best, and most in-demand, graphics processing units in the world and that many pioneering companies have prospered after the exit of an “irreplaceable” chief executive.

Nobody pretends the management job will be easy. Nvidia will be different, not least because the political winds in the US have shifted. But there was no point trying to cling to a chief executive, however successful, who had made himself a busted flush. Huang had to go.

items.title: Participating in art and culture has measurable benefits on our wellbeing | Letter
paragraphs: Reading Emma Brockes’ response to a recent Art Fund study, I felt the significance of the research may have been lost in its packaging (Art is good for your health? Allow me a quick eyeroll, 5 November).

The language of “prescribing” art has its roots in social prescribing. I understand why this might make people uncomfortable, particularly if it suggests that culture is being instrumentalised rather than enjoyed for its own sake.

Yet these findings matter for two reasons. First, they provide evidence for what many of us know intuitively: that participating in and experiencing art and culture are not only enriching, but also have measurable benefits for our health and wellbeing.

Second, with budgets for culture under pressure, this evidence strengthens our case for public investment. Surely that’s another argument for keeping our national museums free and ensuring everyone can access their wellbeing benefits.

Rather than viewing this study cynically, we should recognise the opportunities it presents. As Daisy Fancourt, who is quoted in Brockes’ article, explores in her excellent and insightful book Art Cure, the evidence extends far beyond visiting galleries and museums.

In the London borough of Ealing, we’re piloting a free creative health programme bringing residents and council staff together through activities ranging from clay workshops to Islamic geometric drawing. Almost all participants have reported improved wellbeing following these sessions. But beyond the evaluation, conversations have shown me how even an hour spent being creative can positively change the course of someone’s day, while regular participation can have a lasting impact on their lives.

Art shouldn’t have to justify its existence through its health benefits. But understanding those benefits strengthens the case for everyone to experience, participate in and benefit from art and culture.

And if the thought of visiting a museum makes Brockes’ eyes roll, I’d happily invite her to one of our workshops. She might leave having learned a new skill, but I suspect she’d take away rather more than that. William Rees Culture officer, Ealing council

items.title: Jensen Huang built an AI kingdom. Now he’s gone, will Nvidia’s ramparts be breached?
paragraphs: Can the AI economy survive without its “central bank”? What does Jensen Huang’s fall mean for the world’s second-most valuable company, and what might a tremor in its fortunes mean for the world?

Nvidia’s sky-high valuation is based on the fact that it designs and sells the advanced AI chips, called graphics processing units (GPUs), that underpin the AI economy. Without these, AI models such as ChatGPT and Claude could not be trained and would not run.
This has made the chipmaker arguably the most important player in AI and, at times, the most valuable company in the world. Huang’s departure sent shares in Nvidia plunging 13% in early trading.

Nvidia is not the only company that designs these chips. Most leading tech companies, including Microsoft, Meta and Google, are trying to make their own lines of AI chips. Some of these, such as Google’s tensor processing units, appear to be at least as good as Nvidia’s, and even better for certain purposes.
What makes Nvidia irreplaceable – and far more integral to the AI economy – is its web of relationships, most of these led by Huang himself.

One aspect of this is Nvidia’s complex web of ties with the companies actually building AI infrastructure, a mess of circular finance that implicates US tech giants and many of the world’s governments.

In recent years, Huang has been the kingmaker when it comes to AI. In 2025, he met numerous world leaders – including Mohammed bin Salman, Keir Starmer and Emmanuel Macron – persuading them of the urgency of developing “sovereign AI” with his product. His presence served as a guarantee of those nations’ AI plans. These meetings were followed by deals in which Nvidia announced it had arrangements to supply those governments with precious, hard-to-get chips.

None of these agreements were particularly transparent. While Nvidia appears to have promised 260,000 advanced chips to South Korea, for example, it was never immediately apparent when those chips would be delivered, who would pay for them, and on what terms.

Meanwhile, Nvidia financed a web of companies called “neoclouds” to buy its chips and put them in datacentres, there to be rented to the world’s biggest AI companies. These neoclouds have done wonders for Nvidia, propping up demand and keeping the risk associated with building datacentres and finding customers for them off its balance sheets.

Neoclouds are not the only thing financed by Nvidia. It has become known as the “central bank of AI” because it is enmeshed in almost every layer of the AI economy. Nvidia has invested in a spate of AI startups that could become future customers. It has offered massive sums of cash to companies such as OpenAI, to be used to buy its chips. This investment runs to hundreds of billions of dollars of Nvidia’s money, circling again and again through a limited set of accounts.

Then there is Nvidia’s relationship with a Taiwanese company called TSMC, or the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. TSMC makes the world’s AI chips, churning them out across several fabrication plants on the north-west of the island.

As far as geopolitics goes, TSMC is arguably more important than Nvidia or any other chip designer. Other companies can design AI chips, but TSMC manufactures the overwhelming majority of them and has no real competitor. This is because manufacturing AI chips is one of the most expensive and challenging industrial processes to date.

Each chip is etched with nanometre lines by lasers working in the extreme ultraviolet spectrum, which cost billions of dollars and two decades of research to develop. While TSMC has refined its process to make these chips for more than two decades, it still has only a 60% yield rate for its most advanced chips, which means that 40% of them have defects. It’s a staggeringly high rate for one of the world’s most expensive technologies.

Nvidia has worked closely with TSMC to help it develop its processes and products. Lore has it that Huang wrote the chief executive of TSMC a letter introducing himself in 1997. These are high-trust relationships built over decades.

Will it all be the same without Huang? This is almost impossible to answer because Nvidia’s relationships are so opaque. Investigators following the supply chain of its chips run up against secretive corporate contracts and tangled export records. There is known to be a years-long queue of customers waiting to obtain its chips, but questions regarding who is in that queue, in what order, and how many chips have been shipped remain open.

This murkiness was brought into sharp focus by Megaspeed, a small Singaporean company that was getting access to lots of GPUs, even as other companies struggled. One of Megaspeed’s executives, Alice Huang, was later revealed to be having an affair with Nvidia’s chief executive, and to be an alleged Chinese spy. This relationship appears to have allowed Megaspeed to secure roughly $7.5bn (£5.67bn) worth of Nvidia chips, which were allegedly smuggled into China.

Was Huang and his glad-handing a source of this opacity? Perhaps a new chief executive could bring some transparency and predictability to the business, at least in terms of chips contracts and supply chains.

But what else could be laid bare if the “central bank of AI” became more transparent, or came under external scrutiny? Many questions surround its contracts and relationships; lots of elaborate debt structures and handshake agreements may yet be uncovered.

Huang dazzled the world in his leather jacket; he convinced heads of government that his technology held the keys to transformation and to power. When the patina wears off, will this still seem the case?
